abstract: We are focusing on the development of a highly compact neural net weight function based on the use of EEPROM devices. These devices have already proven useful for analog weight storage, but existing designs rely on the use of conventional voltage multiplication as the weight function, requiring additional transistors per synapse. A parasitic capacitance between the floating gate and the drain of the EEPROM structure leads to an unusual J-V characteristic which can be used to advantage in designing a compact synapse. This novel behavior is well characterized by a model we have developed. A single-device circuit results in a 1-quadrant synapse function which is nonlinear, though monotonic. paragraphs: The paper develops compact neural-network weight functions using EEPROM devices. These devices can already store analog weights, but conventional designs add transistors to perform voltage multiplication. The authors instead investigate whether the storage device's own electrical behavior can also perform the weighting operation, reducing the circuitry needed for each synapse.

The key behavior arises from parasitic capacitance between the floating gate and drain. The authors develop a model that characterizes the resulting unusual electrical response and use it to design a single-device synapse. That circuit provides a one-quadrant weighting function that is nonlinear but monotonic: its response changes consistently in one direction.

An extension using two EEPROM devices provides a two-quadrant function with substantially greater linearity. These alternatives expose a practical tradeoff between device count and the properties of the weighting function. The authors describe the approach as potentially enabling more than a tenfold increase in implementation density. That is a stated opportunity for denser neural hardware, rather than a reported density measurement for a complete network.
summary.tldr: EEPROM electrical behavior can implement compact synaptic weighting functions with one or two devices.

title: Compact EEPROM-based Weight Functions

abstract: We demonstrate a multiscale adaptive network model of motion computation in primate area MT. The model consists of two stages: (l) local velocities are measured across multiple spatio-temporal channels, and (2) the optical flow field is computed by a network of direction(cid:173) selective neurons at multiple spatial resolutions. This model embeds the computational efficiency of Multigrid algorithms within a parallel network as well as adaptively computes the most reliable estimate of the flow field across different spatial scales. Our model neurons show the same nonclassical receptive field properties as Allman's type I MT neurons. Since local velocities are measured across multiple channels, various channels often provide conflicting measurements to the network. We have incorporated a veto scheme for conflict resolution. This mechanism provides a novel explanation for the spatial frequency dependency of the psychophysical phenomenon called Motion Capture. 1 MOTIVATION We previously developed a two-stage model of motion computation in the visual system of primates (Le. magnocellular pathway from retina to V1 and MT; Wang, Mathur & Koch, 1989). This algorithm has these deficiencies: (1) the issue of optimal spatial scale for velocity measurement, and (2) the issue optimal spatial scale for the smoothness of motion field. paragraphs: The paper models motion computation in primate visual area MT by working across several spatial and temporal scales. Scale matters because a motion estimate can be wrong when movement is too large relative to the spacing and timing of measurements. The model addresses both the scale used to measure local velocity and the scale used to assemble a motion field.

The first stage measures local velocities through multiple channels. The second uses direction-selective neurons at several spatial resolutions to estimate optical flow, the pattern of movement across the image. It incorporates the computational efficiency of multigrid algorithms into a parallel network and adaptively combines information across scales to obtain a reliable estimate.

Multiple channels can disagree, so the authors add a veto mechanism to resolve conflicting measurements. They report that model neurons reproduce nonclassical receptive-field properties of a particular class of MT neurons. The conflict-resolution mechanism also offers an explanation for how the perceptual phenomenon of motion capture depends on spatial frequency, connecting the computational design with neural and perceptual observations.
summary.tldr: A multiscale motion network combines velocity measurements and resolves conflicts to explain properties of MT neurons and motion capture.

title: A Multiscale Adaptive Network Model of Motion Computation in Primates

abstract: In salamander retina, the response of On-Off ganglion cells to a central flash is reduced by movement in the receptive field surround. Through computer simulation of a 2-D model which takes into account their anatomical and physiological properties, we show that interactions between four neuron types (two bipolar and two amacrine) may be responsible for the generation and lateral conductance of this change sensitive inhibition. The model shows that the four neuron circuit can account for previously observed movement sensitive reductions in ganglion cell sensitivity and allows visualization and prediction of the spatio-temporal pattern of activity in change sensitive retinal cells.

Through computer simulation of a 2-D model which takes into account their anatomical and physiological properties, we show that interactions between four neuron types (two bipolar and two amacrine) may be responsible for the generation and lateral conductance of this change sensitive inhibition. paragraphs: In the salamander retina, movement around the edge of a ganglion cell's receptive field can weaken its response to a flash in the center. This paper investigates a circuit explanation for that interaction. The question is how activity outside the directly stimulated central region produces inhibition that changes the cell's sensitivity.

The authors construct and simulate a two-dimensional model that incorporates anatomical and physiological properties of retinal cells. They focus on interactions among four neuron types: two bipolar types and two amacrine types. Together, these interactions provide a proposed mechanism both for generating change-sensitive inhibition and for carrying its influence laterally across the retina.

The simulated circuit accounts for previously observed reductions in ganglion-cell sensitivity caused by surrounding movement. It also makes the pattern of activity across space and time available for visualization and prediction. This supports the circuit as a possible explanation of the phenomenon: the model connects a particular arrangement of interacting cell types to the larger retinal response, while preserving the abstract's tentative claim about biological responsibility.
summary.tldr: A simulated circuit involving four retinal neuron types explains how surrounding movement can suppress responses to a central flash.

title: A four neuron circuit accounts for change sensitive inhibition in salamander retina

abstract: This paper applies the theory of Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning to multiple output feedforward threshold networks in which the weights conform to certain equivalences. It is shown that the sample size for reliable learning can be bounded above by a formula similar to that required for single output networks with no equivalences. The best previ(cid:173) ously obtained bounds are improved for all cases.
originalAbstract: This paper applies the theory of Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning to multiple output feedforward threshold networks in which the weights conform to certain equivalences. It is shown that the sample size for reliable learning can be bounded above by a formula similar to that required for single output networks with no equivalences. The best previ(cid:173) ously obtained bounds are improved for all cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much training data is sufficient for reliable learning in feedforward threshold networks. The networks have multiple outputs, and their weights satisfy specified equivalences. The analysis therefore addresses a model class with both several predicted outputs and structural relationships among its weights, rather than treating all weights as unrestricted.

The authors use the Probably Approximately Correct learning framework. In plain language, this asks how many examples suffice to make a sufficiently accurate learned model likely. They derive an upper bound on that sample requirement with a form similar to the bound for single-output networks without weight equivalences.

The paper reports improvements over the previously available bounds in every case considered. A tighter upper bound gives a stronger sufficient guarantee about the amount of data required; it is a statement about reliable learnability rather than a measured training speed. The result shows that multiple outputs and equivalent weights can be handled within a familiar form of sample-complexity analysis while improving the available guarantees.
summary.tldr: PAC analysis improves sample-size upper bounds for multiple-output threshold networks whose weights obey equivalence constraints.

title: Threshold Network Learning in the Presence of Equivalences
Memory-Based Methods for Regression and Classification

abstract: For blind source separation, when the Fisher information matrix is used as the Riemannian metric tensor for the parameter space, the steepest descent algorithm to maximize the likelihood function in this Riemannian parameter space becomes the serial updating rule with equivariant property. This algorithm can be further simplified by using the asymptotic form of the Fisher information matrix around the equilibrium.
originalAbstract: For blind source separation, when the Fisher information matrix is used as the Riemannian metric tensor for the parameter space, the steepest descent algorithm to maximize the likelihood function in this Riemannian parameter space becomes the serial updating rule with equivariant property. This algorithm can be further simplified by using the asymptotic form of the Fisher information matrix around the equilibrium.

paragraphs: Blind source separation seeks to recover underlying signals from observed mixtures. This paper derives a parameter-update rule by examining the geometry of likelihood optimization. Its central choice is to measure distances in parameter space using the Fisher information matrix, which describes how sensitively the modeled distribution changes with the parameters.

With Fisher information serving as the metric, the direction of steepest likelihood improvement is defined by that statistical geometry. The authors show that this construction produces a serial, multiplicative updating rule with an equivariant property. Equivariance expresses a consistent transformation of the algorithm's behavior when the corresponding representation changes. The update is therefore connected to the structure of the statistical problem.

The paper further simplifies the algorithm using the asymptotic form of Fisher information near equilibrium. That qualification matters because the simplification relies on local behavior around that state. The contribution is a derivation connecting a practical form of iterative updating to likelihood and information geometry, together with a route to reducing the update's complexity.
summary.tldr: Using Fisher information to define optimization geometry yields an equivariant multiplicative update for blind source separation.

title: Multiplicative Updating Rule for Blind Separation Derived from the Method of Scoring

abstract: An adaptive on-line algorithm is proposed to estimate hierarchical data structures for non-stationary data sources. The approach is based on the principle of minimum cross entropy to derive a decision tree for data clustering and it employs a metalearning idea (learning to learn) to adapt to changes in data characteristics. Its efficiency is demonstrated by grouping non-stationary artifical data and by hierarchical segmentation of LANDSAT images.
originalAbstract: An adaptive on-line algorithm is proposed to estimate hierarchical data structures for non-stationary data sources. The approach is based on the principle of minimum cross entropy to derive a decision tree for data clustering and it employs a metalearning idea (learning to learn) to adapt to changes in data characteristics. Its efficiency is demonstrated by grouping non-stationary artifical data and by hierarchical segmentation of LANDSAT images.

paragraphs: The paper addresses hierarchical clustering when data arrive over time and their characteristics change. In this setting, the organization discovered from earlier observations may need to adapt as new observations appear. The authors propose an unsupervised online algorithm that estimates a hierarchy through a decision tree.

The tree is derived using the principle of minimum cross entropy. Alongside that statistical criterion, the algorithm uses a metalearning idea, described as learning to learn, to adapt to changes in the data. The approach therefore combines a method for constructing groups with a mechanism for adjusting learning as the source changes, making adaptation central to the clustering procedure.

The authors demonstrate efficiency on two applications: grouping artificial data from a non-stationary source and hierarchical segmentation of LANDSAT images. These examples connect the method to both changing data distributions and image organization. The contribution is an adaptive way to build hierarchical structure online, allowing the grouping process to respond to the characteristics of the data it receives.
summary.tldr: An online clustering algorithm combines minimum cross entropy and metalearning to adapt hierarchical decision trees to changing data.

title: Unsupervised On-line Learning of Decision Trees for Hierarchical Data Analysis

abstract: An essential step in understanding the function of sensory nervous sys- tems is to characterize as accurately as possible the stimulus-response function (SRF) of the neurons that relay and process sensory informa- tion. One increasingly common experimental approach is to present a rapidly varying complex stimulus to the animal while recording the re- sponses of one or more neurons, and then to directly estimate a func- tional transformation of the input that accounts for the neuronal ﬁring. The estimation techniques usually employed, such as Wiener ﬁltering or other correlation-based estimation of the Wiener or Volterra kernels, are equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation in a Gaussian-output-noise regression model. We explore the use of Bayesian evidence-optimization techniques to condition these estimates. We show that by learning hyper- parameters that control the smoothness and sparsity of the transfer func- tion it is possible to improve dramatically the quality of SRF estimates, as measured by their success in predicting responses to novel input.

paragraphs: Understanding a sensory neuron requires estimating how a changing stimulus produces its response. The paper considers experiments that present rapidly varying, complex inputs while recording neuronal activity. The estimation problem is to recover a stimulus-response function that explains the observed firing and can predict responses to new inputs.

The authors connect commonly used correlation-based techniques, including Wiener filtering and Wiener or Volterra kernel estimation, to maximum likelihood regression with Gaussian output noise. They then explore Bayesian evidence optimization as a way to condition these estimates. This introduces learned controls over the structure of the estimated transformation.

Specifically, the method learns hyperparameters governing smoothness and sparsity. These determine how smoothly the estimated function varies and how concentrated its representation is. The authors show that learning these controls can dramatically improve estimate quality, judged by prediction on novel stimuli. The finding matters because the benefit is assessed through responses beyond the inputs used to construct the estimate.
summary.tldr: Bayesian evidence optimization learns smoothness and sparsity controls that can dramatically improve neural response predictions for novel stimuli.

title: Evidence Optimization Techniques for Estimating Stimulus-Response Functions

abstract: This paper provides a foundation for multitask learning using reproducing ker- nel Hilbert spaces of vectorvalued functions. In this setting, the kernel is a matrixvalued function. Some explicit examples will be described which go be- yond our earlier results in [7]. In particular, we characterize classes of matrix valued kernels which are linear and are of the dot product or the translation invari- ant type. We discuss how these kernels can be used to model relations between the tasks and present linear multitask learning algorithms. Finally, we present a novel proof of the representer theorem for a minimizer of a regularization func- tional which is based on the notion of minimal norm interpolation.
originalAbstract: This paper provides a foundation for multitask learning using reproducing ker- nel Hilbert spaces of vectorvalued functions. In this setting, the kernel is a matrixvalued function. Some explicit examples will be described which go be- yond our earlier results in [7]. In particular, we characterize classes of matrix valued kernels which are linear and are of the dot product or the translation invari- ant type. We discuss how these kernels can be used to model relations between the tasks and present linear multitask learning algorithms. Finally, we present a novel proof of the representer theorem for a minimizer of a regularization func- tional which is based on the notion of minimal norm interpolation.

paragraphs: The paper builds a mathematical foundation for learning several related tasks together using vector-valued functions. Instead of representing one prediction at a time, such a function produces a collection of outputs. The framework uses reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, with a matrix-valued kernel that can describe relationships among those outputs.

The authors characterize classes of linear, dot-product, and translation-invariant matrix-valued kernels and provide explicit examples. These constructions matter because the kernel offers a way to express relationships between tasks inside the learning model. The paper also develops linear multitask learning algorithms, connecting the mathematical characterization to procedures for fitting related predictors.

A further contribution is a new proof of the representer theorem for a regularized minimizer. The proof uses minimal-norm interpolation, linking the solution's form to a least-norm fitting principle. Together, the kernel constructions, learning algorithms, and theorem establish a structured basis for specifying task relationships and solving regularized learning problems within the same functional framework.
summary.tldr: Matrix-valued kernels provide a theoretical framework for modeling task relationships and constructing regularized multitask learning algorithms.

title: Kernels for Multi--task Learning

abstract: The additive clustering model is widely used to infer the features of a set of stimuli from their similarities, on the assumption that similarity is a weighted linear function of common features. This paper develops a fully Bayesian formulation of the additive clustering model, using methods from nonparametric Bayesian statistics to allow the number of features to vary. We use this to explore several approaches to parameter estimation, showing that the nonparametric Bayesian approach provides a straightforward way to obtain estimates of both the number of features used in producing similarity judgments and their importance.

This paper develops a fully Bayesian formulation of the additive clustering model, using methods from nonparametric Bayesian statistics to allow the number of features to vary. We use this to explore several approaches to parameter estimation, showing that the nonparametric Bayesian approach provides a straightforward way to obtain estimates of both the number of features used in producing similarity judgments and their importance.

paragraphs: Similarity judgments can provide clues about the features people use to compare stimuli. The additive clustering model makes this idea explicit: similarity is assumed to be a weighted sum of features shared by two stimuli. Features with larger weights contribute more to the similarity predicted by the model.

This paper gives additive clustering a fully Bayesian formulation. Its nonparametric construction allows the number of features to vary, so estimating the representation includes deciding how many features it should contain. The same formulation also addresses the importance assigned to those features, linking the size of the representation with its explanation of the judgments.

The authors use this framework to examine several approaches to parameter estimation. They report that the nonparametric Bayesian approach offers a straightforward way to estimate both feature count and feature importance. These estimates describe similarity through the model's shared-feature assumption: the contribution is a flexible inference framework for that account of similarity, with the number of explanatory features treated as part of the estimation problem.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian additive clustering model jointly estimates how many features explain similarity judgments and how important those features are.

title: A Nonparametric Bayesian Method for Inferring Features From Similarity Judgments

abstract: We show that under suitable assumptions (primarily linearization) a simple and perspicuous online learning rule for Information Bottleneck optimization with spiking neurons can be derived. This rule performs on common benchmark tasks as well as a rather complex rule that has previously been proposed \cite{KlampflETAL:07b}. Furthermore, the transparency of this new learning rule makes a theoretical analysis of its convergence properties feasible. A variation of this learning rule (with sign changes) provides a theoretically founded method for performing Principal Component Analysis {(PCA)} with spiking neurons. By applying this rule to an ensemble of neurons, different principal components of the input can be extracted. In addition, it is possible to preferentially extract those principal components from incoming signals $X$ that are related or are not related to some additional target signal $Y_T$. In a biological interpretation, this target signal $Y_T$ (also called relevance variable) could represent proprioceptive feedback, input from other sensory modalities, or top-down signals.

paragraphs: This paper derives a simpler online learning rule for information bottleneck optimization with spiking neurons. The derivation relies on suitable assumptions, especially linearization. Under that construction, the new rule performs as well on common benchmark tasks as a previously proposed, more complicated rule, while being easier to interpret mathematically.

The simpler form makes theoretical analysis of convergence feasible. Changing signs in the rule produces a theoretically grounded method for principal component analysis with spiking neurons. Applied to an ensemble, this version can extract different principal components of the input, connecting the learning rule to a familiar way of identifying major patterns of variation.

The framework can also favor components that are related, or unrelated, to an additional target signal. This adds a way to select patterns according to their connection with another source of information. Possible biological interpretations of the target include proprioceptive feedback, other sensory inputs, or top-down signals. These are proposed interpretations, while the learning-rule derivation remains tied to its stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Under suitable assumptions, a simple spiking-neuron learning rule supports information bottleneck optimization and a PCA variant guided by target relevance.

title: Simplified Rules and Theoretical Analysis for Information Bottleneck Optimization and PCA with Spiking Neurons

abstract: The human brain can be described as containing a number of functional regions. For a given task, these regions, as well as the connections between them, play a key role in information processing in the brain. However, most existing multi-voxel pattern analysis approaches either treat multiple functional regions as one large uniform region or several independent regions, ignoring the connections between regions. In this paper, we propose to model such connections in an Hidden Conditional Random Field (HCRF) framework, where the classifier of one region of interest (ROI) makes predictions based on not only its voxels but also the classifier predictions from ROIs that it connects to. Furthermore, we propose a structural learning method in the HCRF framework to automatically uncover the connections between ROIs. Experiments on fMRI data acquired while human subjects viewing images of natural scenes show that our model can improve the top-level (the classifier combining information from all ROIs) and ROI-level prediction accuracy, as well as uncover some meaningful connections between ROIs.

paragraphs: The paper examines how classifiers can use information distributed across functional brain regions. Many multi-voxel analysis approaches either combine regions into one uniform collection or analyze them independently. Both choices leave out explicit interactions among regions, even though those interactions can matter for processing information during a task.

The authors use a hidden conditional random field to connect classifiers associated with regions of interest. Each regional classifier makes predictions using both its own voxel measurements and predictions from connected regional classifiers. They also introduce a structure-learning method that discovers the connections automatically within the same framework.

Experiments use fMRI data collected while people view natural-scene images. The model improves prediction accuracy both for individual regions and for the top-level classifier that combines their information, while uncovering some meaningful connections. These results support treating regional predictions as interdependent. The learned connections provide an additional view of how information from different regions contributes to the classification task alongside the gains in predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Connecting regional fMRI classifiers in a learned graphical structure improves predictions and reveals meaningful relationships among brain regions.

title: Hierarchical Mixture of Classification Experts Uncovers Interactions between Brain Regions

abstract: Computing a good strategy in a large extensive form game often demands an extraordinary amount of computer memory, necessitating the use of abstraction to reduce the game size. Typically, strategies from abstract games perform better in the real game as the granularity of abstraction is increased. This paper investigates two techniques for stitching a base strategy in a coarse abstraction of the full game tree, to expert strategies in fine abstractions of smaller subtrees. We provide a general framework for creating static experts, an approach that generalizes some previous strategy stitching efforts. In addition, we show that static experts can create strong agents for both 2-player and 3-player Leduc and Limit Texas Hold'em poker, and that a specific class of static experts can be preferred among a number of alternatives. Furthermore, we describe a poker agent that used static experts and won the 3-player events of the 2010 Annual Computer Poker Competition.

paragraphs: Large extensive-form games can require extraordinary amounts of memory to compute a strategy. Abstraction reduces the game to a more manageable representation, and finer abstractions typically produce stronger strategies in the original game. This paper investigates how to combine a coarse strategy for the whole game with more detailed strategies for selected smaller subtrees.

The authors study two strategy-stitching techniques and provide a general framework for constructing static experts. These experts operate in fine abstractions of smaller parts of the game tree, while the base strategy covers the full tree more coarsely. The framework generalizes some earlier approaches to combining broad strategic coverage with localized detail.

Experiments show that static experts can produce strong agents in both two-player and three-player Leduc and Limit Texas Hold'em poker. The authors also identify a particular class of static experts that can be preferred among the alternatives studied. A poker agent using static experts won the three-player events of the 2010 Annual Computer Poker Competition, providing an additional practical demonstration of the approach.
summary.tldr: Strategy stitching combines a coarse full-game policy with detailed subtree experts to build strong multiplayer poker agents.

title: On Strategy Stitching in Large Extensive Form Multiplayer Games

abstract: We investigate a discriminatively trained model of person-object interactions for recognizing common human actions in still images. We build on the locally order-less spatial pyramid bag-of-features model, which was shown to perform extremely well on a range of object, scene and human action recognition tasks. We introduce three principal contributions. First, we replace the standard quantized local HOG/SIFT features with stronger discriminatively trained body part and object detectors. Second, we introduce new person-object interaction features based on spatial co-occurrences of individual body parts and objects. Third, we address the combinatorial problem of a large number of possible interaction pairs and propose a discriminative selection procedure using a linear support vector machine (SVM) with a sparsity inducing regularizer. Learning of action-specific body part and object interactions bypasses the difficult problem of estimating the complete human body pose configuration. Benefits of the proposed model are shown on human action recognition in consumer photographs, outperforming the strong bag-of-features baseline.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes human actions in individual photographs by learning relationships between body parts and objects. It builds on a spatial pyramid bag-of-features representation, but replaces standard quantized local appearance features with discriminatively trained body-part and object detectors. This gives the action model cues tied more directly to people and the objects involved.

The next step represents spatial co-occurrences between individual body parts and objects. Because many such pairs are possible, the authors introduce a selection procedure using a linear support vector machine with a sparsity-inducing regularizer. This lets learning select useful interaction features from the large set of candidates and associate them with particular actions.

Learning action-specific interactions bypasses the difficult task of estimating an entire human body pose. The model can use relevant part-object relationships without first assembling a complete pose configuration. Experiments on consumer photographs show that the approach outperforms a strong bag-of-features baseline, supporting the value of explicitly representing interactions for the action-recognition setting evaluated.
summary.tldr: Selected spatial interactions between detected body parts and objects improve action recognition in photographs without requiring full-body pose estimation.

title: Learning person-object interactions for action recognition in still images

abstract: Computational analyses of dendritic computations often assume stationary inputs to neurons, ignoring the pulsatile nature of spike-based communication between neurons and the moment-to-moment fluctuations caused by such spiking inputs. Conversely, circuit computations with spiking neurons are usually formalized without regard to the rich nonlinear nature of dendritic processing. Here we address the computational challenge faced by neurons that compute and represent analogue quantities but communicate with digital spikes, and show that reliable computation of even purely linear functions of inputs can require the interplay of strongly nonlinear subunits within the postsynaptic dendritic tree. Our theory predicts a matching of dendritic nonlinearities and synaptic weight distributions to the joint statistics of presynaptic inputs. This approach suggests normative roles for some puzzling forms of nonlinear dendritic dynamics and plasticity.

paragraphs: Neurons face a mismatch between what they compute and how they communicate: their computations can concern continuously varying quantities, while incoming messages arrive as individual spikes. The paper examines the moment-to-moment fluctuations this creates. It connects two perspectives that are often treated separately: nonlinear processing within dendrites and computation in circuits of spiking neurons.

The central result is that reliably computing even a linear function of incoming signals can require strongly nonlinear components within a neuron's dendritic tree. A simple desired relationship between inputs and output therefore does not necessarily imply simple internal machinery. The nonlinear processing can serve the task of computing reliably when communication itself is pulsatile.

The theory predicts that dendritic nonlinearities and distributions of synaptic weights should match the joint statistics of presynaptic inputs. This gives a computational rationale for some otherwise puzzling dendritic dynamics and plasticity. The claim is conditional: nonlinear subunits can be required for reliable linear computation in this setting, rather than being universally necessary for every neuronal computation.
summary.tldr: Nonlinear dendritic processing can help neurons reliably compute linear quantities from fluctuating spike inputs.

title: Active dendrites: adaptation to spike-based communication

abstract: We consider the problem of actively learning \textit{multi-index} functions of the form $f(\vecx) = g(\matA\vecx)= \sum_{i=1}^k g_i(\veca_i^T\vecx)$ from point evaluations of $f$. We assume that the function $f$ is defined on an $\ell_2$-ball in $\Real^d$, $g$ is twice continuously differentiable almost everywhere, and $\matA \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ is a rank $k$ matrix, where $k \ll d$. We propose a randomized, active sampling scheme for estimating such functions with uniform approximation guarantees. Our theoretical developments leverage recent techniques from low rank matrix recovery, which enables us to derive an estimator of the function $f$ along with sample complexity bounds. We also characterize the noise robustness of the scheme, and provide empirical evidence that the high-dimensional scaling of our sample complexity bounds are quite accurate.

paragraphs: The paper studies functions whose inputs have many coordinates but whose values depend on only a few linear combinations of them. More specifically, the function is a sum of component functions, each acting on one such combination. The goal is to learn this structure by choosing input locations and observing the function’s values there.

The authors propose a randomized active sampling method and analyze it using tools from low-rank matrix recovery. Their setting assumes inputs lie in a Euclidean ball, the lower-dimensional function is twice continuously differentiable almost everywhere, and the projection matrix has full row rank. Its number of rows is much smaller than the input dimension, expressing the assumed low-dimensional structure.

Under the studied setting, the method provides uniform approximation guarantees and bounds on the number of evaluations required. The paper also characterizes sensitivity to noise. Empirical results support the predicted dependence of sample requirements on the high input dimension, connecting the theoretical analysis to observed scaling behavior.
summary.tldr: A randomized active sampling method learns functions of a few linear projections with approximation, sample-complexity, and noise-robustness analysis.

title: Active Learning of Multi-Index Function Models

abstract: We investigate three related and important problems connected to machine learning, namely approximating a submodular function everywhere, learning a submodular function (in a PAC like setting [26]), and constrained minimization of submodular functions. In all three problems, we provide improved bounds which depend on the “curvature” of a submodular function and improve on the previously known best results for these problems [9, 3, 7, 25] when the function is not too curved – a property which is true of many real-world submodular functions. In the former two problems, we obtain these bounds through a generic black-box transformation (which can potentially work for any algorithm), while in the case of submodular minimization, we propose a framework of algorithms which depend on choosing an appropriate surrogate for the submodular function. In all these cases, we provide almost matching lower bounds. While improved curvature-dependent bounds were shown for monotone submodular maximization [4, 27], the existence of similar improved bounds for the aforementioned problems has been open. We resolve this question in this paper by showing that the same notion of curvature provides these improved results. Empirical experiments add further support to our claims.

paragraphs: The paper studies three tasks involving submodular functions: approximating a function throughout its domain, learning it in a PAC-like setting, and minimizing it under constraints. Its central idea is to make performance guarantees depend on curvature, a property of the function, rather than relying only on bounds that cover the broader problem class.

For approximation and learning, the authors derive their guarantees through a generic black-box transformation that could potentially apply to any algorithm. For constrained minimization, they develop an algorithmic framework based on selecting an appropriate surrogate function. These approaches yield better bounds than previously known results when the function is not too curved.

The authors also provide lower bounds that nearly match their guarantees, helping establish how much further improvement is possible within the analyzed settings. Curvature-dependent improvements were already known for monotone submodular maximization; this work establishes their relevance to the three additional problems. Experiments offer further support, while the main theoretical improvement remains conditional on the function's curvature.
summary.tldr: Curvature-dependent guarantees improve submodular approximation, learning, and constrained minimization bounds when functions are not too curved.

title: Curvature and Optimal Algorithms for Learning and Minimizing Submodular Functions

abstract: We propose a pre-training technique for recurrent neural networks based on linear autoencoder networks for sequences, i.e. linear dynamical systems modelling the target sequences. We start by giving a closed form solution for the definition of the optimal weights of a linear autoencoder given a training set of sequences. This solution, however, is computationally very demanding, so we suggest a procedure to get an approximate solution for a given number of hidden units. The weights obtained for the linear autoencoder are then used as initial weights for the input-to-hidden connections of a recurrent neural network, which is then trained on the desired task. Using four well known datasets of sequences of polyphonic music, we show that the proposed pre-training approach is highly effective, since it allows to largely improve the state of the art results on all the considered datasets.

paragraphs: The paper proposes initializing a recurrent neural network using a linear autoencoder trained on sequences. These autoencoders are linear dynamical systems that model the target sequences. The approach uses what the simpler sequence model learns to provide initial weights before the recurrent network is trained for its intended task.

The authors first derive a closed-form solution for the optimal linear autoencoder weights given a training set. Computing that solution is very demanding, so they introduce a procedure that approximates it for a specified number of hidden units. The resulting weights initialize the recurrent network's input-to-hidden connections, linking the sequence autoencoder directly to the later training process.

Evaluation uses four established datasets of polyphonic music sequences. The authors report large improvements over the state of the art on all four datasets. These findings support the effectiveness of the proposed initialization in the tested sequence tasks. The contribution combines an analytical characterization of the linear autoencoder with a practical approximation and an empirical demonstration of its value for recurrent network pre-training.
summary.tldr: Linear sequence autoencoders provide effective recurrent-network initialization, substantially improving results on four polyphonic music datasets.

title: Pre-training of Recurrent Neural Networks via Linear Autoencoders

abstract: The idea that animals might use information-driven planning to explore an unknown environment and build an internal model of it has been proposed for quite some time. Recent work has demonstrated that agents using this principle can efficiently learn models of probabilistic environments with discrete, bounded state spaces. However, animals and robots are commonly confronted with unbounded environments. To address this more challenging situation, we study information-based learning strategies of agents in unbounded state spaces using non-parametric Bayesian models. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP) model is able to solve this problem and that an Empirical Bayes version is able to efficiently explore bounded and unbounded worlds by relying on little prior information.

Specifically, we demonstrate that the Chinese Restaurant Process (CRP) model is able to solve this problem and that an Empirical Bayes version is able to efficiently explore bounded and unbounded worlds by relying on little prior information.

paragraphs: An exploring agent can choose actions for the information they provide about an unfamiliar environment. Earlier work showed that this principle can efficiently build models of probabilistic environments with discrete, bounded state spaces. The paper addresses a harder setting in which the space of possible states is unbounded.

The authors use nonparametric Bayesian models to support information-based learning in that setting. Their specific model is the Chinese Restaurant Process. Its role is to provide a way of modeling an environment without requiring a fixed finite collection of possible states, making it relevant when exploration can keep revealing previously unrepresented possibilities.

The paper demonstrates that the Chinese Restaurant Process model can address this learning problem. It further shows that an Empirical Bayes version explores both bounded and unbounded worlds efficiently while relying on little prior information. The findings extend the demonstrated reach of information-driven exploration beyond bounded environments. They support this particular modeling approach rather than establishing that any information-seeking agent will explore an arbitrary unbounded world efficiently.
summary.tldr: A Chinese Restaurant Process model enables information-driven exploration of unbounded state spaces, with an Empirical Bayes version requiring little prior information.

title: Information-based learning by agents in unbounded state spaces

abstract: Blind source separation problems are difficult because they are inherently unidentifiable, yet the entire goal is to identify meaningful sources. We introduce a way of incorporating domain knowledge into this problem, called signal aggregate constraints (SACs). SACs encourage the total signal for each of the unknown sources to be close to a specified value. This is based on the observation that the total signal often varies widely across the unknown sources, and we often have a good idea of what total values to expect. We incorporate SACs into an additive factorial hidden Markov model (AFHMM) to formulate the energy disaggregation problems where only one mixture signal is assumed to be observed. A convex quadratic program for approximate inference is employed for recovering those source signals. On a real-world energy disaggregation data set, we show that the use of SACs dramatically improves the original AFHMM, and significantly improves over a recent state-of-the art approach.

paragraphs: Separating a single mixed signal into meaningful sources is difficult because different source combinations can explain the same observation. The paper introduces signal aggregate constraints to bring domain knowledge into this ambiguity. These constraints encourage each unknown source's total signal to stay close to a specified value.

The idea relies on a useful form of prior knowledge: sources often have substantially different totals, and those totals may be approximately known. The authors incorporate these constraints into an additive factorial hidden Markov model for energy disaggregation, assuming that only one mixture signal is observed. Approximate inference is formulated as a convex quadratic program to recover the individual source signals.

On a real-world energy-disaggregation dataset, adding the constraints dramatically improves the original model and significantly outperforms a recent state-of-the-art approach. The result shows the value of information about aggregate amounts even when the desired output is a set of detailed source signals. The constraints guide an otherwise ambiguous decomposition by expressing expectations about each source's total contribution.
summary.tldr: Constraints on expected source totals improve energy disaggregation from a single mixed signal within an additive factorial hidden Markov model.

title: Signal Aggregate Constraints in Additive Factorial HMMs, with Application to Energy Disaggregation

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent algorithms for training linear and kernel predictors are gaining more and more importance, thanks to their scalability. While various methods have been proposed to speed up their convergence, the model selection phase is often ignored. In fact, in theoretical works most of the time assumptions are made, for example, on the prior knowledge of the norm of the optimal solution, while in the practical world validation methods remain the only viable approach. In this paper, we propose a new kernel-based stochastic gradient descent algorithm that performs model selection while training, with no parameters to tune, nor any form of cross-validation. The algorithm builds on recent advancement in online learning theory for unconstrained settings, to estimate over time the right regularization in a data-dependent way. Optimal rates of convergence are proved under standard smoothness assumptions on the target function as well as preliminary empirical results.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent can train predictors efficiently, but selecting the model’s regularization remains a separate burden. Theoretical analyses may assume knowledge of the optimal solution’s norm, while practical methods rely on validation. This paper brings model selection into the training process through a kernel-based stochastic gradient algorithm.

The algorithm has no parameters to tune and uses no cross-validation. It draws on online learning theory for unconstrained problems to estimate appropriate regularization as training progresses. Because the estimate depends on observed data, the learner adjusts this aspect of model selection during optimization instead of requiring it to be fixed through an external search.

The authors prove optimal convergence rates under standard smoothness assumptions on the target function and provide preliminary empirical results. The theoretical guarantee is therefore tied to those smoothness conditions, while the experimental evidence is explicitly early-stage. The contribution addresses a part of scalable learning that convergence improvements alone leave unresolved: how to choose regularization while retaining an efficient stochastic training procedure.
summary.tldr: A kernel stochastic-gradient method learns regularization during training without tuning or cross-validation, with optimal rates under smoothness assumptions.

title: Simultaneous Model Selection and Optimization through Parameter-free Stochastic Learning

abstract: An active learner is given a class of models, a large set of unlabeled examples, and the ability to interactively query labels of a subset of these examples; the goal of the learner is to learn a model in the class that fits the data well. Previous theoretical work has rigorously characterized label complexity of active learning, but most of this work has focused on the PAC or the agnostic PAC model. In this paper, we shift our attention to a more general setting -- maximum likelihood estimation. Provided certain conditions hold on the model class, we provide a two-stage active learning algorithm for this problem. The conditions we require are fairly general, and cover the widely popular class of Generalized Linear Models, which in turn, include models for binary and multi-class classification, regression, and conditional random fields. We provide an upper bound on the label requirement of our algorithm, and a lower bound that matches it up to lower order terms. Our analysis shows that unlike binary classification in the realizable case, just a single extraround of interaction is sufficient to achieve near-optimal performance in maximum likelihood estimation. On the empirical side, the recent work in (Gu et al. 2012) and (Gu et al. 2014) (on active linear and logistic regression) shows the promise of this approach.

paragraphs: Active learning lets a learner choose which examples receive labels from a large unlabeled collection. This paper studies that choice for maximum likelihood estimation, broadening the theoretical focus beyond the PAC settings emphasized in earlier work. The objective is to fit a model while limiting the number of requested labels.

The authors propose a two-stage algorithm under conditions on the model class. Those conditions cover generalized linear models and encompass binary and multiclass classification, regression, and conditional random fields. The method therefore addresses a range of estimation tasks through one conditional theoretical framework.

An upper bound on the algorithm's label requirement matches a lower bound up to lower-order terms. This establishes near-optimal label use within the analyzed setting. A particularly useful consequence is that just one additional interaction round suffices for near-optimal maximum likelihood estimation. The abstract points to earlier empirical work on active linear and logistic regression as evidence of the approach's promise, rather than presenting that work as new experiments in this paper.
summary.tldr: Under model-class conditions, a two-stage active learner achieves nearly optimal label requirements for maximum likelihood estimation.

title: Convergence Rates of Active Learning for Maximum Likelihood Estimation

abstract: We study accelerated descent dynamics for constrained convex optimization. This dynamics can be described naturally as a coupling of a dual variable accumulating gradients at a given rate $\eta(t)$, and a primal variable obtained as the weighted average of the mirrored dual trajectory, with weights $w(t)$. Using a Lyapunov argument, we give sufficient conditions on $\eta$ and $w$ to achieve a desired convergence rate. As an example, we show that the replicator dynamics (an example of mirror descent on the simplex) can be accelerated using a simple averaging scheme. We then propose an adaptive averaging heuristic which adaptively computes the weights to speed up the decrease of the Lyapunov function. We provide guarantees on adaptive averaging in continuous-time, prove that it preserves the quadratic convergence rate of accelerated first-order methods in discrete-time, and give numerical experiments to compare it with existing heuristics, such as adaptive restarting. The experiments indicate that adaptive averaging performs at least as well as adaptive restarting, with significant improvements in some cases.

paragraphs: The paper examines how averaging can accelerate constrained convex optimization. Its starting point is a continuous-time description with two coupled quantities: a dual variable that accumulates gradients, and a primal variable formed by averaging the mirrored dual trajectory. The gradient accumulation rate and the averaging weights jointly determine how this process evolves.

Using a Lyapunov function, a quantity used to track progress, the authors derive sufficient conditions on these rates and weights for a desired convergence rate. One example shows that averaging can accelerate replicator dynamics, a form of mirror descent on the simplex. This makes the choice of averaging rule an explicit part of the acceleration mechanism.

The authors then propose choosing weights adaptively to make the Lyapunov function decrease faster. They establish continuous-time guarantees and show that the discrete-time version preserves the quadratic convergence rate of accelerated first-order methods. Numerical comparisons indicate performance at least as good as adaptive restarting in the reported experiments, with substantial improvements in some cases.
summary.tldr: Adaptive averaging can accelerate convex optimization while preserving the convergence rate of accelerated first-order methods.

title: Adaptive Averaging in Accelerated Descent Dynamics

abstract: In this paper we aim at facilitating generalization for deep networks while supporting interpretability of the learned representations. Towards this goal, we propose a clustering based regularization that encourages parsimonious representations. Our k-means style objective is easy to optimize and flexible supporting various forms of clustering, including sample and spatial clustering as well as co-clustering. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the tasks of unsupervised learning, classification, fine grained categorization and zero-shot learning.
originalAbstract: In this paper we aim at facilitating generalization for deep networks while supporting interpretability of the learned representations. Towards this goal, we propose a clustering based regularization that encourages parsimonious representations. Our k-means style objective is easy to optimize and flexible supporting various forms of clustering, including sample and spatial clustering as well as co-clustering. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the tasks of unsupervised learning, classification, fine grained categorization and zero-shot learning.

paragraphs: The paper aims to help deep networks generalize while making their learned representations easier to interpret. It approaches both goals through parsimony: encouraging representations to have a more economical organization. The proposed tool is a clustering-based regularizer, which adds a preference for clustered structure to the learning objective.

The regularization objective follows the style of k-means and is described as easy to optimize. It supports several forms of organization, including clustering across samples, spatial clustering, and co-clustering. This flexibility matters because the same broad principle can be applied to different aspects of a learned representation, rather than being tied to only one arrangement of the data.

The authors demonstrate effectiveness on unsupervised learning, classification, fine-grained categorization, and zero-shot learning. The range of tasks supports the usefulness of clustering as a representation-learning constraint across different learning settings. The central contribution is the regularization approach itself: an optimizable way to encourage structured, economical representations in pursuit of better generalization and interpretability, with empirical demonstrations across the listed tasks.
summary.tldr: A flexible k-means-style regularizer encourages economical deep representations, with demonstrations across several learning tasks.

title: Learning Deep Parsimonious Representations

abstract: Recent progress on many imaging and vision tasks has been driven by the use of deep feed-forward neural networks, which are trained by propagating gradients of a loss defined on the final output, back through the network up to the first layer that operates directly on the image. We propose back-propagating one step further---to learn camera sensor designs jointly with networks that carry out inference on the images they capture. In this paper, we specifically consider the design and inference problems in a typical color camera---where the sensor is able to measure only one color channel at each pixel location, and computational inference is required to reconstruct a full color image. We learn the camera sensor's color multiplexing pattern by encoding it as layer whose learnable weights determine which color channel, from among a fixed set, will be measured at each location. These weights are jointly trained with those of a reconstruction network that operates on the corresponding sensor measurements to produce a full color image. Our network achieves significant improvements in accuracy over the traditional Bayer pattern used in most color cameras. It automatically learns to employ a sparse color measurement approach similar to that of a recent design, and moreover, improves upon that design by learning an optimal layout for these measurements.

paragraphs: A typical color-camera sensor measures only one color channel at each pixel, so software must reconstruct the missing channels. The usual learning pipeline takes that sensor layout as fixed. This paper extends backpropagation into the measurement process so that the color sampling pattern and reconstruction network can be learned together.

The sensor is represented as a layer whose trainable weights determine which channel, from a fixed set, is measured at each position. These weights are optimized jointly with a network that converts the resulting measurements into a full-color image. The design objective therefore links physical sampling choices to reconstruction accuracy.

The reported network improves accuracy substantially over the traditional Bayer pattern. It also learns sparse color measurements resembling a recent design and improves that design’s spatial layout. The abstract concerns this specific color-multiplexing setting; it does not establish improvements for every camera component or imaging task.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning a camera’s color sampling pattern and reconstruction network improves color imaging.

title: Learning Sensor Multiplexing Design through Back-propagation

abstract: We study the problem of learning probabilistic first-order logical rules for knowledge base reasoning. This learning problem is difficult because it requires learning the parameters in a continuous space as well as the structure in a discrete space. We propose a framework, Neural Logic Programming, that combines the parameter and structure learning of first-order logical rules in an end-to-end differentiable model. This approach is inspired by a recently-developed differentiable logic called TensorLog [5], where inference tasks can be compiled into sequences of differentiable operations. We design a neural controller system that learns to compose these operations. Empirically, our method outperforms prior work on multiple knowledge base benchmark datasets, including Freebase and WikiMovies.

This learning problem is difficult because it requires learning the parameters in a continuous space as well as the structure in a discrete space. We propose a framework, Neural Logic Programming, that combines the parameter and structure learning of first-order logical rules in an end-to-end differentiable model. This approach is inspired by a recently-developed differentiable logic called TensorLog [5], where inference tasks can be compiled into sequences of differentiable operations. We design a neural controller system that learns to compose these operations. paragraphs: Learning logical rules for a knowledge base involves two coupled decisions: what form a rule should take and what numerical parameters it should have. The first is a discrete structural choice, while the second lies in a continuous space. This mismatch makes it difficult to learn both parts within a single optimization process.

Neural Logic Programming combines rule structure and parameter learning in an end-to-end differentiable framework. It builds on the idea, used in TensorLog, that logical inference can be expressed as a sequence of differentiable operations. A neural controller learns how to compose these operations, connecting the construction of reasoning procedures to trainable numerical components.

The contribution is therefore a way to learn probabilistic first-order rules while keeping the overall model differentiable. Empirical results show improvements over prior work on multiple knowledge-base benchmarks, including Freebase and WikiMovies. These findings support the usefulness of the combined learning approach for the evaluated reasoning tasks, where deciding how to assemble a rule is part of learning.
summary.tldr: Neural Logic Programming jointly learns logical-rule structures and parameters through differentiable operations controlled by a neural model.

title: Differentiable Learning of Logical Rules for Knowledge Base Reasoning

abstract: Self-localization during navigation with noisy sensors in an ambiguous world is computationally challenging, yet animals and humans excel at it. In robotics, {\em Simultaneous Location and Mapping} (SLAM) algorithms solve this problem through joint sequential probabilistic inference of their own coordinates and those of external spatial landmarks. We generate the first neural solution to the SLAM problem by training recurrent LSTM networks to perform a set of hard 2D navigation tasks that require generalization to completely novel trajectories and environments. Our goal is to make sense of how the diverse phenomenology in the brain's spatial navigation circuits is related to their function. We show that the hidden unit representations exhibit several key properties of hippocampal place cells, including stable tuning curves that remap between environments. Our result is also a proof of concept for end-to-end-learning of a SLAM algorithm using recurrent networks, and a demonstration of why this approach may have some advantages for robotic SLAM.

This paper trains recurrent LSTM networks on difficult two-dimensional navigation tasks to investigate a neural solution to that problem.

The tasks require generalization to completely new trajectories and environments. The authors examine the networks' hidden representations to generate hypotheses about how spatial-navigation circuits in the brain relate to their function. Hidden units exhibit several properties associated with hippocampal place cells, including stable tuning curves that change their mapping between environments.

These similarities connect behavior learned for a navigation task with recognizable features of biological spatial representations. Its contribution therefore spans a demonstrated navigation-learning approach and a way to develop functional hypotheses about neural activity.
summary.tldr: LSTMs trained for difficult navigation learn a neural SLAM solution and develop representations resembling several properties of hippocampal place cells.

title: Training recurrent networks to generate hypotheses about how the brain solves hard navigation problems

abstract: We study a novel problem lying at the intersection of two areas: multi-armed bandit and outlier detection. Multi-armed bandit is a useful tool to model the process of incrementally collecting data for multiple objects in a decision space. Outlier detection is a powerful method to narrow down the attention to a few objects after the data for them are collected. However, no one has studied how to detect outlier objects while incrementally collecting data for them, which is necessary when data collection is expensive. We formalize this problem as identifying outlier arms in a multi-armed bandit. We propose two sampling strategies with theoretical guarantee, and analyze their sampling efficiency. Our experimental results on both synthetic and real data show that our solution saves 70-99% of data collection cost from baseline while having nearly perfect accuracy.

paragraphs: Outlier detection usually begins after data have been collected, but obtaining those data can itself be expensive. This paper asks how to identify unusual objects while observations are still arriving. It models each object as an arm in a multi-armed bandit, turning the choice of what to measure next into part of the detection problem.

The authors formalize outlier-arm identification and propose two sampling strategies with theoretical guarantees. They analyze sampling efficiency, connecting the reliability of the eventual detection to the amount of information collected. The key change is that observation decisions and outlier detection are considered together instead of treating data acquisition as a completed preliminary step.

Experiments on synthetic and real data report a 70–99% reduction in data collection cost relative to the baseline, with nearly perfect accuracy. These are empirical findings for the evaluated settings. They show that deciding which objects to sample during detection can substantially reduce measurement costs while retaining strong accuracy, making the approach relevant when collecting observations is a major expense.
summary.tldr: Two bandit sampling strategies identify outliers during data collection, reporting 70–99% cost savings with nearly perfect accuracy in experiments.

title: Identifying Outlier Arms in Multi-Armed Bandit

abstract: The study of private inference has been sparked by growing concern regarding the analysis of data when it stems from sensitive sources. We present the first method for private Bayesian inference in exponential families that properly accounts for noise introduced by the privacy mechanism. It is efficient because it works only with sufficient statistics and not individual data. Unlike other methods, it gives properly calibrated posterior beliefs in the non-asymptotic data regime.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference represents conclusions as posterior beliefs, so the uncertainty introduced by a privacy mechanism matters to the result. This paper addresses private inference for exponential-family models. Its central concern is accounting for privacy noise within the inference procedure, so that the reported beliefs reflect that additional source of uncertainty.

The authors present what they describe as the first method in this setting to account properly for noise introduced by the privacy mechanism. The method operates on sufficient statistics rather than individual data records. These statistics provide the summaries used for inference in the model, and working with them is the stated reason for the method's efficiency.

The main finding is properly calibrated posterior beliefs in the non-asymptotic data regime, where the result does not depend on an effectively unlimited amount of data. That distinction matters because noise from privacy protection remains part of the evidence available for inference. The contribution ties efficient summary-based computation to uncertainty accounting, with exponential families defining the class of models considered.
summary.tldr: The method accounts for privacy noise in exponential-family Bayesian inference to produce calibrated posterior beliefs with finite data.

title: Differentially Private Bayesian Inference for Exponential Families

abstract: Distributed training of massive machine learning models, in particular deep neural networks, via Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is becoming commonplace. Several families of communication-reduction methods, such as quantization, large-batch methods, and gradient sparsification, have been proposed. To date, gradient sparsification methods--where each node sorts gradients by magnitude, and only communicates a subset of the components, accumulating the rest locally--are known to yield some of the largest practical gains. Such methods can reduce the amount of communication per step by up to \emph{three orders of magnitude}, while preserving model accuracy. Yet, this family of methods currently has no theoretical justification. This is the question we address in this paper. We prove that, under analytic assumptions, sparsifying gradients by magnitude with local error correction provides convergence guarantees, for both convex and non-convex smooth objectives, for data-parallel SGD. The main insight is that sparsification methods implicitly maintain bounds on the maximum impact of stale updates, thanks to selection by magnitude. Our analysis and empirical validation also reveal that these methods do require analytical conditions to converge well, justifying existing heuristics.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent can spend substantial resources communicating updates between workers. Gradient sparsification reduces that traffic by sending only selected large-magnitude components and accumulating the others locally. Such methods had already shown communication reductions of up to three orders of magnitude while preserving accuracy, but the paper identifies a lack of theoretical justification.

The authors prove convergence guarantees for magnitude-based sparsification with local error correction in data-parallel SGD. Their results cover smooth convex and nonconvex objectives under analytic assumptions. The key insight is that choosing updates by magnitude implicitly limits the maximum influence of delayed updates, helping explain why withholding some components need not prevent progress.

Both the analysis and empirical validation indicate that these methods require analytical conditions to converge well. This qualification matters: retaining omitted updates and prioritizing large components do not amount to an unconditional guarantee. The paper connects the practical success of sparsification to a mathematical account of stale-update control and provides support for existing heuristics used to make these methods work.
summary.tldr: Magnitude-based gradient sparsification with local error correction has convergence guarantees for smooth convex and nonconvex objectives under analytic assumptions.

title: The Convergence of Sparsified Gradient Methods

abstract: The existence of evasion attacks during the test phase of machine learning algorithms represents a significant challenge to both their deployment and understanding. These attacks can be carried out by adding imperceptible perturbations to inputs to generate adversarial examples and finding effective defenses and detectors has proven to be difficult. In this paper, we step away from the attack-defense arms race and seek to understand the limits of what can be learned in the presence of an evasion adversary. In particular, we extend the Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)-learning framework to account for the presence of an adversary. We first define corrupted hypothesis classes which arise from standard binary hypothesis classes in the presence of an evasion adversary and derive the Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC)-dimension for these, denoted as the adversarial VC-dimension. We then show that sample complexity upper bounds from the Fundamental Theorem of Statistical learning can be extended to the case of evasion adversaries, where the sample complexity is controlled by the adversarial VC-dimension. We then explicitly derive the adversarial VC-dimension for halfspace classifiers in the presence of a sample-wise norm-constrained adversary of the type commonly studied for evasion attacks and show that it is the same as the standard VC-dimension, closing an open question. Finally, we prove that the adversarial VC-dimension can be either larger or smaller than the standard VC-dimension depending on the hypothesis class and adversary, making it an interesting object of study in its own right.

paragraphs: The paper studies the statistical limits of learning when an adversary can alter inputs at test time. It extends the Probably Approximately Correct learning framework to include such evasion attacks. The focus is on how much data is sufficient for learning in this setting and how that requirement depends on both the classifier family and the adversary.

The authors define corrupted hypothesis classes that represent ordinary binary classifiers in the presence of an adversary. They call the VC dimension of these classes the adversarial VC dimension. Standard sample-complexity upper bounds extend to this setting with the new dimension controlling the amount of data required.

More generally, the paper proves that it can be larger or smaller, depending on the hypothesis class and attack model. This distinction matters: the halfspace result does not imply that adversarial perturbations leave statistical complexity unchanged for every learning problem. The framework makes that dependence explicit.
summary.tldr: An adversarial extension of PAC learning characterizes sample-complexity upper bounds through a VC dimension that depends on both classifiers and attacks.

title: PAC-learning in the presence of adversaries

abstract: Boltzmann machines (BMs) are appealing candidates for powerful priors in variational autoencoders (VAEs), as they are capable of capturing nontrivial and multi-modal distributions over discrete variables. However, non-differentiability of the discrete units prohibits using the reparameterization trick, essential for low-noise back propagation. The Gumbel trick resolves this problem in a consistent way by relaxing the variables and distributions, but it is incompatible with BM priors. Here, we propose the GumBolt, a model that extends the Gumbel trick to BM priors in VAEs. GumBolt is significantly simpler than the recently proposed methods with BM prior and outperforms them by a considerable margin. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on permutation invariant MNIST and OMNIGLOT datasets in the scope of models with only discrete latent variables. Moreover, the performance can be further improved by allowing multi-sampled (importance-weighted) estimation of log-likelihood in training, which was not possible with previous models.
