Discrete units, however, prevent direct use of the reparameterization trick needed for low-noise backpropagation. Although the Gumbel trick relaxes discrete variables into a trainable continuous formulation, its existing form is incompatible with Boltzmann-machine priors.

GumBolt extends the Gumbel approach to accommodate those priors. The purpose is to combine expressive dependencies among discrete latent variables with a relaxation suitable for gradient-based training. The authors describe their model as substantially simpler than recently proposed methods using Boltzmann priors, while also reporting a considerable performance improvement over those methods.

On permutation-invariant MNIST and OMNIGLOT, GumBolt achieves state-of-the-art performance within the specified class of models using only discrete latent variables. Its training also supports multiple-sample, importance-weighted estimation of log-likelihood, which the abstract says previous models could not use. Allowing that training approach further improves performance, giving the method both a modeling benefit and an additional training capability.
summary.tldr: GumBolt adapts the Gumbel trick to Boltzmann priors, improving discrete-latent VAEs and enabling importance-weighted training.

title: GumBolt: Extending Gumbel trick to Boltzmann priors

abstract: We present a framework for learning disentangled and interpretable jointly continuous and discrete representations in an unsupervised manner. By augmenting the continuous latent distribution of variational autoencoders with a relaxed discrete distribution and controlling the amount of information encoded in each latent unit, we show how continuous and categorical factors of variation can be discovered automatically from data. Experiments show that the framework disentangles continuous and discrete generative factors on various datasets and outperforms current disentangling methods when a discrete generative factor is prominent.
originalAbstract: We present a framework for learning disentangled and interpretable jointly continuous and discrete representations in an unsupervised manner. By augmenting the continuous latent distribution of variational autoencoders with a relaxed discrete distribution and controlling the amount of information encoded in each latent unit, we show how continuous and categorical factors of variation can be discovered automatically from data. Experiments show that the framework disentangles continuous and discrete generative factors on various datasets and outperforms current disentangling methods when a discrete generative factor is prominent.

paragraphs: The paper addresses unsupervised representation learning when the factors underlying data include both continuous variation and discrete categories. Its goal is a representation in which these factors are separated and interpretable. A joint representation matters because a purely continuous latent space does not explicitly provide both kinds of variables within the proposed learning framework.

The authors extend a variational autoencoder by adding a relaxed discrete distribution to its continuous latent distribution. They also control how much information each latent unit can encode. Together, these choices provide a mechanism for automatically discovering continuous and categorical factors from data without supervised labels for those factors.

Experiments show separation of continuous and discrete generative factors across several datasets. The framework outperforms the compared disentangling methods when a discrete generative factor is prominent. That qualification is central to the result: the reported advantage is particularly associated with data where categorical variation matters, supporting the value of explicitly accommodating discrete structure alongside continuous structure.
summary.tldr: A variational autoencoder with continuous and relaxed discrete latent variables learns interpretable factors, especially benefiting data with prominent categorical variation.

title: Learning Disentangled Joint Continuous and Discrete Representations

abstract: Dimensionality reduction is a classical technique widely used for data analysis. One foundational instantiation is Principal Component Analysis (PCA), which minimizes the average reconstruction error. In this paper, we introduce the multi-criteria dimensionality reduction problem where we are given multiple objectives that need to be optimized simultaneously. As an application, our model captures several fairness criteria for dimensionality reduction such as the Fair-PCA problem introduced by Samadi et al. [NeurIPS18] and the Nash Social Welfare (NSW) problem. In the Fair-PCA problem, the input data is divided into k groups, and the goal is to find a single d-dimensional representation for all groups for which the maximum reconstruction error of any one group is minimized. In NSW the goal is to maximize the product of the individual variances of the groups achieved by the common low-dimensinal space. Our main result is an exact polynomial-time algorithm for the two-criteria dimensionality reduction problem when the two criteria are increasing concave functions. As an application of this result, we obtain a polynomial time algorithm for Fair-PCA for k=2 groups, resolving an open problem of Samadi et al.[NeurIPS18], and a polynomial time algorithm for NSW objective for k=2 groups. We also give approximation algorithms for k>2. Our technical contribution in the above results is to prove new low-rank properties of extreme point solutions to semi-definite programs. We conclude with the results of several experiments indicating improved performance and generalized application of our algorithm on real-world datasets.

This paper instead studies a shared low-dimensional representation that must satisfy several objectives. Its framework captures Fair-PCA, which minimizes the worst group's reconstruction error, and Nash Social Welfare, which maximizes the product of the groups' retained variances.

summary.tldr: A multi-objective dimensionality-reduction framework gives exact polynomial-time solutions for two-group fairness objectives and approximation algorithms for more groups.

title: Multi-Criteria Dimensionality Reduction with Applications to Fairness

abstract: This paper investigates the theory of robustness against adversarial attacks. It focuses on the family of randomization techniques that consist in injecting noise in the network at inference time. These techniques have proven effective in many contexts, but lack theoretical arguments. We close this gap by presenting a theo- retical analysis of these approaches, hence explaining why they perform well in practice. More precisely, we make two new contributions. The first one relates the randomization rate to robustness to adversarial attacks. This result applies for the general family of exponential distributions, and thus extends and unifies the previous approaches. The second contribution consists in devising a new upper bound on the adversarial risk gap of randomized neural networks. We support our theoretical claims with a set of experiments.

paragraphs: Injecting noise into a neural network at prediction time has shown practical promise against adversarial attacks. This paper investigates the theoretical basis for that strategy. It focuses on randomized inference and asks how the amount and form of randomization relate to robustness.

The first contribution establishes a relationship between randomization rate and resistance to adversarial attacks. The result applies to a general family of exponential distributions, extending and bringing together earlier approaches. This gives a broader theoretical account of noise-based defenses rather than an explanation tied to only one particular noise choice.

The second contribution is a new upper bound on the adversarial risk gap for randomized neural networks. Together, the two results provide ways to reason about the robustness consequences of inference-time noise. Experiments support the theoretical claims. The paper's contribution is a mathematical explanation and supporting evidence for this family of techniques, with claims expressed through relationships and bounds rather than an assertion of immunity to attacks.
summary.tldr: The paper relates inference-time randomization to adversarial robustness and derives a new upper bound on randomized networks' adversarial risk gap.

title: Theoretical evidence for adversarial robustness through randomization

abstract: We study a decentralized cooperative stochastic multi-armed bandit problem with K arms on a network of N agents. In our model, the reward distribution of each arm is the same for each agent and rewards are drawn independently across agents and time steps. In each round, each agent chooses an arm to play and subsequently sends a message to her neighbors. The goal is to minimize the overall regret of the entire network. We design a fully decentralized algorithm that uses an accelerated consensus procedure to compute (delayed) estimates of the average of rewards obtained by all the agents for each arm, and then uses an upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm that accounts for the delay and error of the estimates. We analyze the regret of our algorithm and also provide a lower bound. The regret is bounded by the optimal centralized regret plus a natural and simple term depending on the spectral gap of the communication matrix. Our algorithm is simpler to analyze than those proposed in prior work and it achieves better regret bounds, while requiring less information about the underlying network. It also performs better empirically.

paragraphs: This paper studies a network of agents learning which options produce the best rewards. Each agent chooses an option and then communicates with its neighbors. The objective is to reduce the whole network's cumulative regret. The setting assumes that each option has the same reward distribution for every agent, with rewards drawn independently across agents and time.

The proposed algorithm shares information without a central coordinator. An accelerated consensus procedure lets agents estimate the average rewards observed throughout the network. These estimates arrive with delay and error, so the decision rule explicitly accounts for both when using upper confidence bounds to choose options.

The analysis bounds regret by the optimal centralized regret plus a term determined by the communication matrix's spectral gap. This separates the centralized learning benchmark from an additional network-related cost. The authors also provide a lower bound and report improved regret bounds, reduced requirements for network information, simpler analysis, and better empirical performance relative to prior approaches.
summary.tldr: A decentralized bandit algorithm combines consensus with delay-aware confidence bounds, achieving centralized regret plus a network-dependent term.

title: Decentralized Cooperative Stochastic Bandits

abstract: Before sufficient training data is available, fine-tuning neural networks pre-trained on large-scale datasets substantially outperforms training from random initialization. However, fine-tuning methods suffer from two dilemmas, catastrophic forgetting and negative transfer. While several methods with explicit attempts to overcome catastrophic forgetting have been proposed, negative transfer is rarely delved into. In this paper, we launch an in-depth empirical investigation into negative transfer in fine-tuning and find that, for the weight parameters and feature representations, transferability of their spectral components is diverse. For safe transfer learning, we present Batch Spectral Shrinkage (BSS), a novel regularization approach to penalizing smaller singular values so that untransferable spectral components are suppressed. BSS is orthogonal to existing fine-tuning methods and is readily pluggable to them. Experimental results show that BSS can significantly enhance the performance of representative methods, especially with limited training data.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained network can be especially useful when the target task has little training data. However, retaining knowledge from the original task does not ensure that all of it helps the new task. This paper examines negative transfer, alongside the more commonly addressed problem of catastrophic forgetting.

Its empirical investigation finds that spectral components of both network weights and feature representations differ in transferability. These components provide a way to examine different directions within the learned parameters and representations. The finding motivates treating transferred information selectively rather than assuming its usefulness is uniform.

The proposed Batch Spectral Shrinkage method penalizes smaller singular values to suppress components identified as untransferable. It acts as a regularizer and can be added to existing fine-tuning methods. Experiments show significant improvements for representative methods, especially with limited training data. These results support the value of controlling which spectral components are retained during adaptation; they do not establish a universal guarantee that negative transfer disappears.
summary.tldr: Batch Spectral Shrinkage improves fine-tuning by penalizing smaller singular values to suppress poorly transferable components.

title: Catastrophic Forgetting Meets Negative Transfer: Batch Spectral Shrinkage for Safe Transfer Learning

abstract: We prove new explicit upper bounds on the leverage scores of Fourier sparse functions under both the Gaussian and Laplace measures. In particular, we study s-sparse functions of the form $f(x) = \sum_{j=1}^s a_j e^{i \lambda_j x}$ for coefficients $a_j \in C$ and frequencies $\lambda_j \in R$. Bounding Fourier sparse leverage scores under various measures is of pure mathematical interest in approximation theory, and our work extends existing results for the uniform measure [Erd17,CP19a]. Practically, our bounds are motivated by two important applications in machine learning: 1. Kernel Approximation. They yield a new random Fourier features algorithm for approximating Gaussian and Cauchy (rational quadratic) kernel matrices. For low-dimensional data, our method uses a near optimal number of features, and its runtime is polynomial in the *statistical dimension* of the approximated kernel matrix. It is the first ``oblivious sketching method'' with this property for any kernel besides the polynomial kernel, resolving an open question of [AKM+17,AKK+20b]. 2. Active Learning. They can be used as non-uniform sampling distributions for robust active learning when data follows a Gaussian or Laplace distribution. Using the framework of [AKM+19], we provide essentially optimal results for bandlimited and multiband interpolation, and Gaussian process regression. These results generalize existing work that only applies to uniformly distributed data.

Practically, our bounds are motivated by two important applications in machine learning: 1. Kernel Approximation. For low-dimensional data, our method uses a near optimal number of features, and its runtime is polynomial in the *statistical dimension* of the approximated kernel matrix. It is the first ``oblivious sketching method'' with this property for any kernel besides the polynomial kernel, resolving an open question of [AKM+17,AKK+20b]. 2. Active Learning. They can be used as non-uniform sampling distributions for robust active learning when data follows a Gaussian or Laplace distribution. Using the framework of [AKM+19], we provide essentially optimal results for bandlimited and multiband interpolation, and Gaussian process regression. These results generalize existing work that only applies to uniformly distributed data.

paragraphs: The paper studies functions formed by adding a small number of complex exponential terms, each with its own coefficient and frequency. It proves explicit upper bounds on their leverage scores under Gaussian and Laplace measures. These results extend earlier bounds for the uniform measure and provide mathematical tools for choosing informative samples or features.

One application is a new random Fourier features algorithm for approximating Gaussian and Cauchy kernel matrices. For low-dimensional data, it uses a nearly optimal number of features and runs in time polynomial in the matrix's statistical dimension. The authors establish this property for an oblivious sketching method beyond the previously covered polynomial kernel, resolving an open question.

A second application uses the bounds to construct nonuniform sampling distributions for robust active learning with Gaussian- or Laplace-distributed data. Within an existing framework, the authors obtain essentially optimal results for bandlimited interpolation, multiband interpolation, and Gaussian process regression. The significance is that these sampling guarantees extend beyond the uniform-data setting covered by earlier work.
summary.tldr: New Fourier-sparse leverage-score bounds enable efficient kernel approximations and essentially optimal active-learning results for Gaussian and Laplace data.

title: Fourier Sparse Leverage Scores and Approximate Kernel Learning

abstract: Adaptive gradient methods such as AdaGrad, RMSprop and Adam have been optimizers of choice for deep learning due to their fast training speed. However, it was recently observed that their generalization performance is often worse than that of SGD for over-parameterized neural networks. While new algorithms such as AdaBound, SWAT, and Padam were proposed to improve the situation, the provided analyses are only committed to optimization bounds for the training objective, leaving critical generalization capacity unexplored. To close this gap, we propose \textit{\textbf{S}table \textbf{A}daptive \textbf{G}radient \textbf{D}escent} (\textsc{SAGD}) for nonconvex optimization which leverages differential privacy to boost the generalization performance of adaptive gradient methods. Theoretical analyses show that \textsc{SAGD} has high-probability convergence to a population stationary point. We further conduct experiments on various popular deep learning tasks and models. Experimental results illustrate that \textsc{SAGD} is empirically competitive and often better than baselines.

paragraphs: Adaptive optimizers such as AdaGrad, RMSprop, and Adam offer fast training, yet their generalization can be worse than stochastic gradient descent for over-parameterized networks. This paper focuses on the gap between reducing training loss and performing well on the underlying data population. Analyses restricted to the training objective do not directly resolve that gap.

The authors propose Stable Adaptive Gradient Descent, or SAGD, for nonconvex optimization. The method uses differential privacy to improve the generalization behavior of adaptive gradient methods. Its theoretical analysis establishes high-probability convergence to a population stationary point, linking optimization to the population objective rather than only to the particular training sample.

A stationary point is a point where the objective has no first-order direction of change, so the result should not be read as a guarantee of globally optimal predictions. Experiments across several deep learning tasks and models show that SAGD is competitive with, and often better than, the tested baselines. The paper therefore combines a population-level theoretical target with empirical evidence of useful performance.
summary.tldr: SAGD uses differential privacy to strengthen adaptive optimization's generalization guarantees and achieves competitive empirical performance.

title: Towards Better Generalization of Adaptive Gradient Methods

abstract: Probabilistic inference in pairwise Markov Random Fields (MRFs), i.e. computing the partition function or computing a MAP estimate of the variables, is a foundational problem in probabilistic graphical models. Semidefinite programming relaxations have long been a theoretically powerful tool for analyzing properties of probabilistic inference, but have not been practical owing to the high computational cost of typical solvers for solving the resulting SDPs. In this paper, we propose an efficient method for computing the partition function or MAP estimate in a pairwise MRF by instead exploiting a recently proposed coordinate-descent-based fast semidefinite solver. We also extend semidefinite relaxations from the typical binary MRF to the full multi-class setting, and develop a compact semidefinite relaxation that can again be solved efficiently using the solver. We show that the method substantially outperforms (both in terms of solution quality and speed) the existing state of the art in approximate inference, on benchmark problems drawn from previous work. We also show that our approach can scale to large MRF domains such as fully-connected pairwise CRF models used in computer vision.

paragraphs: Pairwise Markov Random Fields describe variables connected through pairwise relationships. Two central inference tasks are finding a most probable assignment, called a MAP estimate, and computing the partition function. Semidefinite programming relaxations offer a theoretically powerful route to these tasks, but the computational expense of conventional solvers has limited their practical use.

This paper makes that route more efficient by using a fast semidefinite solver based on coordinate descent. It also extends semidefinite relaxations beyond binary variables to variables with multiple classes. The authors develop a compact formulation for this broader setting that the same solver can handle efficiently, expanding the range of models the approach can address.

On benchmark problems drawn from earlier work, the method substantially improves both solution quality and speed over existing state-of-the-art approximate inference methods. The authors also demonstrate scaling to large domains, including fully connected pairwise conditional random fields used in vision. The findings support semidefinite relaxation as a practical approximate inference approach when paired with an efficient solver and formulation.
summary.tldr: A fast semidefinite solver and compact multiclass relaxation improve the speed and quality of approximate inference in pairwise graphical models.

title: Efficient semidefinite-programming-based inference for binary and multi-class MRFs

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have been widely used in modeling and generating graphs with latent factors. However there is no clear explanation of what these latent factors are and why they perform well. In this work, we present Dirichlet Graph Variational Autoencoder (DGVAE) with graph cluster memberships as latent factors. Our study connects VAEs based graph generation and balanced graph cut, and provides a new way to understand and improve the internal mechanism of VAEs based graph generation. Specifically, we first interpret the reconstruction term of DGVAE as balanced graph cut in a principled way. Furthermore, motivated by the low pass characteristics in balanced graph cut, we propose a new variant of GNN named Heatts to encode the input graph into cluster memberships. Heatts utilizes the Taylor series for fast computation of Heat kernels and has better low pass characteristics than Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN). Through experiments on graph generation and graph clustering, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework.

paragraphs: Graph-generating variational autoencoders rely on hidden factors, but the meaning of those factors can be unclear. This paper gives them an explicit interpretation: memberships in graph clusters. Its Dirichlet Graph Variational Autoencoder, or DGVAE, makes that interpretation central to both the model and the explanation of how graph reconstruction works.

The authors connect DGVAE's reconstruction term to balanced graph cut, a way of partitioning a graph that also accounts for balance between groups. This connection provides a principled bridge between generating a graph from latent variables and identifying its cluster structure. It also motivates changes to the network used to encode the input graph.

The resulting encoder, Heatts, uses a Taylor-series calculation of heat kernels for fast computation. The authors report better low-pass characteristics than Graph Convolutional Networks, matching the filtering behavior that motivated the design through balanced graph cut. Experiments on graph generation and graph clustering demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The contribution combines interpretable latent factors, a theoretical connection, and an encoder shaped by that connection.
summary.tldr: DGVAE interprets graph latent variables as cluster memberships and uses a balanced-cut connection to design a heat-kernel graph encoder.

title: Dirichlet Graph Variational Autoencoder

abstract: In many real-world scenarios, decision makers seek to efficiently optimize multiple competing objectives in a sample-efficient fashion. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization (BO) is a common approach, but many of the best-performing acquisition functions do not have known analytic gradients and suffer from high computational overhead. We leverage recent advances in programming models and hardware acceleration for multi-objective BO using Expected Hypervolume Improvement (EHVI)---an algorithm notorious for its high computational complexity. We derive a novel formulation of q-Expected Hypervolume Improvement (qEHVI), an acquisition function that extends EHVI to the parallel, constrained evaluation setting. qEHVI is an exact computation of the joint EHVI of q new candidate points (up to Monte-Carlo (MC) integration error). Whereas previous EHVI formulations rely on gradient-free acquisition optimization or approximated gradients, we compute exact gradients of the MC estimator via auto-differentiation, thereby enabling efficient and effective optimization using first-order and quasi-second-order methods. Our empirical evaluation demonstrates that qEHVI is computationally tractable in many practical scenarios and outperforms state-of-the-art multi-objective BO algorithms at a fraction of their wall time.

paragraphs: Optimizing several competing objectives requires choosing evaluations that reveal useful tradeoffs without spending too many samples. Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to guide that choice, but strong acquisition functions can themselves be expensive to optimize. This paper targets Expected Hypervolume Improvement, whose computational demands have made its use challenging.

The authors derive qEHVI for selecting multiple candidate points jointly, including settings with constraints. Its calculation gives the joint expected improvement of the candidate batch, up to Monte Carlo integration error. Crucially, automatic differentiation supplies exact gradients of that Monte Carlo estimator. This distinction matters: the gradients are exact for the estimator, while the expectation still involves sampling error.

Those gradients allow first-order and quasi-second-order optimization methods to search for useful candidate batches. The formulation also takes advantage of modern programming tools and hardware acceleration. The empirical evaluation finds qEHVI computationally practical in many scenarios and reports better performance than state-of-the-art multi-objective Bayesian optimization algorithms at a fraction of their wall time.
summary.tldr: qEHVI makes joint, constrained multi-objective candidate selection practical by differentiating its Monte Carlo estimator and using hardware acceleration.

title: Differentiable Expected Hypervolume Improvement for Parallel Multi-Objective Bayesian Optimization

abstract: The Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) presents a remarkable approach to alleviate the scale variance in object representation by performing instance-level assignments. Nevertheless, this strategy ignores the distinct characteristics of different sub-regions in an instance. To this end, we propose a fine-grained dynamic head to conditionally select a pixel-level combination of FPN features from different scales for each instance, which further releases the ability of multi-scale feature representation. Moreover, we design a spatial gate with the new activation function to reduce computational complexity dramatically through spatially sparse convolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method on several state-of-the-art detection benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/StevenGrove/DynamicHead.

Nevertheless, this strategy ignores the distinct characteristics of different sub-regions in an instance. To this end, we propose a fine-grained dynamic head to conditionally select a pixel-level combination of FPN features from different scales for each instance, which further releases the ability of multi-scale feature representation. Moreover, we design a spatial gate with the new activation function to reduce computational complexity dramatically through spatially sparse convolutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed method on several state-of-the-art detection benchmarks. paragraphs: Object detectors use feature pyramids to represent objects at different scales. Assigning features at the level of a whole object helps address variation in object size, but it overlooks differences among regions within that object. This paper makes the selection of scale information more local.

Its dynamic detection head conditionally combines features from different pyramid scales at individual pixels for each instance. This gives different parts of an object access to different combinations of scale information. The purpose is to make fuller use of the existing multiscale representation by matching feature selection to the characteristics of subregions.

The authors also introduce a spatial gate with a new activation function to enable spatially sparse convolutions and substantially reduce computation. The architecture therefore addresses both the flexibility of feature selection and the cost of applying it. Experiments on several detection benchmarks support the method's effectiveness and efficiency. The stated result is that finer spatial control over multiscale features can be paired with selective computation in an object detector.
summary.tldr: A dynamic detection head selects multiscale features pixel by pixel and uses spatial gating to reduce computation.

title: Fine-Grained Dynamic Head for Object Detection

abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) was first proposed to achieve state-of-the-art performance through the discovery of new architecture patterns, without human intervention. An over-reliance on expert knowledge in the search space design has however led to increased performance (local optima) without significant architectural breakthroughs, thus preventing truly novel solutions from being reached. In this work we 1) are the first to investigate casting NAS as a problem of finding the optimal network generator and 2) we propose a new, hierarchical and graph-based search space capable of representing an extremely large variety of network types, yet only requiring few continuous hyper-parameters. This greatly reduces the dimensionality of the problem, enabling the effective use of Bayesian Optimisation as a search strategy. At the same time, we expand the range of valid architectures, motivating a multi-objective learning approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this strategy on six benchmark datasets and show that our search space generates extremely lightweight yet highly competitive models.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search aims to discover effective network designs automatically, but its search space can still reflect extensive human choices. The paper argues that this dependence can favor local improvements while excluding more novel architectures. It reframes the search target as a network generator, making the rule that produces architectures the object of optimization.

The proposed search space is hierarchical and graph-based. It represents a very large variety of network types using only a small number of continuous hyperparameters. This compact description lowers the dimensionality of the optimization problem enough to support Bayesian optimization as the search strategy. The expanded architectural variety also motivates considering multiple objectives.

Experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that the approach generates extremely lightweight models with highly competitive performance. The result connects two goals that can otherwise pull in different directions: allowing architectural diversity and keeping the search manageable. The contribution is a generator-based formulation and search space, with empirical evidence that its compact parameterization can produce useful and efficient network designs.
summary.tldr: Optimizing a compact network generator enables a broad architecture search that produces lightweight, competitive models.

title: Neural Architecture Generator Optimization

abstract: Gaussian processes are an effective model class for learning unknown functions, particularly in settings where accurately representing predictive uncertainty is of key importance. Motivated by applications in the physical sciences, the widely-used Matérn class of Gaussian processes has recently been generalized to model functions whose domains are Riemannian manifolds, by re-expressing said processes as solutions of stochastic partial differential equations. In this work, we propose techniques for computing the kernels of these processes on compact Riemannian manifolds via spectral theory of the Laplace-Beltrami operator in a fully constructive manner, thereby allowing them to be trained via standard scalable techniques such as inducing point methods. We also extend the generalization from the Matérn to the widely-used squared exponential Gaussian process. By allowing Riemannian Matérn Gaussian processes to be trained using well-understood techniques, our work enables their use in mini-batch, online, and non-conjugate settings, and makes them more accessible to machine learning practitioners.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes model unknown functions while representing predictive uncertainty. For functions defined on Riemannian manifolds, the domain's geometry must be incorporated into the model. Earlier work generalized Matérn Gaussian processes to such domains using stochastic partial differential equations. This paper focuses on making those generalized processes directly computable and accessible to established training methods.

The authors construct their kernels on compact Riemannian manifolds using the spectral theory of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. This provides an explicit computational route from the geometric formulation to the kernel needed for Gaussian process learning. They also extend the approach beyond the Matérn family to squared exponential Gaussian processes.

Computable kernels allow these models to use familiar scalable techniques, including inducing point methods. The work consequently enables training in mini-batch, online, and non-conjugate settings. Its practical significance is the connection between geometry-aware Gaussian process definitions and well-understood machine learning tools, making uncertainty-aware function learning on these domains more accessible without requiring practitioners to work only through the differential-equation formulation.
summary.tldr: Constructive kernels for Gaussian processes on compact Riemannian manifolds make geometry-aware models trainable with standard scalable methods.

title: Matérn Gaussian Processes on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: Variational Bayes (VB) is a popular scalable alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo for Bayesian inference. We study a mean-field spike and slab VB approximation of widely used Bayesian model selection priors in sparse high-dimensional logistic regression. We provide non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees for the VB posterior in both $\ell_2$ and prediction loss for a sparse truth, giving optimal (minimax) convergence rates. Since the VB algorithm does not depend on the unknown truth to achieve optimality, our results shed light on effective prior choices. We confirm the improved performance of our VB algorithm over common sparse VB approaches in a numerical study.

We provide non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees for the VB posterior in both $\ell_2$ and prediction loss for a sparse truth, giving optimal (minimax) convergence rates. Since the VB algorithm does not depend on the unknown truth to achieve optimality, our results shed light on effective prior choices. We confirm the improved performance of our VB algorithm over common sparse VB approaches in a numerical study.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference can quantify uncertainty, but computing it can be expensive in models with many parameters. Variational Bayes offers a scalable approximation. This paper studies a mean-field spike-and-slab approximation for sparse high-dimensional logistic regression, using priors designed for selecting which variables belong in the model.

The authors establish finite-sample theoretical guarantees when the underlying truth is sparse. They measure accuracy both through parameter error in the l2 sense and through prediction loss, obtaining optimal minimax convergence rates. These guarantees show that the approximation can achieve the best worst-case rate in the studied sparse setting, rather than sacrificing that rate simply to gain computational scalability.

The algorithm does not need knowledge of the unknown truth to attain its optimality result. The authors use this to illuminate effective prior choices. A numerical study also reports improved performance over common sparse variational Bayes approaches. The paper thus combines theoretical support for a particular approximation with empirical evidence that its prior structure can improve practical inference.
summary.tldr: Spike-and-slab variational Bayes achieves optimal theoretical rates for sparse logistic regression and improves on common sparse VB approaches in a numerical study.

title: Spike and slab variational Bayes for high dimensional logistic regression

abstract: We study a theory of reinforcement learning (RL) in which the learner receives binary feedback only once at the end of an episode. While this is an extreme test case for theory, it is also arguably more representative of real-world applications than the traditional requirement in RL practice that the learner receive feedback at every time step. Indeed, in many real-world applications of reinforcement learning, such as self-driving cars and robotics, it is easier to evaluate whether a learner's complete trajectory was either ``good'' or ``bad,'' but harder to provide a reward signal at each step. To show that learning is possible in this more challenging setting, we study the case where trajectory labels are generated by an unknown parametric model, and provide a statistically and computationally efficient algorithm that achieves sublinear regret.

Indeed, in many real-world applications of reinforcement learning, such as self-driving cars and robotics, it is easier to evaluate whether a learner's complete trajectory was either ``good'' or ``bad,'' but harder to provide a reward signal at each step. paragraphs: Many reinforcement-learning systems assume a reward signal at every step, but judging individual actions can be harder than judging a complete outcome. This paper studies the extreme case in which the learner receives just one binary assessment at the end of an episode: whether its full trajectory was good or bad.

The theoretical setting assumes those trajectory labels are generated by an unknown parametric model. That assumption supplies structure for learning from the sparse feedback. The authors develop an algorithm that is efficient both statistically and computationally, showing that the learner can make progress despite receiving no separate reward assessment for each intermediate action.

The algorithm achieves sublinear regret, meaning its cumulative performance shortfall grows more slowly than the number of learning episodes. Thus, average regret decreases as learning continues in the analysed setting. The result establishes a route to efficient learning from whole-trajectory judgements, motivated by applications such as robotics and self-driving where such judgements may be easier to obtain than detailed rewards.
summary.tldr: Efficient reinforcement learning with sublinear regret is possible from one binary label per episode under the studied parametric feedback model.

title: On the Theory of Reinforcement Learning with Once-per-Episode Feedback

abstract: Kernel selection plays a central role in determining the performance of Gaussian Process (GP) models, as the chosen kernel determines both the inductive biases and prior support of functions under the GP prior. This work addresses the challenge of constructing custom kernel functions for high-dimensional GP regression models. Drawing inspiration from recent progress in deep learning, we introduce a novel approach named KITT: Kernel Identification Through Transformers. KITT exploits a transformer-based architecture to generate kernel recommendations in under 0.1 seconds, which is several orders of magnitude faster than conventional kernel search algorithms. We train our model using synthetic data generated from priors over a vocabulary of known kernels. By exploiting the nature of the self-attention mechanism, KITT is able to process datasets with inputs of arbitrary dimension. We demonstrate that kernels chosen by KITT yield strong performance over a diverse collection of regression benchmarks.

paragraphs: A Gaussian process model's kernel determines its assumptions about functions and which functions its prior can support. Choosing that kernel is therefore central to regression performance. This paper introduces KITT, a transformer-based system that recommends custom kernels, addressing the cost of kernel selection for regression datasets with many input dimensions.

KITT learns from synthetic datasets generated using priors over a vocabulary of known kernels. This training connects examples of data with the kernel structures that could explain them. The architecture uses self-attention to process datasets whose inputs can have arbitrary dimensionality, allowing the recommendation mechanism to accommodate different numbers of input variables.

The authors report kernel recommendations in less than 0.1 seconds, several orders of magnitude faster than conventional kernel search algorithms. Kernels selected by KITT also perform strongly across a diverse collection of regression benchmarks. The findings support learned kernel recommendation as a fast way to make a consequential modeling choice, combining synthetic training with a transformer architecture suited to varying input dimensions.
summary.tldr: KITT learns to recommend Gaussian process kernels in under 0.1 seconds and produces strong results across the evaluated regression benchmarks.

title: Kernel Identification Through Transformers

abstract: Structured point process data harvested from various platforms poses new challenges to the machine learning community. To cluster repeatedly observed marked point processes, we propose a novel mixture model of multi-level marked point processes for identifying potential heterogeneity in the observed data. Specifically, we study a matrix whose entries are marked log-Gaussian Cox processes and cluster rows of such a matrix. An efficient semi-parametric Expectation-Solution (ES) algorithm combined with functional principal component analysis (FPCA) of point processes is proposed for model estimation. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through simulation studies and real data analyses.

The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through simulation studies and real data analyses.

paragraphs: Some structured datasets contain repeated event observations rather than a single number for each entry. This paper studies a matrix whose entries are marked point processes and seeks to cluster its rows, identifying heterogeneity across the repeatedly observed data.

The proposed mixture model uses multiple levels of marked point processes. More specifically, each matrix entry is modeled as a marked log-Gaussian Cox process. This supplies a statistical framework in which the repeated event patterns can inform the grouping of rows.

For estimation, the authors combine a semiparametric Expectation-Solution algorithm with functional principal component analysis of point processes. The combination is presented as an efficient way to fit the model while working with the functional structure of the event data.

Simulation studies and analyses of real data demonstrate the framework's effectiveness. The central contribution is bringing row clustering to a matrix whose entries have their own stochastic event structure, with a model and estimation procedure designed for that richer form of observation.
summary.tldr: A multilevel mixture model clusters rows of event-process matrices using an efficient estimation procedure built around functional principal components.

title: Row-clustering of a Point Process-valued Matrix

abstract: Named Entity Recognition and Disambiguation (NERD) systems are foundational for information retrieval, question answering, event detection, and other natural language processing (NLP) applications. We introduce TweetNERD, a dataset of 340K+ Tweets across 2010-2021, for benchmarking NERD systems on Tweets. This is the largest and most temporally diverse open sourced dataset benchmark for NERD on Tweets and can be used to facilitate research in this area. We describe evaluation setup with TweetNERD for three NERD tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER), Entity Linking with True Spans (EL), and End to End Entity Linking (End2End); and provide performance of existing publicly available methods on specific TweetNERD splits. TweetNERD is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6617192 under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. Check out more details at https://github.com/twitter-research/TweetNERD.

This is the largest and most temporally diverse open sourced dataset benchmark for NERD on Tweets and can be used to facilitate research in this area. We describe evaluation setup with TweetNERD for three NERD tasks: Named Entity Recognition (NER), Entity Linking with True Spans (EL), and End to End Entity Linking (End2End); and provide performance of existing publicly available methods on specific TweetNERD splits. TweetNERD is available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.6617192 under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) license. Check out more details at https://github.com/twitter-research/TweetNERD.

paragraphs: Named entity recognition and disambiguation help systems identify mentions of entities and determine which entities those mentions refer to. These capabilities support applications such as information retrieval, question answering, and event detection. TweetNERD provides a shared dataset for evaluating this work specifically on tweets.

The dataset contains more than 340,000 tweets spanning 2010 through 2021. The authors describe it as the largest and most temporally diverse open-source benchmark for these tasks on tweets. Its evaluation setup covers three distinct problems: finding entity mentions, linking entities when the correct mention spans are supplied, and performing recognition and linking together.

The paper reports results from existing publicly available methods on specified dataset splits, giving researchers reference evaluations for future comparisons. Separating the three tasks allows evaluation of mention recognition, disambiguation with known spans, and the complete process. Released under a Creative Commons Attribution license, TweetNERD contributes an accessible evaluation resource whose scale and temporal coverage broaden the available basis for studying entity-focused language processing on tweets.
summary.tldr: TweetNERD provides over 340,000 tweets and evaluation setups for entity recognition, entity linking, and end-to-end linking.

title: TweetNERD - End to End Entity Linking Benchmark for Tweets

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) defines the task of learning from a static logged dataset without continually interacting with the environment. The distribution shift between the learned policy and the behavior policy makes it necessary for the value function to stay conservative such that out-of-distribution (OOD) actions will not be severely overestimated. However, existing approaches, penalizing the unseen actions or regularizing with the behavior policy, are too pessimistic, which suppresses the generalization of the value function and hinders the performance improvement. This paper explores mild but enough conservatism for offline learning while not harming generalization. We propose Mildly Conservative Q-learning (MCQ), where OOD actions are actively trained by assigning them proper pseudo Q values. We theoretically show that MCQ induces a policy that behaves at least as well as the behavior policy and no erroneous overestimation will occur for OOD actions. Experimental results on the D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that MCQ achieves remarkable performance compared with prior work. Furthermore, MCQ shows superior generalization ability when transferring from offline to online, and significantly outperforms baselines. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dmksjfl/MCQ.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning learns from a fixed collection of logged experience without continually collecting new interactions. A learned policy may choose actions unlike those taken by the behavior policy that generated the data. Their estimated values can then become overly optimistic. The paper argues that existing safeguards often go too far, suppressing useful generalization along with erroneous estimates.

Mildly Conservative Q-learning addresses this balance by assigning suitable pseudo Q values to out-of-distribution actions and actively training on those targets. Instead of relying only on penalties for unseen actions or restrictions toward the behavior policy, it gives the value function explicit training signals for those actions.

The authors theoretically show that MCQ produces a policy performing at least as well as the behavior policy and avoids erroneous overestimation of out-of-distribution actions. Experiments on D4RL report strong performance relative to prior work. The method also shows better generalization when moving from offline training to online interaction, significantly outperforming the evaluated baselines. Together, the results support calibrating conservatism to preserve opportunities for improvement.
summary.tldr: MCQ trains unseen actions with pseudo Q targets to balance protection against overestimation with better offline reinforcement learning generalization.

title: Mildly Conservative Q-Learning for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The matching principles behind optimal transport (OT) play an increasingly important role in machine learning, a trend which can be observed when OT is used to disambiguate datasets in applications (e.g. single-cell genomics) or used to improve more complex methods (e.g. balanced attention in transformers or self-supervised learning). To scale to more challenging problems, there is a growing consensus that OT requires solvers that can operate on millions, not thousands, of points. The low-rank optimal transport (LOT) approach advocated in \cite{scetbon2021lowrank} holds several promises in that regard, and was shown to complement more established entropic regularization approaches, being able to insert itself in more complex pipelines, such as quadratic OT. LOT restricts the search for low-cost couplings to those that have a low-nonnegative rank, yielding linear time algorithms in cases of interest. However, these promises can only be fulfilled if the LOT approach is seen as a legitimate contender to entropic regularization when compared on properties of interest, where the scorecard typically includes theoretical properties (statistical complexity and relation to other methods) or practical aspects (debiasing, hyperparameter tuning, initialization). We target each of these areas in this paper in order to cement the impact of low-rank approaches in computational OT.

paragraphs: Optimal transport finds low-cost ways to match distributions or collections of points. Its growing use in machine learning creates pressure for methods that can handle millions of points. This paper examines low-rank optimal transport as an approach to making such matching computations more scalable.

Low-rank optimal transport restricts the allowed couplings, or matching plans, to those with low nonnegative rank. This structural restriction yields linear-time algorithms in cases of interest and can fit into more complex transport pipelines. The paper positions this approach alongside entropic regularization, emphasizing that computational promise must be assessed together with statistical and practical properties.

The authors address approximation, statistical complexity, connections to other methods, and practical questions involving debiasing, hyperparameter selection, and initialization. These are consequential because a scalable solver needs a well-understood relationship to the intended matching problem and usable procedures for choosing its settings. The contribution is a broader foundation for evaluating and using low-rank transport, rather than computational scalability considered in isolation.
summary.tldr: The paper develops theoretical and practical foundations for low-rank optimal transport as a scalable matching approach.

title: Low-rank Optimal Transport: Approximation, Statistics and Debiasing

abstract: In the \emph{Distance Oracle} problem, the goal is to preprocess $n$ vectors $x_1, x_2, \cdots, x_n$ in a $d$-dimensional normed space $(\mathbb{X}^d, \| \cdot \|_l)$ into a cheap data structure, so that given a query vector $q \in \mathbb{X}^d$, all distances $\| q - x_i \|_l$ to the data points $\{x_i\}_{i\in [n]}$ can be quickly approximated (faster than the trivial $\sim nd$ query time). This primitive is a basic subroutine in machine learning, data mining and similarity search applications. In the case of $\ell_p$ norms, the problem is well understood, and optimal data structures are known for most values of $p$. Our main contribution is a fast $(1\pm \varepsilon)$ distance oracle for \emph{any symmetric} norm $\|\cdot\|_l$. This class includes $\ell_p$ norms and Orlicz norms as special cases, as well as other norms used in practice, e.g. top-$k$ norms, max-mixture and sum-mixture of $\ell_p$ norms, small-support norms and the box-norm. We propose a novel data structure with $\tilde{O}(n (d + \mathrm{mmc}(l)^2 ) )$ preprocessing time and space, and $t_q = \tilde{O}(d + n \cdot \mathrm{mmc}(l)^2)$ query time, where $\mathrm{mmc}(l)$ is a complexity-measure (modulus) of the symmetric norm under consideration. When $l = \ell_{p}$ , this runtime matches the aforementioned state-of-art oracles.

paragraphs: A distance oracle preprocesses a dataset so that distances from a new query to all stored points can be approximated quickly. Directly processing every coordinate of every point takes roughly nd work for n points in d dimensions. The paper extends efficient distance-oracle constructions from familiar norm families to any symmetric norm.

The proposed data structure returns approximations within a multiplicative factor of 1 ± ε. Its scope includes ℓp and Orlicz norms, as well as top-k norms, mixtures of ℓp norms, small-support norms, and the box-norm. This matters because the distance definition can vary across applications, while the construction provides a common approach across this broader class.

Preprocessing time and storage are approximately n(d + mmc(l)²), and query time is approximately d + n·mmc(l)², with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here mmc(l) measures the complexity of the chosen symmetric norm. The efficiency therefore depends on that norm-specific quantity. For ℓp norms, the runtime matches the previously established state-of-the-art oracles, extending coverage while retaining their known efficiency in that case.
summary.tldr: A distance-oracle construction supports every symmetric norm, with efficiency governed by a norm-specific complexity measure.

title: Fast Distance Oracles for Any Symmetric Norm

abstract: The advent of deep learning has led to significant progress in monocular human reconstruction. However, existing representations, such as parametric models, voxel grids, meshes and implicit neural representations, have difficulties achieving high-quality results and real-time speed at the same time. In this paper, we propose Fourier Occupancy Field (FOF), a novel, powerful, efficient and flexible 3D geometry representation, for monocular real-time and accurate human reconstruction. A FOF represents a 3D object with a 2D field orthogonal to the view direction where at each 2D position the occupancy field of the object along the view direction is compactly represented with the first few terms of Fourier series, which retains the topology and neighborhood relation in the 2D domain. A FOF can be stored as a multi-channel image, which is compatible with 2D convolutional neural networks and can bridge the gap between 3D geometries and 2D images. A FOF is very flexible and extensible, \eg, parametric models can be easily integrated into a FOF as a prior to generate more robust results. Meshes and our FOF can be easily inter-converted. Based on FOF, we design the first 30+FPS high-fidelity real-time monocular human reconstruction framework. We demonstrate the potential of FOF on both public datasets and real captured data. The code is available for research purposes at http://cic.tju.edu.cn/faculty/likun/projects/FOF.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a human's 3D shape from a single view requires a representation that supports both detailed geometry and fast computation. The paper introduces Fourier Occupancy Field, or FOF, to address the difficulty of obtaining high-quality reconstruction at real-time speed with existing representations.

FOF organizes geometry on a 2D field perpendicular to the viewing direction. At each location, a short Fourier series describes occupancy along the corresponding depth direction. Those coefficients can be stored as channels of an image, making the representation compatible with 2D convolutional networks while preserving topology and neighborhood relationships in the 2D domain. This provides a direct connection between image-based processing and the representation of 3D shape.

The representation supports conversion to and from meshes, and can incorporate parametric models as priors for more robust results. Using FOF, the authors build a high-fidelity monocular human reconstruction framework operating above 30 frames per second. Demonstrations on public datasets and captured real data support the representation's potential to combine reconstruction quality, speed, and flexibility.
summary.tldr: FOF encodes depth occupancy as image-like Fourier coefficients, enabling high-fidelity monocular human reconstruction above 30 frames per second.

title: FOF: Learning Fourier Occupancy Field for Monocular Real-time Human Reconstruction

abstract: We introduce a multi-modes tensor clustering method that implements a fused version of the alternating least squares algorithm (Fused-Orth-ALS) for simultaneous tensor factorization and clustering. The statistical convergence rates of recovery and clustering are established when the data are a noise contaminated tensor with a latent low rank CP decomposition structure. Furthermore, we show that a modified alternating least squares algorithm can provably recover the true latent low rank factorization structure when the data form an asymmetric tensor with perturbation. Clustering consistency is also established. Finally, we illustrate the accuracy and computational efficient implementation of the Fused-Orth-ALS algorithm by using both simulations and real datasets.

paragraphs: A tensor organizes data along multiple axes, and clustering such data can involve finding groups along several of those axes. This paper introduces Fused-Orth-ALS, a method that performs tensor factorization and clustering together. Its alternating least squares procedure is designed to recover an underlying compact structure while identifying the associated groups.

The theoretical results concern noisy tensors with a latent low-rank CP decomposition. Under that structure, the authors establish statistical convergence rates for both recovery and clustering. They also show that a modified alternating least squares algorithm can recover the true latent low-rank factorization for asymmetric tensors with perturbations. These guarantees are tied to the stated tensor structure rather than applying to arbitrary multidimensional data.

The paper additionally establishes clustering consistency, connecting the estimated groups to the underlying clustering in the analyzed setting. Simulations and real datasets illustrate accuracy and computational efficiency. Together, the contributions link a joint factorization-and-clustering algorithm with theoretical recovery results, giving both statistical and computational support for analyzing structured tensor data.
summary.tldr: Fused-Orth-ALS jointly factorizes and clusters tensors, with recovery and consistency results under stated low-rank structural assumptions.

title: Fused Orthogonal Alternating Least Squares for Tensor Clustering

abstract: Causal discovery for quantitative data has been extensively studied but less is known for categorical data. We propose a novel causal model for categorical data based on a new classification model, termed classification with optimal label permutation (COLP). By design, COLP is a parsimonious classifier, which gives rise to a provably identifiable causal model. A simple learning algorithm via comparing likelihood functions of causal and anti-causal models suffices to learn the causal direction. Through experiments with synthetic and real data, we demonstrate the favorable performance of the proposed COLP-based causal model compared to state-of-the-art methods. We also make available an accompanying R package COLP, which contains the proposed causal discovery algorithm and a benchmark dataset of categorical cause-effect pairs.

By design, COLP is a parsimonious classifier, which gives rise to a provably identifiable causal model. A simple learning algorithm via comparing likelihood functions of causal and anti-causal models suffices to learn the causal direction. paragraphs: When two variables contain categories rather than numerical measurements, determining which one causes the other calls for a model suited to that data. This paper addresses that two-variable causal discovery problem. Its starting point is a new classifier called classification with optimal label permutation, or COLP, which becomes the building block for a causal model.

COLP is designed to be parsimonious: it represents the classification relationship with a compact model. The authors show that this design produces a causal model whose direction is provably identifiable. To learn the direction, their algorithm fits the causal and reverse-direction models and compares their likelihoods. The identifiability result concerns this proposed model, rather than an unrestricted ability to infer causation from any pair of categorical variables.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show favorable performance compared with leading existing methods. The authors also provide an R package containing the algorithm and a benchmark collection of categorical cause-effect pairs. Together, the model and software make the contribution both theoretical and usable: the paper explains why directional information can exist within its model and supplies a straightforward procedure for extracting it.
summary.tldr: COLP uses a compact classification model to make causal direction identifiable for categorical variable pairs and learns it by comparing directional likelihoods.

title: Bivariate Causal Discovery for Categorical Data via Classification with Optimal Label Permutation

abstract: In unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA), directly adapting from the source to the target domain usually suffers significant discrepancies and leads to insufficient alignment. Thus, many UDA works attempt to vanish the domain gap gradually and softly via various intermediate spaces, dubbed domain bridging (DB). However, for dense prediction tasks such as domain adaptive semantic segmentation (DASS), existing solutions have mostly relied on rough style transfer and how to elegantly bridge domains is still under-explored. In this work, we resort to data mixing to establish a deliberated domain bridging (DDB) for DASS, through which the joint distributions of source and target domains are aligned and interacted with each in the intermediate space. At the heart of DDB lies a dual-path domain bridging step for generating two intermediate domains using the coarse-wise and the fine-wise data mixing techniques, alongside a cross-path knowledge distillation step for taking two complementary models trained on generated intermediate samples as ‘teachers’ to develop a superior ‘student’ in a multi-teacher distillation manner. These two optimization steps work in an alternating way and reinforce each other to give rise to DDB with strong adaptation power. Extensive experiments on adaptive segmentation tasks with different settings demonstrate that our DDB significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns categories across an image, making differences between training and deployment imagery especially consequential. This paper studies unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model must transfer from a source domain to a target domain. Its starting point is that a direct transfer often leaves substantial differences insufficiently aligned.

Deliberated Domain Bridging creates intermediate domains by mixing source and target data at two levels of granularity. One path uses coarse mixing and the other uses fine mixing. Models trained on these two intermediate domains act as complementary teachers. A student then learns from both through cross-path knowledge distillation, bringing together information obtained along the two routes.

The method alternates between constructing these bridges and transferring knowledge across them. The intended benefit is a reinforcing process: intermediate training connects the domains, while distillation combines the complementary models. Experiments across different adaptive segmentation settings report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. These findings support using structured data mixing and multiple teachers to address the domain gap in dense prediction.
summary.tldr: DDB combines coarse and fine data mixing with alternating multi-teacher distillation to improve domain-adaptive segmentation.

title: Deliberated Domain Bridging for Domain Adaptive Semantic Segmentation

abstract: In offline model-based reinforcement learning (offline MBRL), we learn a dynamic model from historically collected data, and subsequently utilize the learned model and fixed datasets for policy learning, without further interacting with the environment. Offline MBRL algorithms can improve the efficiency and stability of policy learning over the model-free algorithms. However, in most of the existing offline MBRL algorithms, the learning objectives for the dynamic models and the policies are isolated from each other. Such an objective mismatch may lead to inferior performance of the learned agents. In this paper, we address this issue by developing an iterative offline MBRL framework, where we maximize a lower bound of the true expected return, by alternating between dynamic-model training and policy learning. With the proposed unified model-policy learning framework, we achieve competitive performance on a wide range of continuous-control offline reinforcement learning datasets. Source code is released at https://github.com/Shentao-YANG/AMPL_NeurIPS2022.

paragraphs: Offline model-based reinforcement learning uses previously collected data to learn how an environment changes, then uses that model and the fixed data to learn a policy. No further interaction with the environment is available. The paper examines a mismatch in many existing approaches: the objective used to train the environment model is separate from the objective used to improve the policy.

That separation can matter because improving a model according to its own training objective may not translate into better decisions. The proposed framework connects the two learning processes through a lower bound on the policy’s true expected return. It alternates between updating the dynamics model and updating the policy while pursuing this common objective.

The contribution is therefore a unified way to organize offline learning, with model training and policy improvement explicitly linked. Experiments on a broad range of continuous-control offline datasets show competitive performance. This supports the practical value of addressing objective mismatch, while the stated result remains competitive performance rather than a claim that the framework universally surpasses other offline reinforcement-learning methods.
summary.tldr: The framework alternates dynamics-model training and policy learning around a shared lower bound on expected return.

title: A Unified Framework for Alternating Offline Model Training and Policy Learning

abstract: We develop a rigorous mathematical analysis of zero-shot learning with attributes. In this setting, the goal is to label novel classes with no training data, only detectors for attributes and a description of how those attributes are correlated with the target classes, called the class-attribute matrix. We develop the first non-trivial lower bound on the worst-case error of the best map from attributes to classes for this setting, even with perfect attribute detectors. The lower bound characterizes the theoretical intrinsic difficulty of the zero-shot problem based on the available information---the class-attribute matrix---and the bound is practically computable from it. Our lower bound is tight, as we show that we can always find a randomized map from attributes to classes whose expected error is upper bounded by the value of the lower bound. We show that our analysis can be predictive of how standard zero-shot methods behave in practice, including which classes will likely be confused with others.

The lower bound characterizes the theoretical intrinsic difficulty of the zero-shot problem based on the available information---the class-attribute matrix---and the bound is practically computable from it. Our lower bound is tight, as we show that we can always find a randomized map from attributes to classes whose expected error is upper bounded by the value of the lower bound. paragraphs: Attribute-based zero-shot learning assigns examples to classes for which no training examples are available. It relies on attribute detectors and a matrix describing how attributes correlate with classes. This paper asks how much error is unavoidable given that information, even if the attribute detectors themselves work perfectly.

The authors derive a nontrivial lower bound on the worst-case error of the best mapping from attributes to classes. The bound can be computed from the class-attribute matrix, turning that matrix into a way to assess the intrinsic difficulty of the task. Perfectly identifying attributes therefore does not, by itself, settle how reliably those attributes distinguish the target classes.

The lower bound is tight: the authors show that a randomized mapping always exists whose expected error is no larger than the bound. This connects an impossibility result with an achievable guarantee. They also show that the analysis can predict practical behavior of standard zero-shot methods, including likely class confusions. The contribution helps separate difficulty inherent in the available attribute information from the behavior of a particular prediction method.
summary.tldr: A computable, tight worst-case error bound reveals the intrinsic difficulty of attribute-based zero-shot classification, even with perfect attribute detectors.

title: Tight Lower Bounds on Worst-Case Guarantees for Zero-Shot Learning with Attributes

abstract: An effective aggregation of node features into a graph-level representation via readout functions is an essential step in numerous learning tasks involving graph neural networks. Typically, readouts are simple and non-adaptive functions designed such that the resulting hypothesis space is permutation invariant. Prior work on deep sets indicates that such readouts might require complex node embeddings that can be difficult to learn via standard neighborhood aggregation schemes. Motivated by this, we investigate the potential of adaptive readouts given by neural networks that do not necessarily give rise to permutation invariant hypothesis spaces. We argue that in some problems such as binding affinity prediction where molecules are typically presented in a canonical form it might be possible to relax the constraints on permutation invariance of the hypothesis space and learn a more effective model of the affinity by employing an adaptive readout function. Our empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of neural readouts on more than 40 datasets spanning different domains and graph characteristics. Moreover, we observe a consistent improvement over standard readouts (i.e., sum, max, and mean) relative to the number of neighborhood aggregation iterations and different convolutional operators.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often need to combine representations of individual nodes into one representation of the whole graph. Standard readouts such as sum, mean, and maximum are simple and insensitive to node ordering. However, prior work suggests that these readouts can require node representations that are difficult for ordinary neighborhood aggregation to learn.

The paper investigates learned neural readouts that do not necessarily enforce invariance to every node permutation. The authors argue that relaxing this constraint may be useful in settings where inputs already have a canonical form, such as molecules used for binding-affinity prediction. A learned readout can then take on more of the work of constructing an effective graph representation.

Experiments across more than forty datasets show that neural readouts are effective across varied domains and graph properties. The authors observe consistent improvements over standard readouts across different convolution operators and numbers of neighborhood aggregation steps. The results support reconsidering the readout as a trainable modeling component, with the permissibility of relaxing permutation invariance depending on how graphs are presented in the application.
summary.tldr: Learned neural readouts improve graph prediction across many datasets, with canonical graph representations motivating relaxation of strict permutation invariance.

title: Graph Neural Networks with Adaptive Readouts

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning algorithms often use two networks for value function optimization: an online network, and a target network that tracks the online network with some delay. Using two separate networks enables the agent to hedge against issues that arise when performing bootstrapping. In this paper we endow two popular deep reinforcement learning algorithms, namely DQN and Rainbow, with updates that incentivize the online network to remain in the proximity of the target network. This improves the robustness of deep reinforcement learning in presence of noisy updates. The resultant agents, called DQN Pro and Rainbow Pro, exhibit significant performance improvements over their original counterparts on the Atari benchmark demonstrating the effectiveness of this simple idea in deep reinforcement learning. The code for our paper is available here: Github.com/amazon-research/fast-rl-with-slow-updates.
