paragraphs: Many deep reinforcement learning methods optimize value estimates using two networks. The online network learns from updates, while a target network follows it with a delay. This separation helps manage bootstrapping, in which learning uses estimates produced by the system itself. Even with this arrangement, noisy updates can disrupt the online network's learning.

The paper changes the updates so that the online network is encouraged to stay close to the target network. The slower-moving target therefore influences not only what the agent learns toward, but also how far the online network moves during learning. The authors apply this idea to DQN and Rainbow, producing the variants DQN Pro and Rainbow Pro.

The resulting agents show significantly better performance than their original counterparts on the Atari benchmark. The authors connect the improvement to greater robustness in the presence of noisy updates. The contribution is a simple modification to the relationship between two networks already used in these algorithms: restraining changes in the online network can support more effective learning, despite making that network move more cautiously.
summary.tldr: Encouraging DQN and Rainbow's online networks to remain near their target networks improves robustness to noisy updates and Atari performance.

title: Faster Deep Reinforcement Learning with Slower Online Network

abstract: For a self-driving car to operate reliably, its perceptual system must generalize to the end-user's environment --- ideally without additional annotation efforts. One potential solution is to leverage unlabeled data (e.g., unlabeled LiDAR point clouds) collected from the end-users' environments (i.e. target domain) to adapt the system to the difference between training and testing environments. While extensive research has been done on such an unsupervised domain adaptation problem, one fundamental problem lingers: there is no reliable signal in the target domain to supervise the adaptation process. To overcome this issue we observe that it is easy to collect unsupervised data from multiple traversals of repeated routes. While different from conventional unsupervised domain adaptation, this assumption is extremely realistic since many drivers share the same roads. We show that this simple additional assumption is sufficient to obtain a potent signal that allows us to perform iterative self-training of 3D object detectors on the target domain. Concretely, we generate pseudo-labels with the out-of-domain detector but reduce false positives by removing detections of supposedly mobile objects that are persistent across traversals. Further, we reduce false negatives by encouraging predictions in regions that are not persistent. We experiment with our approach on two large-scale driving datasets and show remarkable improvement in 3D object detection of cars, pedestrians, and cyclists, bringing us a step closer to generalizable autonomous driving.

The key finding is that repeated route observations can provide sufficient additional structure for useful self-training without new annotations. The approach's adaptation signal depends on the availability of those repeated traversals, which the authors argue is realistic because many drivers use the same roads.
summary.tldr: Repeated drives along the same routes provide signals that improve pseudo-labels and adapt 3D object detectors without new annotations.

title: Unsupervised Adaptation from Repeated Traversals for Autonomous Driving

abstract: We design a predictive layer for structured-output prediction (SOP) that can be plugged into any neural network guaranteeing its predictions are consistent with a set of predefined symbolic constraints. Our Semantic Probabilistic Layer (SPL) can model intricate correlations, and hard constraints, over a structured output space all while being amenable to end-to-end learning via maximum likelihood.SPLs combine exact probabilistic inference with logical reasoning in a clean and modular way, learning complex distributions and restricting their support to solutions of the constraint. As such, they can faithfully, and efficiently, model complex SOP tasks beyond the reach of alternative neuro-symbolic approaches. We empirically demonstrate that SPLs outperform these competitors in terms of accuracy on challenging SOP tasks such as hierarchical multi-label classification, pathfinding and preference learning, while retaining perfect constraint satisfaction.

paragraphs: Structured prediction produces outputs with interacting parts, and some combinations may violate known rules. This paper introduces a Semantic Probabilistic Layer that can be attached to a neural network to guarantee consistency with predefined symbolic constraints. The layer is designed to represent both complex dependencies among outputs and rules that must always be satisfied.

Its mechanism combines exact probabilistic inference with logical reasoning. The learned distribution assigns support only to outputs that satisfy the constraints, while allowing the full network to be trained end to end through maximum likelihood. This places validity inside the predictive model itself and gives the model room to learn correlations among the remaining permissible outputs.

Experiments cover hierarchical multi-label classification, pathfinding, and preference learning. The authors report higher accuracy than competing neuro-symbolic approaches while maintaining perfect constraint satisfaction. These results distinguish two aspects of success: obeying the specified rules and choosing accurate outputs among those rules' valid solutions. The paper's contribution is a modular layer that addresses both aspects within a probabilistic learning framework.
summary.tldr: Semantic Probabilistic Layers learn structured predictions while guaranteeing compliance with predefined symbolic constraints.

title: Semantic Probabilistic Layers for Neuro-Symbolic Learning

abstract: The efficient exploration of chemical space to design molecules with intended properties enables the accelerated discovery of drugs, materials, and catalysts, and is one of the most important outstanding challenges in chemistry. Encouraged by the recent surge in computer power and artificial intelligence development, many algorithms have been developed to tackle this problem. However, despite the emergence of many new approaches in recent years, comparatively little progress has been made in developing realistic benchmarks that reflect the complexity of molecular design for real-world applications. In this work, we develop a set of practical benchmark tasks relying on physical simulation of molecular systems mimicking real-life molecular design problems for materials, drugs, and chemical reactions. Additionally, we demonstrate the utility and ease of use of our new benchmark set by demonstrating how to compare the performance of several well-established families of algorithms. Overall, we believe that our benchmark suite will help move the field towards more realistic molecular design benchmarks, and move the development of inverse molecular design algorithms closer to the practice of designing molecules that solve existing problems in both academia and industry alike.

paragraphs: Inverse molecular design starts with desired properties and searches for molecules that could provide them. Many algorithms address this challenge, but evaluating them meaningfully requires tasks that reflect practical chemistry. This paper identifies a gap between the growth of design algorithms and the development of realistic benchmarks for comparing them.

Tartarus supplies benchmark tasks based on physical simulations of molecular systems. The tasks mimic design problems involving materials, drugs, and chemical reactions. This connects evaluation to simulated physical behavior relevant to intended applications, giving researchers a common setting for testing how their algorithms explore chemical space.

The authors demonstrate the benchmark suite by comparing several established families of algorithms, illustrating both its utility and ease of use. The contribution is an evaluation platform rather than a claim that molecular design has been solved. Its intended impact is to bring algorithm development closer to practical design needs in research and industry by making realistic problem settings available for systematic comparison.
summary.tldr: Tartarus benchmarks molecular-design algorithms on physically simulated tasks intended to reflect practical chemistry problems.

title: Tartarus: A Benchmarking Platform for Realistic And Practical Inverse Molecular Design

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are commonly described as being permutation equivariant with respect to node relabeling in the graph. This symmetry of GNNs is often compared to the translation equivariance of Euclidean convolution neural networks (CNNs). However, these two symmetries are fundamentally different: The translation equivariance of CNNs corresponds to symmetries of the fixed domain acting on the image signals (sometimes known as active symmetries), whereas in GNNs any permutation acts on both the graph signals and the graph domain (sometimes described as passive symmetries). In this work, we focus on the active symmetries of GNNs, by considering a learning setting where signals are supported on a fixed graph. In this case, the natural symmetries of GNNs are the automorphisms of the graph. Since real-world graphs tend to be asymmetric, we relax the notion of symmetries by formalizing approximate symmetries via graph coarsening. We present a bias-variance formula that quantifies the tradeoff between the loss in expressivity and the gain in the regularity of the learned estimator, depending on the chosen symmetry group. To illustrate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on image inpainting, traffic flow prediction, and human pose estimation with different choices of symmetries. We show theoretically and empirically that the best generalization performance can be achieved by choosing a suitably larger group than the graph automorphism, but smaller than the permutation group.

paragraphs: Graph networks usually treat node relabeling consistently: changing node names changes the output labels accordingly. This paper distinguishes that property from transformations of a signal on a fixed domain. When the graph stays fixed, the relevant exact symmetries are its automorphisms, transformations that preserve the graph itself. Real graphs often have few such symmetries.

The authors therefore study approximate symmetries, formalized through graph coarsening. This creates a way to impose useful shared structure even when the original graph lacks exact symmetry. A bias-variance formula describes the resulting tradeoff: stronger symmetry constraints can make an estimator more regular, while also reducing the range of functions it can express.

Together with the theory, they show that the best generalization can come from a suitably chosen group larger than the exact automorphism group but smaller than all node permutations. The result makes the amount of imposed symmetry a meaningful modeling choice.
summary.tldr: Approximate graph symmetries offer a tunable tradeoff between expressivity and regularity that can improve generalization beyond exact graph symmetries.

title: Approximately Equivariant Graph Networks

abstract: Generalizable implicit neural representation (INR) enables a single continuous function, i.e., a coordinate-based neural network, to represent multiple data instances by modulating its weights or intermediate features using latent codes. However, the expressive power of the state-of-the-art modulation is limited due to its inability to localize and capture fine-grained details of data entities such as specific pixels and rays. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework for generalizable INR that combines a transformer encoder with a locality-aware INR decoder. The transformer encoder predicts a set of latent tokens from a data instance to encode local information into each latent token. The locality-aware INR decoder extracts a modulation vector by selectively aggregating the latent tokens via cross-attention for a coordinate input and then predicts the output by progressively decoding with coarse-to-fine modulation through multiple frequency bandwidths. The selective token aggregation and the multi-band feature modulation enable us to learn locality-aware representation in spatial and spectral aspects, respectively. Our framework significantly outperforms previous generalizable INRs and validates the usefulness of the locality-aware latents for downstream tasks such as image generation.

paragraphs: A generalizable implicit neural representation uses a coordinate-based network to represent multiple data instances, adapting the network with latent codes. The paper identifies a weakness in existing adaptation methods: they struggle to associate those codes with specific local details, such as individual pixels or rays.

The proposed framework combines a transformer encoder with a decoder designed around locality. The encoder produces several latent tokens that capture local information. For each queried coordinate, cross-attention selects and combines the relevant tokens into a modulation vector. The decoder then uses modulation across multiple frequency bands to build its prediction progressively from coarse structure to fine detail.

These two mechanisms address different aspects of detail: token selection determines which spatial information matters, while frequency-based modulation controls the scales of information being decoded. The authors report substantial improvements over previous generalizable implicit representations. They also demonstrate that the learned local latent representations are useful for downstream tasks such as image generation.
summary.tldr: Coordinate-specific token selection and coarse-to-fine modulation improve the local detail captured by generalizable implicit neural representations.

title: Locality-Aware Generalizable Implicit Neural Representation

abstract: Diffusion models have recently shown remarkable success in high-quality image generation. Sometimes, however, a pre-trained diffusion model exhibits partial misalignment in the sense that the model can generate good images, but it sometimes outputs undesirable images. If so, we simply need to prevent the generation of the bad images, and we call this task censoring. In this work, we present censored generation with a pre-trained diffusion model using a reward model trained on minimal human feedback. We show that censoring can be accomplished with extreme human feedback efficiency and that labels generated with a mere few minutes of human feedback are sufficient.

In this work, we present censored generation with a pre-trained diffusion model using a reward model trained on minimal human feedback. We show that censoring can be accomplished with extreme human feedback efficiency and that labels generated with a mere few minutes of human feedback are sufficient.

paragraphs: A diffusion model can produce appealing images while still occasionally generating outputs that people do not want. This paper studies that particular situation: a pretrained generator already has useful capabilities, but its output only partly matches human preferences. The authors call the task of preventing those undesirable generations censoring.

Their approach uses a reward model trained with a small amount of human feedback to support censored generation from the pretrained diffusion model. The feedback supplies judgments about desirable and undesirable outputs. This gives the censoring process a learned signal for distinguishing acceptable images from the unwanted part of the generator’s output.

The reported finding is that labels collected through only a few minutes of human feedback can be sufficient for this task. Its significance is the small human effort needed to address partial misalignment in the studied setting. The result concerns censoring an already capable generator; it does not establish that a few minutes of feedback can resolve every kind of mismatch between image generation and human preferences.
summary.tldr: A reward model learned from a few minutes of human feedback can support suppressing unwanted outputs from an already capable diffusion model.

title: Censored Sampling of Diffusion Models Using 3 Minutes of Human Feedback

abstract: Neural sequence models based on the transformer architecture have demonstrated remarkable \emph{in-context learning} (ICL) abilities, where they can perform new tasks when prompted with training and test examples, without any parameter update to the model. This work first provides a comprehensive statistical theory for transformers to perform ICL. Concretely, we show that transformers can implement a broad class of standard machine learning algorithms in context, such as least squares, ridge regression, Lasso, learning generalized linear models, and gradient descent on two-layer neural networks, with near-optimal predictive power on various in-context data distributions. Using an efficient implementation of in-context gradient descent as the underlying mechanism, our transformer constructions admit mild size bounds, and can be learned with polynomially many pretraining sequences. Building on these ``base'' ICL algorithms, intriguingly, we show that transformers can implement more complex ICL procedures involving \emph{in-context algorithm selection}, akin to what a statistician can do in real life---A \emph{single} transformer can adaptively select different base ICL algorithms---or even perform qualitatively different tasks---on different input sequences, without any explicit prompting of the right algorithm or task. We both establish this in theory by explicit constructions, and also observe this phenomenon experimentally. In theory, we construct two general mechanisms for algorithm selection with concrete examples: pre-ICL testing, and post-ICL validation. As an example, we use the post-ICL validation mechanism to construct a transformer that can perform nearly Bayes-optimal ICL on a challenging task---noisy linear models with mixed noise levels. Experimentally, we demonstrate the strong in-context algorithm selection capabilities of standard transformer architectures.

title: Transformers as Statisticians: Provable In-Context Learning with In-Context Algorithm Selection

abstract: Stochastic gradients closely relate to both optimization and generalization of deep neural networks (DNNs). Some works attempted to explain the success of stochastic optimization for deep learning by the arguably heavy-tail properties of gradient noise, while other works presented theoretical and empirical evidence against the heavy-tail hypothesis on gradient noise. Unfortunately, formal statistical tests for analyzing the structure and heavy tails of stochastic gradients in deep learning are still under-explored. In this paper, we mainly make two contributions. First, we conduct formal statistical tests on the distribution of stochastic gradients and gradient noise across both parameters and iterations. Our statistical tests reveal that dimension-wise gradients usually exhibit power-law heavy tails, while iteration-wise gradients and stochastic gradient noise caused by minibatch training usually do not exhibit power-law heavy tails. Second, we further discover that the covariance spectra of stochastic gradients have the power-law structures overlooked by previous studies and present its theoretical implications for training of DNNs. While previous studies believed that the anisotropic structure of stochastic gradients matters to deep learning, they did not expect the gradient covariance can have such an elegant mathematical structure. Our work challenges the existing belief and provides novel insights on the structure of stochastic gradients in deep learning.

paragraphs: Arguments about why stochastic optimization works in deep learning have sometimes focused on whether gradient noise has heavy tails. This paper investigates that question with formal statistical tests and emphasizes that the answer depends on how gradients are examined: across parameter dimensions or across training iterations.

The tests find that dimension-wise gradients usually show power-law heavy tails. In contrast, iteration-wise gradients and gradient noise introduced by minibatch training usually do not. These qualified findings distinguish properties of the gradients themselves from properties of their noise, and distinguish variation across coordinates from variation over time.

The authors also identify power-law structure in the covariance spectra of stochastic gradients and discuss theoretical implications for network training. This adds a more specific description to the broader observation that gradient variability differs across directions. Together, the results suggest that understanding stochastic gradients requires attention to their organization across dimensions and correlations, rather than assigning one heavy-tail label to every aspect of the training process.
summary.tldr: Statistical tests distinguish heavy tails across gradient dimensions from their usual absence across iterations and reveal power-law covariance structure.

title: On the Overlooked Structure of Stochastic Gradients

abstract: Persistent homology (PH) provides topological descriptors for geometric data, such as weighted graphs, which are interpretable, stable to perturbations, and invariant under, e.g., relabeling. Most applications of PH focus on the one-parameter case---where the descriptors summarize the changes in topology of data as it is filtered by a single quantity of interest---and there is now a wide array of methods enabling the use of one-parameter PH descriptors in data science, which rely on the stable vectorization of these descriptors as elements of a Hilbert space. Although the multiparameter PH (MPH) of data that is filtered by several quantities of interest encodes much richer information than its one-parameter counterpart, the scarceness of stability results for MPH descriptors has so far limited the available options for the stable vectorization of MPH. In this paper, we aim to bring together the best of both worlds by showing how the interpretation of signed barcodes---a recent family of MPH descriptors---as signed Radon measures leads to natural extensions of vectorization strategies from one parameter to multiple parameters. The resulting feature vectors are easy to define and to compute, and provably stable. While, as a proof of concept, we focus on simple choices of signed barcodes and vectorizations, we already see notable performance improvements when comparing our feature vectors to state-of-the-art topology-based methods on various types of data.

Using several filtering quantities can capture richer information, but converting those multiparameter descriptions into useful numerical vectors has been constrained by limited stability results. Stability matters because small changes in the input should not cause uncontrolled changes in the resulting representation.

This mathematical interpretation allows vectorization strategies from the one-parameter setting to extend naturally to multiple parameters. The contribution supplies both a principled route to stable multiparameter features and initial evidence that the extra topological information can be useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Interpreting signed barcodes as measures yields computable, provably stable feature vectors for multiparameter persistent homology.

title: Stable Vectorization of Multiparameter Persistent Homology using Signed Barcodes as Measures

abstract: Distributional shifts pose a significant challenge to achieving robustness in contemporary machine learning. To overcome this challenge, robust satisficing (RS) seeks a robust solution to an unspecified distributional shift while achieving a utility above a desired threshold. This paper focuses on the problem of RS in contextual Bayesian optimization when there is a discrepancy between the true and reference distributions of the context. We propose a novel robust Bayesian satisficing algorithm called RoBOS for noisy black-box optimization. Our algorithm guarantees sublinear lenient regret under certain assumptions on the amount of distribution shift. In addition, we define a weaker notion of regret called robust satisficing regret, in which our algorithm achieves a sublinear upper bound independent of the amount of distribution shift. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we apply it to various learning problems and compare it to other approaches, such as distributionally robust optimization.

Our algorithm guarantees sublinear lenient regret under certain assumptions on the amount of distribution shift. In addition, we define a weaker notion of regret called robust satisficing regret, in which our algorithm achieves a sublinear upper bound independent of the amount of distribution shift. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, we apply it to various learning problems and compare it to other approaches, such as distributionally robust optimization.

paragraphs: When the distribution of operating conditions changes, a decision that looked good under a reference distribution may become unreliable. Robust satisficing addresses this by seeking robustness to an unspecified distributional shift while maintaining utility above a desired threshold. This paper brings that objective into contextual Bayesian optimization with noisy black-box evaluations.

The proposed RoBOS algorithm handles a discrepancy between the true distribution of context and the reference distribution used for optimization. Its goal is organized around meeting a desired level of utility under distributional uncertainty. This gives the optimization problem a threshold-based notion of success, alongside the need to learn from noisy observations of an unknown objective.

The authors prove sublinear lenient regret under assumptions about the amount of distribution shift. They also introduce a weaker measure, robust satisficing regret, and prove a sublinear upper bound that is independent of the shift amount. The distinction matters: the shift-independent statement uses the weaker criterion. Applications to several learning problems and comparisons with approaches including distributionally robust optimization are used to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.
summary.tldr: RoBOS targets satisfactory utility under context-distribution shifts, with conditional lenient-regret guarantees and a shift-independent bound for a weaker regret measure.

title: Robust Bayesian Satisficing

abstract: 3D spatial understanding is highly valuable in the context of semantic modeling of environments, agents, and their relationships. Semantic modeling approaches employed on monocular video often ingest outputs from off-the-shelf SLAM/SfM pipelines, which are anecdotally observed to perform poorly or fail completely on some fraction of the videos of interest. These target videos may vary widely in complexity of scenes, activities, camera trajectory, etc. Unfortunately, such semantically-rich video data often comes with no ground-truth 3D information, and in practice it is prohibitively costly or impossible to obtain ground truth reconstructions or camera pose post-hoc. This paper proposes a novel evaluation protocol, Object Reprojection Error (ORE) to benchmark camera trajectories; ORE computes reprojection error for static objects within the video and requires only lightweight object tracklet annotations. These annotations are easy to gather on new or existing video, enabling ORE to be calculated on essentially arbitrary datasets. We show that ORE maintains high rank correlation with standard metrics based on groundtruth. Leveraging ORE, we source videos and annotations from Ego4D-EgoTracks, resulting in EgoStatic, a large-scale diverse dataset for evaluating camera trajectories in-the-wild.

The contribution combines a more accessible evaluation signal with a dataset built around that signal.
summary.tldr: ORE evaluates camera trajectories using lightweight static-object tracks and correlates strongly with rankings from ground-truth-based metrics.

title: Object Reprojection Error (ORE): Camera pose benchmarks from lightweight tracking annotations

abstract: Real-world geometry and 3D vision tasks are replete with challenging symmetries that defy tractable analytical expression. In this paper, we introduce Neural Isometries, an autoencoder framework which learns to map the observation space to a general-purpose latent space wherein encodings are related by isometries whenever their corresponding observations are geometrically related in world space. Specifically, we regularize the latent space such that maps between encodings preserve a learned inner product and commute with a learned functional operator, in the same manner as rigid-body transformations commute with the Laplacian. This approach forms an effective backbone for self-supervised representation learning, and we demonstrate that a simple off-the-shelf equivariant network operating in the pre-trained latent space can achieve results on par with meticulously-engineered, handcrafted networks designed to handle complex, nonlinear symmetries. Furthermore, isometric maps capture information about the respective transformations in world space, and we show that this allows us to regress camera poses directly from the coefficients of the maps between encodings of adjacent views of a scene.

paragraphs: Geometric transformations in real-world vision can be difficult to describe with manageable equations. Neural Isometries addresses this by learning a representation in which geometrically related observations are connected by simpler, structure-preserving transformations. An autoencoder maps observations into this latent space, moving part of the difficulty into representation learning.

The training constraints make transformations between encodings preserve a learned inner product and commute with a learned functional operator. In plain terms, the transformations must respect both a learned notion of geometry and an additional operation on the representation. The construction parallels the relationship between rigid transformations and the Laplacian.

The learned space supports self-supervised representation learning. A standard equivariant network operating within it achieves results comparable to carefully handcrafted networks for complex nonlinear symmetries. The transformations between encodings also retain information about motion in the world: the authors use their coefficients to predict camera poses between adjacent scene views. This shows that the representation can support both downstream processing and direct estimation of geometric relationships.
summary.tldr: Neural Isometries learns a latent space where complex geometric transformations become structured maps usable for equivariant learning and camera-pose estimation.

title: Neural Isometries: Taming Transformations for Equivariant ML

abstract: How can we test AI performance? This question seems trivial, but it isn't. Standard benchmarks often have problems such as in-distribution and small-size test sets, oversimplified metrics, unfair comparisons, and short-term outcome pressure. As a consequence, good performance on standard benchmarks does not guarantee success in real-world scenarios. To address these problems, we present Touchstone, a large-scale collaborative segmentation benchmark of 9 types of abdominal organs. This benchmark is based on 5,195 training CT scans from 76 hospitals around the world and 5,903 testing CT scans from 11 additional hospitals. This diverse test set enhances the statistical significance of benchmark results and rigorously evaluates AI algorithms across various out-of-distribution scenarios. We invited 14 inventors of 19 AI algorithms to train their algorithms, while our team, as a third party, independently evaluated these algorithms on three test sets. In addition, we also evaluated pre-existing AI frameworks---which, differing from algorithms, are more flexible and can support different algorithms—including MONAI from NVIDIA, nnU-Net from DKFZ, and numerous other open-source frameworks. We are committed to expanding this benchmark to encourage more innovation of AI algorithms for the medical domain.

paragraphs: Touchstone addresses whether medical image benchmarks provide convincing evidence of performance beyond their own test sets. Small or closely matched test sets, simplified metrics, and unfair comparisons can make strong benchmark results an unreliable guide to real-world success. The authors introduce a large collaborative benchmark for segmenting nine types of abdominal organs.

The benchmark uses 5,195 training CT scans from 76 hospitals and 5,903 testing scans from 11 additional hospitals. This separation and diversity support evaluation under multiple distribution shifts and strengthen the statistical significance of comparisons. The evaluation therefore examines performance across varied testing conditions rather than relying only on data similar to the training set.

The authors invited 14 inventors to train 19 algorithms, while an independent team evaluated them on three test sets. They also assessed existing frameworks, including MONAI and nnU-Net, distinguishing these adaptable systems from individual algorithms. The contribution is an evaluation resource and process designed to improve the credibility of medical-segmentation comparisons, with continued expansion intended to support further algorithm development.
summary.tldr: Touchstone evaluates abdominal-organ segmentation through large, diverse hospital datasets and independent testing of inventor-trained algorithms.

title: Touchstone Benchmark: Are We on the Right Way for Evaluating AI Algorithms for Medical Segmentation?

abstract: Policy Mirror Descent (PMD) stands as a versatile algorithmic framework encompassing several seminal policy gradient algorithms such as natural policy gradient, with connections with state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms such as TRPO and PPO. PMD can be seen as a soft Policy Iteration algorithm implementing regularized 1-step greedy policy improvement. However, 1-step greedy policies might not be the best choice and recent remarkable empirical successes in RL such as AlphaGo and AlphaZero have demonstrated that greedy approaches with respect to multiple steps outperform their 1-step counterpart. In this work, we propose a new class of PMD algorithms called $h$-PMD which incorporates multi-step greedy policy improvement with lookahead depth $h$ to the PMD update rule. To solve discounted infinite horizon Markov Decision Processes with discount factor $\gamma$, we show that $h$-PMD which generalizes the standard PMD enjoys a faster dimension-free $\gamma^h$-linear convergence rate, contingent on the computation of multi-step greedy policies. We propose an inexact version of $h$-PMD where lookahead action values are estimated. Under a generative model, we establish a sample complexity for $h$-PMD which improves over prior work. Finally, we extend our result to linear function approximation to scale to large state spaces. Under suitable assumptions, our sample complexity only involves dependence on the dimension of the feature map space instead of the state space size.

Its usual update makes a regularized one-step greedy improvement. This paper extends that update to consider several steps ahead before choosing how to improve the policy.

The resulting h-PMD algorithm uses lookahead depth h. summary.tldr: h-PMD adds multistep lookahead to Policy Mirror Descent and proves faster convergence and improved sample complexity under stated computational and modeling assumptions.

title: Policy Mirror Descent with Lookahead

abstract: In the Inertial Confinement Fusion (ICF) process, roughly a 2mm spherical shell made of high-density carbon is used as a target for laser beams, which compress and heat it to energy levels needed for high fusion yield in nuclear fusion. These shells are polished meticulously to meet the standards for a fusion shot. However, the polishing of these shells involves multiple stages, with each stage taking several hours. To make sure that the polishing process is advancing in the right direction, we are able to measure the shell surface roughness. This measurement, however, is very labor-intensive, time-consuming, and requires a human operator. To help improve the polishing process we have released the first dataset to the public that consists of raw vibration signals with the corresponding polishing surface roughness changes. We show that this dataset can be used with a variety of neural network based methods for prediction of the change of polishing surface roughness, hence eliminating the need for the time-consuming manual process. This is the first dataset of its kind to be released in public and its use will allow the operator to make any necessary changes to the ICF polishing process for optimal results. This dataset contains the raw vibration data of multiple polishing runs with their extracted statistical features and the corresponding surface roughness values. Additionally, to generalize the prediction models to different polishing conditions, we also apply domain adaptation techniques to improve prediction accuracy for conditions unseen by the trained model. The dataset is available in \url{https://junzeliu.github.io/Diamond-Polishing-Dataset/}.

The paper releases a dataset linking raw polishing vibration signals with surface roughness measurements and changes. These paired observations support learning a relationship between signals recorded during polishing and the surface condition that operators need to monitor.

The authors demonstrate that several neural-network methods can predict changes in surface roughness from the dataset, offering a way to replace the manual measurement step. They also apply domain adaptation to improve prediction under polishing conditions unseen during training. The dataset's practical contribution is to make this prediction problem publicly accessible and support timely adjustments to the polishing process using information from vibration signals.
summary.tldr: A public dataset pairs polishing vibrations with fusion-shell surface roughness, enabling neural prediction of polishing progress.

title: Nuclear Fusion Diamond Polishing Dataset

abstract: Advancements in multimodal learning, particularly in video understanding and generation, require high-quality video-text datasets for improved model performance. Vript addresses this issue with a meticulously annotated corpus of 12K high-resolution videos, offering detailed, dense, and script-like captions for over 420K clips. Each clip has a caption of ~145 words, which is over 10x longer than most video-text datasets. Unlike captions only documenting static content in previous datasets, we enhance video captioning to video scripting by documenting not just the content, but also the camera operations, which include the shot types (medium shot, close-up, etc) and camera movements (panning, tilting, etc). By utilizing the Vript, we explore three training paradigms of aligning more text with the video modality rather than clip-caption pairs. This results in Vriptor, a top-performing video captioning model among open-source models, comparable to GPT-4V in performance. Vriptor is also a powerful model capable of end-to-end generation of dense and detailed captions for long videos. Moreover, we introduce Vript-Hard, a benchmark consisting of three video understanding tasks that are more challenging than existing benchmarks: Vript-HAL is the first benchmark evaluating action and object hallucinations in video LLMs, Vript-RR combines reasoning with retrieval resolving question ambiguity in long-video QAs, and Vript-ERO is a new task to evaluate the temporal understanding of events in long videos rather than actions in short videos in previous works. All code, models, and datasets are available in https://github.com/mutonix/Vript.

Together, the dataset, model, and benchmark address both richer video-language training and more demanding evaluation of the resulting capabilities.
summary.tldr: Vript provides detailed video scripts, supports a strong captioning model, and introduces tests of hallucination, reasoning, and long-video temporal understanding.

title: Vript: A Video Is Worth Thousands of Words

abstract: As a prominent category of imitation learning methods, adversarial imitation learning (AIL) has garnered significant practical success powered by neural network approximation. However, existing theoretical studies on AIL are primarily limited to simplified scenarios such as tabular and linear function approximation and involve complex algorithmic designs that hinder practical implementation, highlighting a gap between theory and practice. In this paper, we explore the theoretical underpinnings of online AIL with general function approximation. We introduce a new method called optimization-based AIL (OPT-AIL), which centers on performing online optimization for reward functions and optimism-regularized Bellman error minimization for Q-value functions. Theoretically, we prove that OPT-AIL achieves polynomial expert sample complexity and interaction complexity for learning near-expert policies. To our best knowledge, OPT-AIL is the first provably efficient AIL method with general function approximation. Practically, OPT-AIL only requires the approximate optimization of two objectives, thereby facilitating practical implementation. Empirical studies demonstrate that OPT-AIL outperforms previous state-of-the-art deep AIL methods in several challenging tasks.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning learns behavior from expert demonstrations and has worked well with neural networks in practice. Its theoretical guarantees, however, have largely focused on simpler tabular or linear models, sometimes with algorithms that are difficult to implement. OPT-AIL aims to close that gap by studying online adversarial imitation learning with general function approximation.

The method combines online optimization of reward functions with optimism-regularized Bellman-error minimization for Q-value functions. The latter functions assess the value of actions, and their optimization incorporates the method's optimism term. Practically, the algorithm requires approximate optimization of only two objectives, making its theoretical construction more directly usable than a complex sequence of specialized procedures.

The authors prove polynomial bounds on the expert samples and environment interactions needed to learn near-expert policies. To their knowledge, this is the first provably efficient adversarial imitation learning method with general function approximation. Experiments also show better performance than previous leading deep imitation-learning methods on several challenging tasks, pairing the efficiency analysis with empirical evidence of practical effectiveness.
summary.tldr: OPT-AIL combines a practical two-objective algorithm with polynomial sample and interaction guarantees for imitation learning using general function approximation.

title: Provably and Practically Efficient Adversarial Imitation Learning with General Function Approximation

abstract: We consider a constrained Markov Decision Problem (CMDP) where the goal of an agent is to maximize the expected discounted sum of rewards over an infinite horizon while ensuring that the expected discounted sum of costs exceeds a certain threshold. Building on the idea of momentum-based acceleration, we develop the Primal-Dual Accelerated Natural Policy Gradient (PD-ANPG) algorithm that ensures an $\epsilon$ global optimality gap and $\epsilon$ constraint violation with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((1-\gamma)^{-7}\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for general parameterized policies where $\gamma$ denotes the discount factor. This improves the state-of-the-art sample complexity in general parameterized CMDPs by a factor of $\mathcal{O}((1-\gamma)^{-1}\epsilon^{-2})$ and achieves the theoretical lower bound in $\epsilon^{-1}$.
originalAbstract: We consider a constrained Markov Decision Problem (CMDP) where the goal of an agent is to maximize the expected discounted sum of rewards over an infinite horizon while ensuring that the expected discounted sum of costs exceeds a certain threshold. Building on the idea of momentum-based acceleration, we develop the Primal-Dual Accelerated Natural Policy Gradient (PD-ANPG) algorithm that ensures an $\epsilon$ global optimality gap and $\epsilon$ constraint violation with $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}((1-\gamma)^{-7}\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for general parameterized policies where $\gamma$ denotes the discount factor. paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with an objective and a constraint that both extend over an infinite horizon. The agent seeks a large expected discounted reward while keeping its expected discounted cost above a specified threshold. This lower-bound requirement is part of the stated problem. Discounting determines how strongly future rewards and costs contribute to these totals.

The authors introduce Primal-Dual Accelerated Natural Policy Gradient, or PD-ANPG, using momentum-based acceleration. For general parameterized policies, they establish an epsilon global optimality gap and epsilon constraint violation with sample complexity of order (1−gamma)⁻⁷ epsilon⁻², up to logarithmic factors. Here gamma is the discount factor, and epsilon specifies the desired accuracy for both performance and constraint satisfaction.

The bound improves the previous state of the art by a factor of order (1−gamma)⁻¹ epsilon⁻². It also matches the theoretical lower bound in its dependence on inverse accuracy. This is a specific sample-efficiency result: the claimed optimality concerns the epsilon dependence, while the bound separately retains its stated dependence on the discount factor.
summary.tldr: PD-ANPG improves sample-complexity guarantees for constrained reinforcement learning and matches the theoretical lower bound in accuracy dependence.

title: Sample-Efficient Constrained Reinforcement Learning with General Parameterization

abstract: In reinforcement learning with image-based inputs, it is crucial to establish a robust and generalizable state representation. Recent advancements in metric learning, such as deep bisimulation metric approaches, have shown promising results in learning structured low-dimensional representation space from pixel observations, where the distance between states is measured based on task-relevant features. However, these approaches face challenges in demanding generalization tasks and scenarios with non-informative rewards. This is because they fail to capture sufficient long-term information in the learned representations. To address these challenges, we propose a novel State Chrono Representation (SCR) approach. SCR augments state metric-based representations by incorporating extensive temporal information into the update step of bisimulation metric learning. It learns state distances within a temporal framework that considers both future dynamics and cumulative rewards over current and long-term future states. Our learning strategy effectively incorporates future behavioral information into the representation space without introducing a significant number of additional parameters for modeling dynamics. Extensive experiments conducted in DeepMind Control and Meta-World environments demonstrate that SCR achieves better performance comparing to other recent metric-based methods in demanding generalization tasks. The codes of SCR are available in https://github.com/jianda-chen/SCR.

paragraphs: An agent learning from images needs a compact state representation that preserves what matters for its task. Metric-learning approaches organize states by task-relevant similarity, but the paper argues that existing methods can miss enough long-term information to struggle with difficult generalization settings and rewards that provide little useful guidance.

State Chrono Representation extends bisimulation-based metric learning by adding temporal information to the update process. Its state distances account for future dynamics and cumulative rewards across current and longer-term future states. The resulting representation is intended to reflect future behavior as well as the information captured by existing state metrics.

The authors report incorporating this information without a significant increase in parameters for modeling dynamics. The contribution is therefore a change in what the representation learns to preserve: longer-term consequences become part of the similarity structure used to support control from visual observations.
summary.tldr: State Chrono Representation adds long-term dynamics and reward information to state metrics, improving visual reinforcement-learning generalization.

title: State Chrono Representation for Enhancing Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Vision-language models have shown impressive progress in recent years. However, existing models are largely limited to turn-based interactions, where each turn must be stepped (i.e., prompted) by the user. Open-ended, asynchronous interactions, where an AI model may proactively deliver timely responses or feedback based on the unfolding situation in real-time, are an open challenge. In this work, we present the QEVD benchmark and dataset, which explores human-AI interaction in the challenging, yet controlled, real-world domain of fitness coaching – a task which intrinsically requires monitoring live user activity and providing immediate feedback. The benchmark requires vision-language models to recognize complex human actions, identify possible mistakes, and provide appropriate feedback in real-time. Our experiments reveal the limitations of existing state-of-the-art vision-language models for such asynchronous situated interactions. Motivated by this, we propose a simple end-to-end streaming baseline that can respond asynchronously to human actions with appropriate feedback at the appropriate time.

However, existing models are largely limited to turn-based interactions, where each turn must be stepped (i.e., prompted) by the user. Open-ended, asynchronous interactions, where an AI model may proactively deliver timely responses or feedback based on the unfolding situation in real-time, are an open challenge. In this work, we present the QEVD benchmark and dataset, which explores human-AI interaction in the challenging, yet controlled, real-world domain of fitness coaching – a task which intrinsically requires monitoring live user activity and providing immediate feedback. The benchmark requires vision-language models to recognize complex human actions, identify possible mistakes, and provide appropriate feedback in real-time. Our experiments reveal the limitations of existing state-of-the-art vision-language models for such asynchronous situated interactions. Motivated by this, we propose a simple end-to-end streaming baseline that can respond asynchronously to human actions with appropriate feedback at the appropriate time.

paragraphs: Most vision-language interactions require a user to prompt each response. Live coaching introduces another requirement: a system must monitor an unfolding activity and decide when feedback is useful. This paper uses fitness coaching to study that form of asynchronous interaction in a real-world setting that is challenging but controlled.

The authors introduce the QEVD dataset and benchmark. Models must recognize complex human actions, identify possible mistakes, and provide suitable feedback in real time. Success therefore depends on both message content and timing. Recognizing an action alone is insufficient for the benchmark's broader goal of delivering relevant guidance during the activity.

Experiments reveal limitations in existing state-of-the-art vision-language models on these interaction demands. The authors respond with a simple end-to-end streaming baseline that can react asynchronously to human actions with appropriate feedback at an appropriate moment. The contribution combines an evaluation setting with a concrete baseline, making proactive response timing part of the modeling problem alongside visual understanding and language generation.
summary.tldr: QEVD evaluates real-time fitness coaching, and a streaming baseline addresses the joint challenge of choosing useful feedback and delivering it at the right time.

title: What to Say and When to Say it: Live Fitness Coaching as a Testbed for Situated Interaction

abstract: Electronic health records (EHRs) are stored in various database systems with different database models on heterogeneous storage architectures, such as relational databases, document stores, or graph databases. These different database models have a big impact on query complexity and performance. While this has been a known fact in database research, its implications for the growing number of Text-to-Query systems have surprisingly not been investigated so far.In this paper, we present SM3-Text-to-Query, the first multi-model medical Text-to-Query benchmark based on synthetic patient data from Synthea, following the SNOMED-CT taxonomy---a widely used knowledge graph ontology covering medical terminology. SM3-Text-to-Query provides data representations for relational databases (PostgreSQL), document stores (MongoDB), and graph databases (Neo4j and GraphDB (RDF)), allowing the evaluation across four popular query languages, namely SQL, MQL, Cypher, and SPARQL.We systematically and manually develop 408 template questions, which we augment to construct a benchmark of 10K diverse natural language question/query pairs for these four query languages (40K pairs overall). On our dataset, we evaluate several common in-context-learning (ICL) approaches for a set of representative closed and open-source LLMs.Our evaluation sheds light on the trade-offs between database models and query languages for different ICL strategies and LLMs. Last,SM3-Text-to-Query is easily extendable to additional query languages or real, standard-based patient databases.

These choices affect query complexity and performance, yet their implications for systems translating natural language into queries have received little investigation. SM3-Text-to-Query creates a benchmark for examining those differences across several database representations.

The benchmark uses synthetic patient data from Synthea and follows the SNOMED-CT medical terminology ontology. It provides representations for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Neo4j, and GraphDB, supporting SQL, MQL, Cypher, and SPARQL. The authors manually develop 408 question templates and augment them into 10,000 natural-language question/query pairs per language, giving 40,000 pairs overall.

Using this resource, the authors evaluate common in-context-learning approaches with representative open-source and closed language models. The evaluation examines how database models and query languages interact with the chosen model and prompting strategy. The resulting contribution is a way to study these trade-offs within one medical benchmark. Its design also supports extension to further query languages or real patient databases that follow standards.
summary.tldr: SM3-Text-to-Query enables medical natural-language query evaluation across four query languages using 40,000 synthetic question/query pairs.

title: SM3-Text-to-Query: Synthetic Multi-Model Medical Text-to-Query Benchmark

abstract: Histopathology Whole Slide Image (WSI) analysis serves as the gold standard for clinical cancer diagnosis in the daily routines of doctors. To develop computer-aided diagnosis model for histopathology WSIs, previous methods typically employ Multi-Instance Learning to enable slide-level prediction given only slide-level labels.Among these models, vanilla attention mechanisms without pairwise interactions have traditionally been employed but are unable to model contextual information. More recently, self-attention models have been utilized to address this issue. To alleviate the computational complexity of long sequences in large WSIs, methods like HIPT use region-slicing, and TransMIL employs Nystr\"{o}mformer as an approximation of full self-attention. Both approaches suffer from suboptimal performance due to the loss of key information. Moreover, their use of absolute positional embedding struggles to effectively handle long contextual dependencies in shape-varying WSIs.In this paper, we first analyze how the low-rank nature of the long-sequence attention matrix constrains the representation ability of WSI modelling. Then, we demonstrate that the rank of attention matrix can be improved by focusing on local interactions via a local attention mask. Our analysis shows that the local mask aligns with the attention patterns in the lower layers of the Transformer. Furthermore, the local attention mask can be implemented during chunked attention calculation, reducing the quadratic computational complexity to linear with a small local bandwidth. Additionally, this locality helps the model generalize to unseen or under-fitted positions more easily.Building on this, we propose a local-global hybrid Transformer for both computational acceleration and local-global information interactions modelling. Our method, Long-contextual MIL (LongMIL), is evaluated through extensive experiments on various WSI tasks to validate its superiority in: 1) overall performance, 2) memory usage and speed, and 3) extrapolation ability compared to previous methods.

paragraphs: Whole-slide pathology images contain long sequences of visual information, making contextual modeling computationally demanding. Existing methods may divide slides into regions or approximate full attention, potentially losing useful information. This paper investigates how the low rank of long-sequence attention matrices constrains representation and uses that analysis to motivate a different attention design.

The approach connects efficiency to representation quality: local structure is used both to manage long inputs and to improve how their information is modeled.
summary.tldr: LongMIL combines local and global attention to improve whole-slide image modeling, efficiency, and extrapolation.

title: Rethinking Transformer for Long Contextual Histopathology Whole Slide Image Analysis

abstract: Existing Vision-Language Compositionality (VLC) benchmarks like SugarCrepe are formulated as image-to-text retrieval problems, where, given an image, the models need to select between the correct textual description and a synthetic hard negative text. In this work, we present the Bidirectional Vision-Language Compositionality (BiVLC) dataset. The novelty of BiVLC is to add a synthetic hard negative image generated from the synthetic text, resulting in two image-to-text retrieval examples (one for each image) and, more importantly, two text-to-image retrieval examples (one for each text). Human annotators filter out ill-formed examples ensuring the validity of the benchmark. The experiments on BiVLC uncover a weakness of current multimodal models, as they perform poorly in the text-to-image direction. In fact, when considering both retrieval directions, the conclusions obtained in previous works change significantly. In addition to the benchmark, weshow that a contrastive model trained using synthetic images and texts significantly improves over the base model in SugarCrepe and in BiVLC for both retrieval directions. The gap to human performance in BiVLC confirms that Vision-Language Compositionality is still a challenging problem.

paragraphs: Vision-language compositionality benchmarks test whether models connect images with descriptions that correctly express their contents. Existing benchmarks such as SugarCrepe ask a model to choose between a correct description and a deliberately difficult incorrect one. BiVLC expands this evaluation so that matching runs in both directions: from images to text and from text to images.

The authors generate an additional image from the difficult incorrect description. Each resulting pair of images and descriptions supplies two image-to-text decisions and two text-to-image decisions. Human annotators remove ill-formed examples. This construction makes the reverse matching task part of the benchmark, exposing capabilities that image-to-text evaluation alone does not measure.

Experiments reveal particularly weak performance when models must select an image from text, and including both directions substantially changes conclusions from earlier evaluations. Training a contrastive model with synthetic images and text improves over its base model on SugarCrepe and on both BiVLC directions. A remaining gap to human performance shows that the evaluated models still struggle with this capability.
summary.tldr: BiVLC adds text-to-image matching to compositionality evaluation, revealing weaknesses that image-to-text benchmarks can miss.

title: BiVLC: Extending Vision-Language Compositionality Evaluation with Text-to-Image Retrieval

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success with their billion-level parameters, yet they incur high inference overheads. The emergence of activation sparsity in LLMs provides a natural approach to reduce this cost by involving only parts of the parameters for inference. However, existing methods only focus on utilizing this naturally formed activation sparsity in a post-training setting, overlooking the potential for further amplifying this inherent sparsity. In this paper, we hypothesize that LLMs can learn to be efficient by achieving more structured activation sparsity. To achieve this, we introduce a novel training algorithm, Learn-To-be-Efficient (LTE), designed to train efficiency-aware LLMs to learn to activate fewer neurons and achieve a better trade-off between sparsity and performance. Furthermore, unlike SOTA MoEfication methods, which mainly focus on ReLU-based models, LTE can also be applied to LLMs like LLaMA using non-ReLU activations. Extensive evaluation on language understanding, language generation, and instruction tuning tasks show that LTE consistently outperforms SOTA baselines. Along with our hardware-aware custom kernel implementation, LTE reduces LLaMA2-7B inference latency by 25% at 50% sparsity.

paragraphs: Large language models can be expensive to run because inference involves enormous numbers of parameters. Activation sparsity offers a way to reduce this work by using only parts of the model for a given computation. Existing approaches exploit sparsity that emerges naturally after training; this paper investigates whether training can deliberately encourage more structured sparsity.

Learn-To-be-Efficient, or LTE, trains models to activate fewer neurons while balancing sparsity against task performance. Its aim is to make computational efficiency something the model learns. The method also applies to non-ReLU activation functions, including those used in LLaMA, extending beyond the ReLU-focused scope of the MoEfication methods discussed in the abstract.

Evaluations on language understanding, generation, and instruction tuning show LTE consistently outperforming the compared state-of-the-art baselines. Combined with a hardware-aware custom kernel, it reduces LLaMA2-7B inference latency by 25% at 50% sparsity. That result connects the learned reduction in active computation to measured execution speed for the reported model and implementation.
summary.tldr: LTE trains language models to activate fewer neurons and, with a custom kernel, reduces LLaMA2-7B inference latency by 25% at 50% sparsity.

title: Learn To be Efficient: Build Structured Sparsity in Large Language Models

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have recently achieved remarkable advancements in time series forecasting (TSF) due to their powerful ability of sequence dependence modeling. To date, existing DNN-based TSF methods still suffer from unreliable predictions for real-world data due to its non-stationarity characteristics, i.e., data distribution varies quickly over time. To mitigate this issue, several normalization methods (e.g., SAN) have recently been specifically designed by normalization in a fixed period/window in the time domain. However, these methods still struggle to capture distribution variations, due to the complex time patterns of time series in the time domain. Based on the fact that wavelet transform can decompose time series into a linear combination of different frequencies, which exhibits distribution variations with time-varying periods, we propose a novel Dual-domain Dynamic Normalization (DDN) to dynamically capture distribution variations in both time and frequency domains. Specifically, our DDN tries to eliminate the non-stationarity of time series via both frequency and time domain normalization in a sliding window way. Besides, our DDN can serve as a plug-in-play module, and thus can be easily incorporated into other forecasting models. Extensive experiments on public benchmark datasets under different forecasting models demonstrate the superiority of our DDN over other normalization methods. Code will be made available following the review process.

paragraphs: Forecasting becomes unreliable when the statistical distribution of a time series changes quickly. Normalization methods try to reduce these changes before a forecasting model processes the data. The paper argues that methods using fixed periods or windows in the time domain can struggle because the underlying temporal patterns are complex.

Dual-domain Dynamic Normalization, or DDN, uses a wavelet transform to separate the series into components at different frequencies. This representation exposes distribution changes associated with periods that vary over time. DDN then applies normalization in both the frequency and time domains using sliding windows, aiming to reduce non-stationarity through both views of the same signal.

The method is designed as a module that can be incorporated into other forecasting models. Experiments on public benchmarks with different forecasting models show advantages over the other normalization methods evaluated. The findings suggest that preprocessing can benefit from accounting for changing frequency structure as well as local time-domain behavior, without requiring an entirely new forecasting architecture.
summary.tldr: DDN normalizes changing time series in both time and frequency domains, improving forecasting across the tested models and benchmarks.

title: DDN: Dual-domain Dynamic Normalization for Non-stationary Time Series Forecasting

abstract: We consider sequential treatment regimes where each unit is exposed to combinations of interventions over time. When interventions are described by qualitative labels, such as "close schools for a month due to a pandemic" or "promote this podcast to this user during this week", it is unclear which appropriate structural assumptions allow us to generalize behavioral predictions to previously unseen combinations of interventions. Standard black-box approaches mapping sequences of categorical variables to outputs are applicable, but they rely on poorly understood assumptions on how reliable generalization can be obtained, and may underperform under sparse sequences, temporal variability, and large action spaces. To approach that, we pose an explicit model for composition, that is, how the effect of sequential interventions can be isolated into modules, clarifying which data conditions allow for the identification of their combined effect at different units and time steps. We show the identification properties of our compositional model, inspired by advances in causal matrix factorization methods. Our focus is on predictive models for novel compositions of interventions instead of matrix completion tasks and causal effect estimation. We compare our approach to flexible but generic black-box models to illustrate how structure aids prediction in sparse data conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies prediction when a unit receives combinations of interventions over time. Interventions may be represented only by qualitative labels, such as a temporary school closure or a weekly promotion. The challenge is to predict responses to combinations that have not previously appeared, especially when observed sequences are sparse and the action space is large.

The authors introduce an explicit model of composition that separates the effects of sequential interventions into modules. This structure makes it possible to state which data conditions allow combined effects to be identified for different units and times. The model draws inspiration from causal matrix factorization, while directing its attention to predictions for novel intervention compositions.

The paper establishes identification properties and compares the structured approach with flexible, generic black-box models. Those comparisons illustrate how explicit structure can help prediction under sparse data. The intended contribution is predictive generalization to new compositions, rather than causal effect estimation or matrix completion. Its guarantees are tied to the model's stated compositional structure and identification conditions.
summary.tldr: An explicit compositional model clarifies when sequential intervention effects can be identified and helps predict unseen combinations under sparse data.

title: Structured Learning of Compositional Sequential Interventions

abstract: In federated learning (FL), accommodating clients' varied computational capacities poses a challenge, often limiting the participation of those with constrained resources in global model training. To address this issue, the concept of model heterogeneity through submodel extraction has emerged, offering a tailored solution that aligns the model's complexity with each client's computational capacity. In this work, we propose Federated Importance-Aware Submodel Extraction (FIARSE), a novel approach that dynamically adjusts submodels based on the importance of model parameters, thereby overcoming the limitations of previous static and dynamic submodel extraction methods. Compared to existing works, the proposed method offers a theoretical foundation for the submodel extraction and eliminates the need for additional information beyond the model parameters themselves to determine parameter importance, significantly reducing the overhead on clients. Extensive experiments are conducted on various datasets to showcase the superior performance of the proposed FIARSE.

In this work, we propose Federated Importance-Aware Submodel Extraction (FIARSE), a novel approach that dynamically adjusts submodels based on the importance of model parameters, thereby overcoming the limitations of previous static and dynamic submodel extraction methods. Compared to existing works, the proposed method offers a theoretical foundation for the submodel extraction and eliminates the need for additional information beyond the model parameters themselves to determine parameter importance, significantly reducing the overhead on clients. paragraphs: Federated learning must accommodate clients with different computational capacities. A model that fits a powerful client may be too demanding for a resource-constrained one, limiting participation in shared training. Submodel extraction addresses this mismatch by giving each client a model whose complexity matches its available resources.

FIARSE makes that extraction depend dynamically on the importance of model parameters. The method adjusts which submodels are used as training proceeds, rather than relying solely on a fixed extraction choice. Its importance assessment uses the model parameters themselves, eliminating the need for additional information to determine which parameters matter. The authors connect this choice to substantially lower overhead for clients.

The paper also supplies a theoretical foundation for its extraction approach and evaluates it across multiple datasets. The experiments report superior performance relative to existing methods. Taken together, these contributions support parameter importance as a useful basis for accommodating heterogeneous clients: the selection process considers both the client's computational capacity and which parts of the model are important.
summary.tldr: FIARSE dynamically extracts client-sized federated submodels using parameter importance assessed from the model parameters alone.

title: FIARSE: Model-Heterogeneous Federated Learning via Importance-Aware Submodel Extraction

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capabilities across various tasks. However, training LLMs from scratch requires significant computational power and extensive memory capacity. Recent studies have explored low-rank structures on weights for efficient fine-tuning in terms of parameters and memory, either through low-rank adaptation or factorization. While effective for fine-tuning, low-rank structures are generally less suitable for pretraining because they restrict parameters to a low-dimensional subspace. In this work, we propose to parameterize the weights as a sum of low-rank and sparse matrices for pretraining, which we call SLTrain. The low-rank component is learned via matrix factorization, while for the sparse component, we employ a simple strategy of uniformly selecting the sparsity support at random and learning only the non-zero entries with the fixed support. While being simple, the random fixed-support sparse learning strategy significantly enhances pretraining when combined with low-rank learning. Our results show that SLTrain adds minimal extra parameters and memory costs compared to pretraining with low-rank parameterization, yet achieves substantially better performance, which is comparable to full-rank training. Remarkably, when combined with quantization and per-layer updates, SLTrain can reduce memory requirements by up to 73% when pretraining the LLaMA 7B model.

paragraphs: Low-rank weight representations can reduce the parameters and memory needed to train language models, but they restrict weights to a low-dimensional space. The authors argue that this restriction is generally more problematic for pretraining from scratch than for fine-tuning. SLTrain addresses it by representing each weight matrix as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix.

The low-rank part is learned through matrix factorization. For the sparse part, the method randomly selects a fixed set of positions and learns only their values. Those positions do not need to change during training. This simple addition gives the representation flexibility beyond the low-rank component while introducing relatively few extra trainable entries.

The authors report substantially better pretraining performance than low-rank parameterization alone, with minimal additional parameter and memory costs and performance comparable to full-rank training. Combined with quantization and per-layer updates, SLTrain reduces memory requirements by up to 73% when pretraining LLaMA 7B. That memory result applies to the combined configuration described in the paper.
summary.tldr: SLTrain combines low-rank weights with a fixed sparse component to make language-model pretraining more parameter- and memory-efficient.

title: SLTrain: a sparse plus low rank approach for parameter and memory efficient pretraining

abstract: We introduce SELF-DISCOVER, a general framework for LLMs to self-discover the task-intrinsic reasoning structures to tackle complex reasoning problems that are challenging for typical prompting methods. Core to the framework is a self-discovery process where LLMs select multiple atomic reasoning modules such as critical thinking and step-by-step thinking, and compose them into an explicit reasoning structure for LLMs to follow during decoding. SELF-DISCOVER substantially improves GPT-4 and PaLM 2’s performance on challenging reasoning benchmarks such as BigBench-Hard, grounded agent reasoning, and MATH, by as much as 32% compared to Chain of Thought (CoT). Furthermore, SELF-DISCOVER outperforms inference-intensive methods such as CoT-Self-Consistency by more than 20%, while requiring 10-40x fewer inference compute. Finally, we show that the self-discovered reasoning structures are universally applicable across model families: from PaLM 2-L to GPT-4, and from GPT-4 to Llama2, and share commonalities with human reasoning patterns.
