paragraphs: Tensor balancing rescales a nonnegative multidimensional array so that every fiber sums to one. For an Nth-order tensor, the rescaling uses N tensors of order N−1. The paper generalizes matrix balancing, a process used to make matrices comparable across applications ranging from biology to economics.

The authors represent tensors as probability distributions on a statistical manifold. In that representation, balancing becomes projection onto a submanifold. This geometric view supports a proof of correctness and an efficient Newton-based algorithm. A key step is obtaining the required Jacobian analytically through the Möbius inversion formula, making the geometric formulation useful for actual computation.

The proposed algorithm has quadratic convergence, and numerical experiments show it running several orders of magnitude faster than existing methods. The authors also describe the underlying model as broader than tensor balancing, encompassing models such as weighted directed acyclic graphs and Boltzmann machines. Thus, the immediate result is a faster balancing procedure, while the probability-based geometric representation offers a framework with wider stated applicability.
summary.tldr: A statistical-manifold formulation yields a quadratically convergent Newton algorithm for tensor balancing with substantial experimental speedups.

title: Tensor Balancing on Statistical Manifold

abstract: Double machine learning provides n^{1/2}-consistent estimates of parameters of interest even when high-dimensional or nonparametric nuisance parameters are estimated at an n^{-1/4} rate. The key is to employ Neyman-orthogonal moment equations which are first-order insensitive to perturbations in the nuisance parameters. We show that the n^{-1/4} requirement can be improved to n^{-1/(2k+2)} by employing a k-th order notion of orthogonality that grants robustness to more complex or higher-dimensional nuisance parameters. In the partially linear regression setting popular in causal inference, we show that we can construct second-order orthogonal moments if and only if the treatment residual is not normally distributed. Our proof relies on Stein’s lemma and may be of independent interest. We conclude by demonstrating the robustness benefits of an explicit doubly-orthogonal estimation procedure for treatment effect.

paragraphs: Estimating a parameter of interest often requires first estimating other, potentially complex nuisance quantities. Double machine learning uses Neyman-orthogonal moment equations to reduce sensitivity to errors in those quantities. First-order orthogonality allows root-n-consistent estimation of the target even when nuisance estimates converge at the slower n⁻¹/⁴ rate.

This paper extends the idea to higher-order orthogonality. With a k-th order notion, the required nuisance rate becomes n⁻¹/(2k+2), allowing slower nuisance estimation while retaining the target estimation guarantee. The result identifies a route to greater robustness when nuisance components are more complex or higher dimensional: suppress sensitivity to additional orders of estimation error.

The paper also identifies a precise boundary in partially linear regression, a setting used in causal inference. Second-order orthogonal moments can be constructed if and only if the treatment residual is not normally distributed. The proof uses Stein’s lemma. An explicit doubly orthogonal treatment-effect procedure demonstrates robustness benefits, while the distributional condition shows that access to higher-order protection depends on the structure of the problem.
summary.tldr: Higher-order orthogonality tolerates slower nuisance estimation, but second-order construction in partially linear regression requires nonnormal treatment residuals.

title: Orthogonal Machine Learning: Power and Limitations

abstract: We consider the problem of discrete-time signal denoising, focusing on a specific family of non-linear convolution-type estimators. Each such estimator is associated with a time-invariant filter which is obtained adaptively, by solving a certain convex optimization problem. Adaptive convolution-type estimators were demonstrated to have favorable statistical properties, see (Juditsky & Nemirovski, 2009; 2010; Harchaoui et al., 2015b; Ostrovsky et al., 2016). Our first contribution is an efficient implementation of these estimators via the known first-order proximal algorithms. Our second contribution is a computational complexity analysis of the proposed procedures, which takes into account their statistical nature and the related notion of statistical accuracy. The proposed procedures and their analysis are illustrated on a simulated data benchmark.

paragraphs: This paper examines how to remove noise from discrete-time signals using a family of adaptive convolution estimators. Each estimator uses a time-invariant filter, but the filter itself is learned from the data by solving a convex optimization problem. The overall estimator can therefore be nonlinear even though the resulting filter is time-invariant.

Previous work had established favorable statistical properties for these estimators. The authors focus on making them computationally efficient, implementing them with established first-order proximal algorithms. This connects an estimator family with statistical appeal to optimization procedures that can carry out the required fitting. The contribution concerns how to compute the estimators efficiently, rather than introducing their statistical motivation.

The paper also analyzes computational complexity in relation to statistical accuracy. This ties the effort spent solving the optimization problem to the accuracy relevant for estimating a noisy signal. A simulated benchmark illustrates both the proposed procedures and their analysis, bringing the computational and statistical aspects of denoising into the same account.
summary.tldr: The paper makes adaptive convolution denoisers efficient to compute and analyzes their cost in terms of statistical accuracy.

title: Efficient First-Order Algorithms for Adaptive Signal Denoising

abstract: We propose a targeted communication architecture for multi-agent reinforcement learning, where agents learn both what messages to send and whom to address them to while performing cooperative tasks in partially-observable environments. This targeting behavior is learnt solely from downstream task-specific reward without any communication supervision. We additionally augment this with a multi-round communication approach where agents coordinate via multiple rounds of communication before taking actions in the environment. We evaluate our approach on a diverse set of cooperative multi-agent tasks, of varying difficulties, with varying number of agents, in a variety of environments ranging from 2D grid layouts of shapes and simulated traffic junctions to 3D indoor environments, and demonstrate the benefits of targeted and multi-round communication. Moreover, we show that the targeted communication strategies learned by agents are interpretable and intuitive. Finally, we show that our architecture can be easily extended to mixed and competitive environments, leading to improved performance and sample complexity over recent state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: TarMAC addresses communication among reinforcement learning agents cooperating in environments where each agent has only partial information. Its architecture learns both message content and intended recipients. The targeting behavior is learned from the reward for completing the task, without separate supervision specifying how the agents should communicate.

The architecture also supports several communication rounds before agents act. This gives the group repeated opportunities to coordinate within a decision step. Learning recipients and allowing multiple exchanges address different parts of the communication problem: directing information toward particular agents and enabling coordination to develop over more than one round.

Evaluations span tasks with different difficulties and agent counts, including two-dimensional shape layouts, simulated traffic junctions, and three-dimensional indoor environments. The authors report benefits from targeted and multi-round communication and describe the learned strategies as interpretable and intuitive. Extensions to mixed and competitive environments also improve performance and sample complexity over recent state-of-the-art approaches in the reported evaluations, suggesting usefulness beyond purely cooperative tasks.
summary.tldr: TarMAC learns what agents should communicate and to whom, using task rewards and multiple communication rounds to improve coordination.

title: TarMAC: Targeted Multi-Agent Communication

abstract: Policy gradient methods are powerful reinforcement learning algorithms and have been demonstrated to solve many complex tasks. However, these methods are also data-inefficient, afflicted with high variance gradient estimates, and frequently get stuck in local optima. This work addresses these weaknesses by combining recent improvements in the reuse of off-policy data and exploration in parameter space with deterministic behavioral policies. The resulting objective is amenable to standard neural network optimization strategies like stochastic gradient descent or stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Incorporation of previous rollouts via importance sampling greatly improves data-efficiency, whilst stochastic optimization schemes facilitate the escape from local optima. We evaluate the proposed approach on a series of continuous control benchmark tasks. The results show that the proposed algorithm is able to successfully and reliably learn solutions using fewer system interactions than standard policy gradient methods.

paragraphs: Policy-gradient methods can solve complex control tasks, but learning may require many interactions and suffer from noisy gradient estimates or poor local solutions. This paper combines reuse of earlier experience with exploration in policy-parameter space. The approach uses deterministic behavioral policies as part of that combination.

Previous trajectories are incorporated through importance sampling, allowing rollouts collected under other policies to contribute to learning. The resulting objective supports standard neural-network optimization methods, including stochastic gradient descent and stochastic gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Reusing trajectories addresses data efficiency, while stochastic optimization is intended to help the learning process escape local optima.

The authors evaluate the method on continuous-control benchmarks and report reliable successful learning with fewer system interactions than standard policy-gradient approaches. These results support the combined approach in the tested tasks. Its central contribution is to make earlier trajectories useful within an objective that accommodates established optimizers, joining experience reuse and parameter-space exploration in a single learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Reusing trajectories through importance sampling and exploring policy parameters reduces environment interactions in the reported continuous-control experiments.

title: Trajectory-Based Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The Wasserstein distance serves as a loss function for unsupervised learning which depends on the choice of a ground metric on sample space. We propose to use the Wasserstein distance itself as the ground metric on the sample space of images. This ground metric is known as an effective distance for image retrieval, that correlates with human perception. We derive the Wasserstein ground metric on pixel space and define a Riemannian Wasserstein gradient penalty to be used in the Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (WGAN) framework. The new gradient penalty is computed efficiently via convolutions on the $L^2$ gradients with negligible additional computational cost. The new formulation is more robust to the natural variability of the data and provides for a more continuous discriminator in sample space.

We propose to use the Wasserstein distance itself as the ground metric on the sample space of images. This ground metric is known as an effective distance for image retrieval, that correlates with human perception. We derive the Wasserstein ground metric on pixel space and define a Riemannian Wasserstein gradient penalty to be used in the Wasserstein Generative Adversarial Network (WGAN) framework. The new gradient penalty is computed efficiently via convolutions on the $L^2$ gradients with negligible additional computational cost. paragraphs: A Wasserstein loss compares distributions using an underlying distance between individual samples, called the ground metric. For images, that choice determines what kinds of differences the loss treats as large or small. This paper proposes using a Wasserstein distance between images as the ground metric within a Wasserstein generative-modeling objective.

The authors motivate this nested construction through the image distance’s established usefulness for retrieval and its correlation with human perception. They derive the Wasserstein ground metric on pixel space and formulate a corresponding Riemannian Wasserstein gradient penalty for the WGAN framework. This adapts the discriminator’s regularization to the proposed geometry of image differences.

The new penalty can be calculated efficiently by applying convolutions to L2 gradients, with negligible additional computational cost. The authors report greater robustness to natural data variability and a more continuous discriminator over the sample space. The contribution is therefore a change to the geometry underlying the loss, together with a computationally inexpensive way to incorporate that geometry into training.
summary.tldr: Using Wasserstein distance between images as a WGAN ground metric yields an efficient gradient penalty and improved robustness to natural variability.

title: Wasserstein of Wasserstein Loss for Learning Generative Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning agents are prone to undesired behaviors due to reward mis-specification. Finding a set of reward functions to properly guide agent behaviors is particularly challenging in multi-agent scenarios. Inverse reinforcement learning provides a framework to automatically acquire suitable reward functions from expert demonstrations. Its extension to multi-agent settings, however, is difficult due to the more complex notions of rational behaviors. In this paper, we propose MA-AIRL, a new framework for multi-agent inverse reinforcement learning, which is effective and scalable for Markov games with high-dimensional state-action space and unknown dynamics. We derive our algorithm based on a new solution concept and maximum pseudolikelihood estimation within an adversarial reward learning framework. In the experiments, we demonstrate that MA-AIRL can recover reward functions that are highly correlated with the ground truth rewards, while significantly outperforms prior methods in terms of policy imitation.

paragraphs: Poorly specified rewards can lead reinforcement learning agents toward unwanted behavior. Choosing suitable rewards becomes especially difficult when multiple agents interact, because the meaning of rational behavior is more complicated. This paper develops MA-AIRL, a framework for learning reward functions from expert demonstrations in multi-agent settings rather than specifying all those rewards by hand.

The method targets Markov games with high-dimensional state and action spaces and unknown dynamics. Its derivation combines a new solution concept with maximum pseudolikelihood estimation inside an adversarial reward-learning framework. These components provide a way to formulate and estimate rewards while accounting for the interacting-agent setting that makes a direct extension of inverse reinforcement learning difficult.

In experiments, MA-AIRL recovers rewards that are highly correlated with the ground-truth rewards and substantially improves policy imitation over prior methods. These are complementary findings: one concerns agreement with the underlying reward signal, and the other concerns reproducing demonstrated behavior. Together, they support the framework's usefulness for multi-agent reward learning and imitation.
summary.tldr: MA-AIRL learns rewards from multi-agent demonstrations, recovering highly correlated reward functions and improving policy imitation in the reported experiments.

title: Multi-Agent Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: A commonly cited inefficiency of neural network training by back-propagation is the update locking problem: each layer must wait for the signal to propagate through the network before updating. In recent years multiple authors have considered alternatives that can alleviate this issue. In this context, we consider a simpler, but more effective, substitute that uses minimal feedback, which we call Decoupled Greedy Learning (DGL). It is based on a greedy relaxation of the joint training objective, recently shown to be effective in the context of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) on large-scale image classification. We consider an optimization of this objective that permits us to decouple the layer training, allowing for layers or modules in networks to be trained with a potentially linear parallelization in layers. We show theoretically and empirically that this approach converges. Then, we empirically find that it can lead to better generalization than sequential greedy optimization and sometimes end-to-end back-propagation. We show an extension of this approach to asynchronous settings, where modules can operate with large communication delays, is possible with the use of a replay buffer. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DGL on the CIFAR-10 dataset against alternatives and on the large-scale ImageNet dataset.

paragraphs: Back-propagation creates a scheduling dependency: a layer must wait for a learning signal to travel through the network before it can update. Decoupled Greedy Learning, or DGL, addresses this update locking by changing how the training objective is optimized. It builds on a greedy relaxation of joint training that had shown promise for large-scale image classification.

The method separates training across layers or modules using minimal feedback. This creates the possibility of parallelization that grows linearly with the number of layers, rather than requiring every update to follow the full network's sequence. The paper supports convergence with both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence.

Experiments find that DGL can generalize better than sequential greedy training and, in some cases, end-to-end back-propagation. The authors also extend the approach to asynchronous operation using a replay buffer, allowing modules to work despite large communication delays. Results on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, while the parallelization claim remains a potential benefit rather than a guaranteed realized speedup.
summary.tldr: DGL decouples neural-network module training, supports convergence and asynchronous operation, and sometimes improves generalization over end-to-end back-propagation.

title: Decoupled Greedy Learning of CNNs

abstract: Higher-order tensors arise frequently in applications such as neuroimaging, recommendation system, and social network analysis. We consider the problem of low-rank tensor estimation from possibly incomplete, ordinal-valued observations. Two related problems are studied, one on tensor denoising and another on tensor completion. We propose a multi-linear cumulative link model, develop a rank-constrained M-estimator, and obtain theoretical accuracy guarantees. Our mean squared error bound enjoys a faster convergence rate than previous results, and we show that the proposed estimator is minimax optimal under the class of low-rank models. Furthermore, the procedure developed serves as an efficient completion method which guarantees consistent recovery of an order-K (d,...,d)-dimensional low-rank tensor using only O(Kd) noisy, quantized observations. We demonstrate the outperformance of our approach over previous methods on the tasks of clustering and collaborative filtering.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimation of low-rank tensors when observations are ordinal and may be incomplete. Ordinal measurements provide ordered categories rather than unrestricted numerical values. The authors address both denoising, which estimates structure despite noisy observations, and completion, which recovers a tensor when some observations are missing.

They propose a multilinear cumulative link model and a rank-constrained M-estimator. The analysis provides accuracy guarantees, including a mean squared error bound that converges faster than previous results. The estimator is also shown to be minimax optimal within the class of low-rank models, establishing an optimality result tied to that model class.

For an order-K tensor with dimension d along each axis, the completion procedure guarantees consistent recovery using O(Kd) noisy, quantized observations under the stated low-rank setup. This is a favorable scaling with tensor order and dimension. Experiments on clustering and collaborative filtering show better performance than previous methods, complementing the estimation guarantees with evidence on applied tasks.
summary.tldr: A rank-constrained ordinal tensor estimator achieves improved error guarantees, minimax optimality for low-rank models, and efficient completion.

title: Tensor denoising and completion based on ordinal observations

abstract: Devising indicative evaluation metrics for the image generation task remains an open problem. The most widely used metric for measuring the similarity between real and generated images has been the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) score. Since it does not differentiate the fidelity and diversity aspects of the generated images, recent papers have introduced variants of precision and recall metrics to diagnose those properties separately. In this paper, we show that even the latest version of the precision and recall metrics are not reliable yet. For example, they fail to detect the match between two identical distributions, they are not robust against outliers, and the evaluation hyperparameters are selected arbitrarily. We propose density and coverage metrics that solve the above issues. We analytically and experimentally show that density and coverage provide more interpretable and reliable signals for practitioners than the existing metrics.

The most widely used metric for measuring the similarity between real and generated images has been the Frechet Inception Distance (FID) score. Since it does not differentiate the fidelity and diversity aspects of the generated images, recent papers have introduced variants of precision and recall metrics to diagnose those properties separately. In this paper, we show that even the latest version of the precision and recall metrics are not reliable yet. For example, they fail to detect the match between two identical distributions, they are not robust against outliers, and the evaluation hyperparameters are selected arbitrarily. We propose density and coverage metrics that solve the above issues. We analytically and experimentally show that density and coverage provide more interpretable and reliable signals for practitioners than the existing metrics.

paragraphs: Evaluating an image generator requires understanding both the fidelity of its outputs and the diversity they capture. A single similarity score can obscure that distinction. The paper examines metrics intended to separate these properties and asks whether their signals are reliable enough to guide practitioners.

The authors identify problems with existing precision-and-recall variants: they can fail to recognize identical distributions, react poorly to outliers, and depend on arbitrarily chosen evaluation hyperparameters. These issues matter because an evaluation method should provide meaningful results even in basic comparison cases. Otherwise, a reported difference can be difficult to interpret as evidence about the generator.

The proposed alternatives are density and coverage metrics, designed to address those problems while preserving separate information about fidelity and diversity. The authors support them with analytical and experimental evidence, reporting more interpretable and reliable signals than the existing metrics. The contribution is an improved diagnostic approach to generated images, helping evaluation describe the kinds of agreement between real and generated data.
summary.tldr: Density and coverage offer more reliable, interpretable diagnostics of image-generation fidelity and diversity in the reported analysis.

title: Reliable Fidelity and Diversity Metrics for Generative Models

abstract: We introduce a novel regularization approach for deep learning that incorporates and respects the underlying graphical structure of the neural network. Existing regularization methods often focus on penalizing weights in a global/uniform manner that ignores the connectivity structure of the neural network. We propose to use the Fiedler value of the neural network’s underlying graph as a tool for regularization. We provide theoretical support for this approach via spectral graph theory. We show several useful properties of the Fiedler value that make it suitable for regularization. We provide an approximate, variational approach for faster computation during training. We provide an alternative formulation of this framework in the form of a structurally weighted L1 penalty, thus linking our approach to sparsity induction. We performed experiments on datasets that compare Fiedler regularization with traditional regularization methods such as Dropout and weight decay. Results demonstrate the efficacy of Fiedler regularization.

We show several useful properties of the Fiedler value that make it suitable for regularization. We provide an approximate, variational approach for faster computation during training. We provide an alternative formulation of this framework in the form of a structurally weighted L1 penalty, thus linking our approach to sparsity induction. We performed experiments on datasets that compare Fiedler regularization with traditional regularization methods such as Dropout and weight decay. paragraphs: Regularization influences what a neural network learns by penalizing aspects of its parameters or structure. Many familiar penalties treat weights uniformly and do not account for how those weights connect the network. This paper develops a regularizer that explicitly uses the network's underlying graph.

The proposed quantity is the graph's Fiedler value. The authors use spectral graph theory to justify this choice and establish properties that make it suitable for regularization. Because evaluating the quantity during training can be costly, they also introduce an approximate variational method for faster computation.

An alternative formulation expresses the framework as an L1 penalty with weights determined by structure, connecting the approach to encouraging sparse networks. This gives a concrete interpretation of how graph information can influence which connections are penalized. Experiments compare Fiedler regularization with methods including Dropout and weight decay, and the reported results support its effectiveness. The contribution combines a structural motivation, theoretical support, and a practical approximation for incorporating that motivation into training.
summary.tldr: Fiedler regularization uses neural network graph structure to guide sparsity, with theoretical support and an approximation for practical training.

title: Fiedler Regularization: Learning Neural Networks with Graph Sparsity

abstract: Formation mechanisms are fundamental to the study of complex networks, but learning them from observations is challenging. In real-world domains, one often has access only to the final constructed graph, instead of the full construction process, and observed graphs exhibit complex structural properties. In this work, we propose GraphOpt, an end-to-end framework that jointly learns an implicit model of graph structure formation and discovers an underlying optimization mechanism in the form of a latent objective function. The learned objective can serve as an explanation for the observed graph properties, thereby lending itself to transfer across different graphs within a domain. GraphOpt poses link formation in graphs as a sequential decision-making process and solves it using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning algorithm. Further, it employs a novel continuous latent action space that aids scalability. Empirically, we demonstrate that GraphOpt discovers a latent objective transferable across graphs with different characteristics. GraphOpt also learns a robust stochastic policy that achieves competitive link prediction performance without being explicitly trained on this task and further enables construction of graphs with properties similar to those of the observed graph.

The framework treats adding links as a sequence of decisions. It uses maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning to discover an objective underlying those decisions, jointly learning an implicit formation model. title: GraphOpt: Learning Optimization Models of Graph Formation

abstract: Estimating the score, i.e., the gradient of log density function, from a set of samples generated by an unknown distribution is a fundamental task in inference and learning of probabilistic models that involve flexible yet intractable densities. Kernel estimators based on Stein’s methods or score matching have shown promise, however their theoretical properties and relationships have not been fully-understood. We provide a unifying view of these estimators under the framework of regularized nonparametric regression. It allows us to analyse existing estimators and construct new ones with desirable properties by choosing different hypothesis spaces and regularizers. A unified convergence analysis is provided for such estimators. Finally, we propose score estimators based on iterative regularization that enjoy computational benefits from curl-free kernels and fast convergence.

paragraphs: The score of a probability distribution is the gradient of its log density. Estimating it from samples is useful when a probabilistic model has a flexible density that is difficult to work with directly. This paper studies kernel-based score estimators, including approaches based on Stein's methods and score matching, whose relationships and theoretical properties had not been fully understood.

The authors place these estimators within regularized nonparametric regression. This shared framework makes it possible to analyze existing methods together and construct new estimators by changing the hypothesis space or the regularizer. Those choices determine the functions available to the estimator and how their fitting is controlled.

The paper provides a unified convergence analysis and proposes additional estimators based on iterative regularization. These methods obtain computational benefits from curl-free kernels and fast convergence. The contribution is both explanatory and constructive: it organizes seemingly separate score-estimation approaches under one framework, then uses that framework to develop methods with desirable computational and convergence properties.
summary.tldr: A regularized regression framework unifies kernel score estimators and supports new methods with favorable convergence and computation.

title: Nonparametric Score Estimators

abstract: We analyze the problem of active covering, where the learner is given an unlabeled dataset and can sequentially label query examples. The objective is to label query all of the positive examples in the fewest number of total label queries. We show under standard non-parametric assumptions that a classical support estimator can be repurposed as an offline algorithm attaining an excess query cost of $\widetilde{\Theta}(n^{D/(D+1)})$ compared to the optimal learner, where $n$ is the number of datapoints and $D$ is the dimension. We then provide a simple active learning method that attains an improved excess query cost of $\widetilde{O}(n^{(D-1)/D})$. Furthermore, the proposed algorithms only require access to the positive labeled examples, which in certain settings provides additional computational and privacy benefits. Finally, we show that the active learning method consistently outperforms offline methods as well as a variety of baselines on a wide range of benchmark image-based datasets.

paragraphs: Active covering starts with an unlabeled dataset and lets a learner request labels sequentially. Its objective is to query every positive example while spending as few total label queries as possible. The central issue is therefore how to direct labeling effort toward positive examples without overlooking those that remain.

Under standard nonparametric assumptions, the authors first repurpose a classical support estimator as an offline method. Its excess query cost relative to the optimal learner scales as n raised to D/(D+1), up to logarithmic factors, where n is dataset size and D is dimension. Their active method improves the upper bound to n raised to (D−1)/D, again suppressing logarithmic factors.

These bounds measure additional queries beyond the optimal learner's cost, rather than total labeling effort. The algorithms require access only to positively labeled examples, which can bring computational and privacy benefits in some settings. On a broad range of image benchmarks, the active method consistently outperformed the evaluated offline methods and other baselines, supporting the value of sequentially directing queries.
summary.tldr: An active labeling method improves theoretical excess-query bounds and empirical performance when searching for every positive example in a dataset.

title: Active Covering

abstract: Recent works apply Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to graph matching tasks and show promising results. Considering that model outputs are complex matchings, we devise several techniques to improve the learning of GNNs and obtain a new model, Stochastic Iterative Graph MAtching (SIGMA). Our model predicts a distribution of matchings, instead of a single matching, for a graph pair so the model can explore several probable matchings. We further introduce a novel multi-step matching procedure, which learns how to refine a graph pair’s matching results incrementally. The model also includes dummy nodes so that the model does not have to find matchings for nodes without correspondence. We fit this model to data via scalable stochastic optimization. We conduct extensive experiments across synthetic graph datasets as well as biochemistry and computer vision applications. Across all tasks, our results show that SIGMA can produce significantly improved graph matching results compared to state-of-the-art models. Ablation studies verify that each of our components (stochastic training, iterative matching, and dummy nodes) offers noticeable improvement.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondences between nodes in two graphs, so its output is a structured collection of assignments. SIGMA builds on graph neural networks to handle this complexity. It predicts a distribution over matchings, allowing several plausible correspondence patterns to be explored instead of producing only a single candidate.

The model also refines a matching over multiple steps, learning to improve the graph pair’s assignments incrementally. Dummy nodes provide a way to leave nodes without real counterparts unmatched, avoiding the requirement that every node have a correspondence. Scalable stochastic optimization trains these components together, combining uncertainty over assignments with iterative refinement and explicit handling of unmatched nodes.

Experiments span synthetic graphs, biochemistry, and computer vision applications. The authors report significantly improved matching results over state-of-the-art models across all evaluated tasks. Ablation studies show noticeable benefits from each component: stochastic training, iterative matching, and dummy nodes. These findings support the combined design while also attributing gains to its individual ingredients.
summary.tldr: SIGMA improves graph matching by exploring distributions of assignments, refining them iteratively, and allowing nodes to remain unmatched.

title: Stochastic Iterative Graph Matching

abstract: We develop a rigorous approach for using a set of arbitrarily correlated weak supervision sources in order to solve a multiclass classification task when only a very small set of labeled data is available. Our learning algorithm provably converges to a model that has minimum empirical risk with respect to an adversarial choice over feasible labelings for a set of unlabeled data, where the feasibility of a labeling is computed through constraints defined by rigorously estimated statistics of the weak supervision sources. We show theoretical guarantees for this approach that depend on the information provided by the weak supervision sources. Notably, this method does not require the weak supervision sources to have the same labeling space as the multiclass classification task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with experiments on various image classification tasks.

Notably, this method does not require the weak supervision sources to have the same labeling space as the multiclass classification task. paragraphs: This paper addresses multiclass classification when only a very small labeled dataset is available, but several weak supervision sources provide additional information. Those sources may be arbitrarily correlated, so the approach does not depend on treating their outputs as independent evidence. The task is to turn imperfect supervision into a learning problem with performance guarantees.

The method rigorously estimates statistics of the supervision sources and uses them to constrain possible labelings of unlabeled examples. Training then considers an adversarial choice among the labelings that satisfy those constraints. The authors prove that their algorithm converges to a model minimizing empirical risk under this adversarial formulation.

The theoretical guarantees depend on the information supplied by the weak sources, connecting the strength of the result to the available supervision. Sources also need not use the same label space as the final classification task, allowing information expressed through different categories to contribute. Experiments on multiple image-classification tasks demonstrate the approach’s effectiveness.
summary.tldr: An adversarial learning formulation combines correlated weak supervision sources with guarantees tied to the information they provide.

title: Adversarial Multi Class Learning under Weak Supervision with Performance Guarantees

abstract: We study the problem of designing autonomous agents that can learn to cooperate effectively with a potentially suboptimal partner while having no access to the joint reward function. This problem is modeled as a cooperative episodic two-agent Markov decision process. We assume control over only the first of the two agents in a Stackelberg formulation of the game, where the second agent is acting so as to maximise expected utility given the first agent’s policy. How should the first agent act in order to learn the joint reward function as quickly as possible and so that the joint policy is as close to optimal as possible? We analyse how knowledge about the reward function can be gained in this interactive two-agent scenario. We show that when the learning agent’s policies have a significant effect on the transition function, the reward function can be learned efficiently.

paragraphs: The paper studies cooperation when an autonomous agent does not know the reward function shared with its partner. The partner may also act suboptimally. The learning agent must therefore discover what the pair is trying to achieve while choosing behavior that helps them perform well together.

The problem is modeled as an episodic two-agent Markov decision process, with control over only the first agent. In the Stackelberg formulation, the second agent seeks to maximize expected utility in response to the first agent’s policy. This makes interaction informative: changing the controlled agent’s policy can change the situation to which the partner responds.

The authors analyze how those interactions reveal the joint reward function. They show efficient reward learning when the learning agent’s policies have a significant effect on the transition function, which governs how the environment evolves. This condition identifies a useful role for influence over the interaction. It is a sufficient setting for efficient learning, rather than a claim that every cooperative pairing permits fast reward discovery.
summary.tldr: An agent can efficiently learn a shared reward through cooperation when its policies significantly influence the environment’s transitions.

title: Interactive Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Games

abstract: We discover that neural networks exhibit approximate logical dependencies among neurons, and we introduce Neuron Dependency Graphs (NDG) that extract and present them as directed graphs. In an NDG, each node corresponds to the boolean activation value of a neuron, and each edge models an approximate logical implication from one node to another. We show that the logical dependencies extracted from the training dataset generalize well to the test set. In addition to providing symbolic explanations to the neural network’s internal structure, NDGs can represent a Structural Causal Model. We empirically show that an NDG is a causal abstraction of the corresponding neural network that "unfolds" the same way under causal interventions using the theory by Geiger et al. (2021). Code is available at https://github.com/phimachine/ndg.

paragraphs: This paper studies approximate logical relationships among neurons inside a neural network. Its Neuron Dependency Graph represents each neuron through a Boolean activation value and draws a directed edge when one activation approximately implies another. The graph turns internal activity into a symbolic description of dependencies that can be inspected at the level of individual neurons.

The authors find that dependencies extracted using training data generalize well to test data. This matters because a description of internal structure is more useful when its relationships extend beyond the examples used to discover them. The resulting graph provides an interpretable account of how activation patterns relate within the network.

The paper also connects these graphs to Structural Causal Models. Empirical tests show that an NDG can behave as a causal abstraction of its corresponding neural network, responding consistently with that network under interventions in the framework used by the authors. The claim is supported empirically, and the graph’s logical implications remain approximate rather than exact universal rules.
summary.tldr: Neuron Dependency Graphs summarize approximate logical activation relationships and empirically support a causal abstraction of neural networks.

title: Neuron Dependency Graphs: A Causal Abstraction of Neural Networks

abstract: We consider the task of accurately modeling strong human policies in multi-agent decision-making problems, given examples of human behavior. Imitation learning is effective at predicting human actions but may not match the strength of expert humans (e.g., by sometimes committing blunders), while self-play learning and search techniques such as AlphaZero lead to strong performance but may produce policies that differ markedly from human behavior. In chess and Go, we show that regularized search algorithms that penalize KL divergence from an imitation-learned policy yield higher prediction accuracy of strong humans and better performance than imitation learning alone. We then introduce a novel regret minimization algorithm that is regularized based on the KL divergence from an imitation-learned policy, and show that using this algorithm for search in no-press Diplomacy yields a policy that matches the human prediction accuracy of imitation learning while being substantially stronger.

Imitation learning is effective at predicting human actions but may not match the strength of expert humans (e.g., by sometimes committing blunders), while self-play learning and search techniques such as AlphaZero lead to strong performance but may produce policies that differ markedly from human behavior. paragraphs: Predicting expert human play and playing strongly are related but distinct goals. Imitation learning can reproduce human choices yet still make costly mistakes. Search and self-play can produce strong decisions whose style differs substantially from human behavior. This paper combines imitation with search to address both objectives together.

The search procedure penalizes KL divergence from a policy learned through imitation. This penalty encourages the searched policy to remain close to human behavioral patterns while search improves decisions. In chess and Go, the authors find that this regularized search both predicts strong humans more accurately and plays better than imitation learning alone.

The paper also introduces a regret-minimization algorithm with regularization based on the same divergence from an imitation policy. Used for search in no-press Diplomacy, it matches imitation learning's human-action prediction accuracy while producing a substantially stronger policy. The results show different benefits across the evaluated games: improved prediction and strength in chess and Go, and preserved prediction accuracy with greater strength in Diplomacy.
summary.tldr: Search regularized toward an imitation-learned policy improves playing strength while preserving or improving human-action prediction in the evaluated games.

title: Modeling Strong and Human-Like Gameplay with KL-Regularized Search

abstract: Gaussian Process (GP) models are a class of flexible non-parametric models that have rich representational power. By using a Gaussian process with additive structure, complex responses can be modelled whilst retaining interpretability. Previous work showed that additive Gaussian process models require high-dimensional interaction terms. We propose the orthogonal additive kernel (OAK), which imposes an orthogonality constraint on the additive functions, enabling an identifiable, low-dimensional representation of the functional relationship. We connect the OAK kernel to functional ANOVA decomposition, and show improved convergence rates for sparse computation methods. With only a small number of additive low-dimensional terms, we demonstrate the OAK model achieves similar or better predictive performance compared to black-box models, while retaining interpretability.

paragraphs: Additive Gaussian processes represent a complex response through a collection of component functions. This structure can make predictions easier to interpret, because the relationship is expressed through individual effects and interactions. The paper revisits a difficulty highlighted by earlier work: additive Gaussian processes can require interactions involving many input dimensions, weakening the appeal of a simple component-based explanation.

The authors propose the orthogonal additive kernel, or OAK. It constrains the additive functions to be orthogonal, allowing an identifiable representation built from low-dimensional components. Identifiability matters because the component functions should provide a well-defined account of the relationship, rather than allowing their contributions to be ambiguously redistributed. The paper connects this construction to functional analysis of variance.

The theoretical results include improved convergence rates for sparse computational methods. Empirically, models using only a small collection of low-dimensional additive terms achieve predictive performance similar to or better than the compared black-box models. These findings support the possibility of retaining interpretable structure without sacrificing predictive quality in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: An orthogonal additive kernel gives Gaussian processes identifiable, low-dimensional components while preserving strong predictive performance in the reported evaluations.

title: Additive Gaussian Processes Revisited

abstract: With the success of Transformers in the computer vision field, the automated design of vision Transformers has attracted significant attention. Recently, MetaFormer found that simple average pooling can achieve impressive performance, which naturally raises the question of how to design a search space to search diverse and high-performance Transformer-like architectures. By revisiting typical search spaces, we design micro-meso-macro space to search for Transformer-like architectures, namely BurgerFormer. Micro, meso, and macro correspond to the granularity levels of operation, block and stage, respectively. At the microscopic level, we enrich the atomic operations to include various normalizations, activation functions, and basic operations (e.g., multi-head self attention, average pooling). At the mesoscopic level, a hamburger structure is searched out as the basic BurgerFormer block. At the macroscopic level, we search for the depth, width, and expansion ratio of the network based on the multi-stage architecture. Meanwhile, we propose a hybrid sampling method for effectively training the supernet. Experimental results demonstrate that the searched BurgerFormer architectures achieve comparable even superior performance compared with current state-of-the-art Transformers on the ImageNet and COCO datasets. The codes can be available at https://github.com/xingxing-123/BurgerFormer.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to automate the design of effective Transformer-like vision models. Its motivation includes the observation that even simple average pooling can perform impressively within such architectures. That raises a design question: how should an architecture search represent a sufficiently diverse set of operations and structures?

BurgerFormer searches at three levels. At the operation level, choices include normalization, activation functions, attention, and average pooling. At the block level, the search produces a hamburger-shaped basic structure. At the stage level, it chooses network depth, width, and expansion ratio within a multistage architecture. These levels let the search jointly explore local computation and broader network organization.

The authors also introduce hybrid sampling to train the supernet effectively, supporting the search over candidate architectures. Experiments on ImageNet and COCO show that the resulting BurgerFormer models achieve performance comparable to, and sometimes better than, current state-of-the-art Transformers. The contribution combines a search-space design with a training strategy, demonstrating that choices at several architectural scales can yield competitive vision models.
summary.tldr: BurgerFormer searches operations, blocks, and stages together to discover Transformer-like vision architectures with competitive or superior benchmark performance.

title: Searching for BurgerFormer with Micro-Meso-Macro Space Design

abstract: Many improvements on GNNs can be deemed as operations on the spectrum of the underlying graph matrix, which motivates us to directly study the characteristics of the spectrum and their effects on GNN performance. By generalizing most existing GNN architectures, we show that the correlation issue caused by the unsmooth spectrum becomes the obstacle to leveraging more powerful graph filters as well as developing deep architectures, which therefore restricts GNNs’ performance. Inspired by this, we propose the correlation-free architecture which naturally removes the correlation issue among different channels, making it possible to utilize more sophisticated filters within each channel. The final correlation-free architecture with more powerful filters consistently boosts the performance of learning graph representations. Code is available at https://github.com/qslim/gnn-spectrum.

paragraphs: This paper examines why making graph neural networks deeper or giving them more powerful graph filters does not necessarily improve their performance. Its starting point is that many changes to these networks can be understood as changes to the spectrum of the underlying graph matrix. Studying that spectrum therefore offers a common way to analyze different architectures.

Using a formulation that generalizes most existing architectures, the authors identify a correlation problem associated with an unsmooth spectrum. Correlations between different channels become an obstacle to using richer filters and developing deeper networks. The analysis connects a property of the graph matrix to a specific architectural difficulty, rather than treating depth and filter choice as independent design decisions.

The proposed architecture removes this correlation issue between channels, allowing more sophisticated filters within each channel. The authors report that the resulting combination consistently improves graph representation learning. The contribution is both an explanation of what can restrict existing architectures and a design that addresses the identified restriction.
summary.tldr: A graph neural network architecture removes spectrum-related correlations between channels so that richer graph filters can improve representation learning.

title: A New Perspective on the Effects of Spectrum in Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Multi-task Imitation Learning (MIL) aims to train a policy capable of performing a distribution of tasks based on multi-task expert demonstrations, which is essential for general-purpose robots. Existing MIL algorithms suffer from low data efficiency and poor performance on complex long-horizontal tasks. We develop Multi-task Hierarchical Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning (MH-AIRL) to learn hierarchically-structured multi-task policies, which is more beneficial for compositional tasks with long horizons and has higher expert data efficiency through identifying and transferring reusable basic skills across tasks. To realize this, MH-AIRL effectively synthesizes context-based multi-task learning, AIRL (an IL approach), and hierarchical policy learning. Further, MH-AIRL can be adopted to demonstrations without the task or skill annotations (i.e., state-action pairs only) which are more accessible in practice. Theoretical justifications are provided for each module of MH-AIRL, and evaluations on challenging multi-task settings demonstrate superior performance and transferability of the multi-task policies learned with MH-AIRL as compared to SOTA MIL baselines.

paragraphs: Multi-task imitation learning aims to learn a policy for a range of tasks from expert demonstrations. Existing methods can use expert data inefficiently and struggle with complex tasks extending over many steps. This paper proposes MH-AIRL to learn hierarchical policies that identify and transfer reusable basic skills across tasks.

The method combines context-based multi-task learning, adversarial inverse reinforcement learning, and hierarchical policy learning. Its hierarchy is intended to support compositional tasks, where reusable skills contribute to longer behaviors. Sharing those skills across tasks also provides a route to greater expert-data efficiency, because useful behavior learned in one task can contribute to others.

MH-AIRL can use demonstrations containing only state-action pairs, without task or skill annotations. The authors provide theoretical justifications for each module and evaluate the method in challenging multi-task settings. The learned policies show better performance and transferability than leading multi-task imitation baselines, supporting the proposed combination of reusable skills, hierarchy, and learning from more readily available demonstrations.
summary.tldr: MH-AIRL learns reusable hierarchical skills from multi-task demonstrations, improving reported performance and transferability without requiring task or skill labels.

title: Multi-task Hierarchical Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) enables the transfer of models trained on source domains to unlabeled target domains. However, transferring complex time series models presents challenges due to the dynamic temporal structure variations across domains. This leads to feature shifts in the time and frequency representations. Additionally, the label distributions of tasks in the source and target domains can differ significantly, posing difficulties in addressing label shifts and recognizing labels unique to the target domain. Effectively transferring complex time series models remains a formidable problem. We present RAINCOAT, the first model for both closed-set and universal domain adaptation on complex time series. RAINCOAT addresses feature and label shifts by considering both temporal and frequency features, aligning them across domains, and correcting for misalignments to facilitate the detection of private labels. Additionally, RAINCOAT improves transferability by identifying label shifts in target domains. Our experiments with 5 datasets and 13 state-of-the-art UDA methods demonstrate that RAINCOAT can improve transfer learning performance by up to 16.33% and can handle both closed-set and universal domain adaptation.
originalAbstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) enables the transfer of models trained on source domains to unlabeled target domains. However, transferring complex time series models presents challenges due to the dynamic temporal structure variations across domains. This leads to feature shifts in the time and frequency representations. Additionally, the label distributions of tasks in the source and target domains can differ significantly, posing difficulties in addressing label shifts and recognizing labels unique to the target domain. Effectively transferring complex time series models remains a formidable problem. We present RAINCOAT, the first model for both closed-set and universal domain adaptation on complex time series. RAINCOAT addresses feature and label shifts by considering both temporal and frequency features, aligning them across domains, and correcting for misalignments to facilitate the detection of private labels. Additionally, RAINCOAT improves transferability by identifying label shifts in target domains. Our experiments with 5 datasets and 13 state-of-the-art UDA methods demonstrate that RAINCOAT can improve transfer learning performance by up to 16.33% and can handle both closed-set and universal domain adaptation.

paragraphs: A time-series model transferred to a new domain may encounter changes in both signal structure and labels. Patterns can shift in their timing and frequency content, while the relative prevalence of labels can change or new labels can appear. RAINCOAT addresses these difficulties when the target domain has no labels available for adaptation.

The method considers temporal and frequency features together, aligns them between source and target domains, and corrects misalignments to help detect labels private to the target. It also identifies label shifts to improve transferability. This supports both closed-set adaptation, where the label sets match, and universal adaptation, where the method must accommodate differences between those sets.

Experiments across five datasets and comparisons with 13 existing adaptation methods show transfer-learning improvements of up to 16.33%. This figure is a reported maximum, rather than an improvement promised for every transfer. The results support the value of addressing signal changes and label changes together, and demonstrate that RAINCOAT can handle both adaptation settings within the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: RAINCOAT adapts time-series models to unlabeled domains by jointly addressing temporal and frequency feature shifts and changes in labels.

title: Domain Adaptation for Time Series Under Feature and Label Shifts

abstract: Subgraph matching is a fundamental building block for graph-based applications and is challenging due to its high-order combinatorial nature. Existing studies usually tackle it by combinatorial optimization or learning-based methods. However, they suffer from exponential computational costs or searching the matching without theoretical guarantees. In this paper, we develop $D^2$Match by leveraging the efficiency of Deep learning and Degeneracy for subgraph matching. More specifically, we first prove that subgraph matching can degenerate to subtree matching, and subsequently is equivalent to finding a perfect matching on a bipartite graph. We can then yield an implementation of linear time complexity by the built-in tree-structured aggregation mechanism on graph neural networks. Moreover, circle structures and node attributes can be easily incorporated in $D^2$Match to boost the matching performance. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments to show the superior performance of our $D^2$Match and confirm that our $D^2$Match indeed exploits the subtrees and differs from existing GNNs-based subgraph matching methods that depend on memorizing the data distribution divergence.

paragraphs: Subgraph matching asks whether a graph contains a structure corresponding to another graph. Its difficulty comes from the many interacting choices involved in matching nodes and connections. The paper describes a tension between combinatorial approaches with exponential computational costs and learning approaches whose searches lack theoretical guarantees. D²Match aims to connect efficient learning with a structural account of matching.

The authors establish a reduction from subgraph matching to subtree matching, followed by an equivalence to finding a perfect matching in a bipartite graph. They use the tree-shaped aggregation already built into graph neural networks to obtain a linear-time implementation of their approach. Cycle structures and node attributes can also be incorporated to improve matching performance.

Experiments report superior performance and examine what the method uses to make its decisions. The authors find that D²Match exploits subtree information, distinguishing it from existing graph neural network approaches that depend on memorizing differences between data distributions. The contribution therefore concerns both computational design and evidence that matching behavior draws on relevant graph structure.
summary.tldr: D²Match connects subgraph matching to subtree and bipartite matching, using graph neural network aggregation for an efficient implementation.

title: D2Match: Leveraging Deep Learning and Degeneracy for Subgraph Matching

abstract: Many problems in machine learning require an estimate of the gradient of an expectation in discrete random variables with respect to the sampling distribution. This work is motivated by the development of the Gumbel-Softmax family of estimators, which use a temperature-controlled relaxation of discrete variables. The state-of-the art in this family, the Gumbel-Rao estimator uses an extra internal sampling to reduce the variance, which may be costly. We analyze this estimator and show that it possesses a zero temperature limit with a surprisingly simple closed form. The limit estimator, called ZGR, has favorable bias and variance properties, it is easy to implement and computationally inexpensive. It decomposes as the average of the straight through (ST) estimator and DARN estimator — two basic but not very well performing on their own estimators. We demonstrate that the simple ST–ZGR family of estimators practically dominates in the bias-variance tradeoffs the whole GR family while also outperforming SOTA unbiased estimators.

paragraphs: Learning with discrete random choices often requires estimating how an expected outcome changes when the sampling distribution changes. Gumbel-Softmax estimators address this using a relaxation controlled by a temperature parameter. The Gumbel-Rao estimator adds internal sampling to reduce variability in the gradient estimate, but that extra sampling can be computationally costly.

The authors analyze what happens as its temperature approaches zero. They show that the estimator has a limit with a simple closed-form expression, which they call ZGR. This limiting estimator is inexpensive and easy to implement, with favorable bias and variance properties. Its simplicity makes the mathematical limit useful as a practical estimator.

ZGR also has an unexpected structure: it averages the straight-through and DARN estimators, even though those two estimators perform relatively poorly individually. The authors report that the ST–ZGR family practically dominates the Gumbel-Rao family in bias–variance tradeoffs and outperforms state-of-the-art unbiased estimators. The findings show how analyzing a limiting case can produce a simpler computational method with strong empirical tradeoffs.
summary.tldr: Analyzing Gumbel-Rao at zero temperature yields a simple, inexpensive gradient estimator with favorable reported bias–variance tradeoffs.

title: Cold Analysis of Rao-Blackwellized Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax Gradient Estimator

abstract: The performance of a bandit algorithm is usually measured by the cumulative rewards of the actions chosen by the algorithm. However, in many real-world applications, the rewards in each round should be good enough for reasons such as safety and fairness. In this paper, we investigate the contextual conservative interleaving bandit problem, which has a performance constraint that requires the chosen actions to be not much worse than given baseline actions in each round. This work is the first to simultaneously consider the following practical situations: (1) multiple actions are chosen in a round, (2) the feature vectors associated with given actions depend on the round, and (3) the performance constraints in each round that depend only on the actions chosen in that round. We propose a meta-algorithm, Greedy on Confidence Widths (GCW), that satisfies the performance constraints with high probability. GCW uses a standard bandit algorithm and achieves minimax optimal regret up to logarithmic factors if the algorithm used is also minimax optimal. We improve the existing analyses for the C${}^2$UCB algorithm and the Thompson sampling to combine with GCW. We show that these algorithms achieve near-optimal regret when the feasible sets of given actions are the bases of a matroid. Our numerical experiments on a real-world dataset demonstrate that GCW with the standard bandit algorithms efficiently improves performance while satisfying the performance constraints.

paragraphs: A bandit algorithm can earn strong total rewards while making some poor individual decisions. This paper studies a stricter requirement: in each round, the selected actions must perform close enough to supplied baseline actions. The setting combines multiple actions per round, action features that change between rounds, and constraints evaluated using only the current round's choices.

The proposed Greedy on Confidence Widths, or GCW, is a meta-algorithm that works with a standard bandit algorithm. It satisfies the round-by-round performance constraints with high probability. If its underlying algorithm has minimax-optimal regret, GCW preserves that optimality up to logarithmic factors, linking conservative behavior to a qualified learning guarantee.

The authors also improve analyses of C²UCB and Thompson sampling for use with GCW. They establish near-optimal regret when feasible action sets are bases of a matroid, a particular combinatorial structure. Experiments on a real-world dataset show performance improving efficiently while the constraints remain satisfied, supporting the practical value of learning under a per-round safeguard.
summary.tldr: GCW adds high-probability per-round performance safeguards to bandit learning while preserving near-optimal regret under stated conditions.

title: Contextual Conservative Interleaving Bandits

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are instruction followers but the performance varies under different instructions. It is challenging to create the best instruction, especially for black-box LLMs on which backpropagation is forbidden. Instead of directly optimizing the discrete instruction, we optimize a low-dimensional soft prompt applied to an open-source LLM to generate the instruction for the black-box LLM. In each optimization step of the proposed method InstructZero, a soft prompt is converted into an instruction by the open-source LLM, which is then submitted to the black-box LLM for zero-shot evaluation, whose result is sent to Bayesian optimization to produce new soft prompts improving the zero-shot performance. We evaluate InstructZero on different combinations of open-source LLMs and APIs including Vicuna and ChatGPT. InstructZero outperforms SOTA auto-instruction methods across a variety of downstream tasks.

paragraphs: An instruction-following language model can perform very differently depending on how a task is phrased. Finding a good instruction becomes harder when the model is accessible only as a black box and gradients cannot be used. InstructZero tackles this by searching through an open-source model that generates instructions for the target model.

The search operates on a low-dimensional soft prompt rather than directly editing discrete instruction text. At each step, the open-source model turns that soft prompt into an instruction. The instruction is evaluated on the black-box model in a zero-shot setting, and the resulting performance feeds a Bayesian optimization procedure that proposes subsequent soft prompts.

This arrangement connects a continuous search space to usable natural-language instructions, with target-model evaluations guiding the process. The authors test different combinations of open-source models and APIs, including Vicuna and ChatGPT. They report improvements over state-of-the-art automatic instruction methods across varied downstream tasks, supporting the use of an accessible model as an intermediary for optimizing instructions to an inaccessible one.
summary.tldr: InstructZero uses Bayesian optimization and an open-source language model to discover better instructions for a black-box model.

title: InstructZero: Efficient Instruction Optimization for Black-Box Large Language Models

abstract: Offline design optimization problem arises in numerous science and engineering applications including material and chemical design, where expensive online experimentation necessitates the use of in silico surrogate functions to predict and maximize the target objective over candidate designs. Although these surrogates can be learned from offline data, their predictions are often inaccurate outside the offline data regime. This challenge raises a fundamental question about the impact of imperfect surrogate model on the performance gap between its optima and the true optima, and to what extent the performance loss can be mitigated. Although prior work developed methods to improve the robustness of surrogate models and their associated optimization processes, a provably quantifiable relationship between an imperfect surrogate and the corresponding performance gap, as well as whether prior methods directly address it, remain elusive. To shed light on this important question, we present a theoretical framework to understand offline black-box optimization, by explicitly bounding the optimization quality based on how well the surrogate matches the latent gradient field that underlines the offline data. Inspired by our theoretical analysis, we propose a principled black-box gradient matching algorithm to create effective surrogate models for offline optimization, improving over prior approaches on various real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: Offline design optimization uses existing observations to search for better designs when new experiments are expensive. A surrogate model predicts the objective for candidate designs and guides that search. The difficulty is that its predictions can become inaccurate beyond the observed data, so a design that looks excellent to the surrogate may fall short under the true objective.

The paper develops a theoretical framework connecting surrogate error to optimization quality. Its bound depends on how closely the surrogate matches the underlying gradient field: the pattern of directions in which the true objective changes. This provides a way to analyze the gap between optimizing the learned model and reaching the true optimum.

Motivated by that analysis, the authors propose a black-box gradient-matching algorithm for training surrogates. They report improvements over previous approaches on multiple real-world benchmarks. The contribution connects a theoretical measure of what makes a surrogate useful for optimization with a training method designed around that measure, rather than relying solely on the surrogate's predicted objective values.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds offline optimization quality through gradient-field matching and uses that analysis to train better surrogate models.

title: Learning Surrogates for Offline Black-Box Optimization via Gradient Matching

abstract: Variational families with full-rank covariance approximations are known not to work well in black-box variational inference (BBVI), both empirically and theoretically. In fact, recent computational complexity results for BBVI have established that full-rank variational families scale poorly with the dimensionality of the problem compared to e.g. mean-field families. This is particularly critical to hierarchical Bayesian models with local variables; their dimensionality increases with the size of the datasets. Consequently, one gets an iteration complexity with an explicit $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$ dependence on the dataset size $N$. In this paper, we explore a theoretical middle ground between mean-field variational families and full-rank families: structured variational families. We rigorously prove that certain scale matrix structures can achieve a better iteration complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(N\right)$, implying better scaling with respect to $N$. We empirically verify our theoretical results on large-scale hierarchical models.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a difficult probability distribution using a more manageable family of distributions. Choosing that family affects both flexibility and computational cost. In black-box variational inference, full-rank covariance approximations scale poorly with problem dimension. This becomes especially important in hierarchical Bayesian models with local variables, where dimension grows with dataset size.

The paper studies structured variational families as a middle ground between mean-field and full-rank approximations. Its focus is on how the structure of the scale matrix affects iteration complexity. For the setting discussed, full-rank families lead to an explicit quadratic dependence, O(N²), on the number of data points N.

The authors prove that certain scale-matrix structures improve this dependence to O(N). This establishes a theoretical scaling advantage for the specified structures, rather than for every structured family. Experiments on large hierarchical models support the theoretical findings. The result makes the choice of approximation structure a concrete computational decision: it can change how the required number of iterations grows as the dataset expands.
summary.tldr: Certain structured variational families reduce BBVI’s dataset-size dependence in iteration complexity from quadratic to linear.

title: Provably Scalable Black-Box Variational Inference with Structured Variational Families

abstract: Compositionality is a critical aspect of scalable system design. Here, we focus on Boolean composition of learned tasks as opposed to functional or sequential composition. Existing Boolean composition for Reinforcement Learning focuses on reaching a satisfying absorbing state in environments with discrete action spaces, but does not support composable safety (i.e., avoidance) constraints. We provide three contributions: i) introduce two distinct notions of compositional safety semantics; ii) show how to enforce either safety semantics, prove correctness, and analyze the trade-offs between the two safety notions; and iii) extend Boolean composition from discrete action spaces to continuous action spaces. We demonstrate these techniques using modified versions of value iteration in a grid world, Deep Q-Network (DQN) in a grid world with image observations, and Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) in a continuous-observation and continuous-action Bullet physics environment
