paragraphs: Combining learned tasks through Boolean logic offers a way to build more complex behavior from reusable parts. Earlier reinforcement learning approaches focused on reaching a satisfying terminal state in environments with discrete actions. They did not support composing avoidance constraints, leaving safety requirements outside that task-combination framework.

This paper introduces two distinct meanings of safety for Boolean task composition. The authors show how to enforce each meaning, prove the correctness of the corresponding constructions, and analyze their trade-offs. Making the safety semantics explicit matters because a composed task needs a clear account of what its avoidance requirements mean.

The work also extends Boolean composition to continuous action spaces. Demonstrations span modified value iteration in a grid world, a Deep Q-Network using image observations in a grid world, and TD3 in a Bullet physics environment with continuous observations and actions. These examples connect the formal treatment to multiple learning settings, showing how task composition with defined safety semantics can extend beyond discrete-state planning examples.
summary.tldr: The paper gives Boolean task composition two enforceable safety semantics and extends the framework to continuous actions.

title: Run-Time Task Composition with Safety Semantics

abstract: Traditionally, graph neural networks have been trained using a single observed graph. However, the observed graph represents only one possible realization. In many applications, the graph may encounter uncertainties, such as having erroneous or missing edges, as well as edge weights that provide little informative value. To address these challenges and capture additional information previously absent in the observed graph, we introduce latent variables to parameterize and generate multiple graphs. The parameters follow an unknown distribution to be estimated. We propose a formulation in terms of maximum likelihood estimation of the network parameters. Therefore, it is possible to devise an algorithm based on Expectation-Maximization (EM). Specifically, we iteratively determine the distribution of the graphs using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, incorporating the principles of PAC-Bayesian theory. Numerical experiments demonstrate improvements in performance against baseline models on node classification for both heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs.

paragraphs: A graph supplied to a neural network may have missing links, incorrect links, or edge weights that convey little useful information. Training on that single observed graph treats just one possible realization as the available structure. This paper instead represents uncertainty by introducing latent variables that parameterize multiple possible graphs.

The distribution governing those parameters is unknown and must be estimated. The authors formulate learning through maximum likelihood estimation of the network parameters, which supports an Expectation-Maximization algorithm. Their procedure iteratively estimates the graph distribution using Markov Chain Monte Carlo and incorporates principles from PAC-Bayesian theory. Graph structure thus becomes part of what the learning procedure estimates.

Numerical experiments show better node classification performance than baseline models on both homogeneous and heterogeneous graphs. These findings support learning with a distribution of graph structures when a single observed graph may be incomplete or unreliable. The central contribution is a probabilistic formulation that can capture information absent from the original graph while training the predictive model.
summary.tldr: The method learns a distribution of possible graphs to improve node classification when the observed graph may be unreliable.

title: Graph Neural Networks with a Distribution of Parametrized Graphs

abstract: Knowledge graph reasoning plays a vital role in various applications and has garnered considerable attention. Recently, path-based methods have achieved impressive performance. However, they may face limitations stemming from constraints in message-passing neural networks, such as missing paths and information over-squashing. In this paper, we revisit the application of transformers for knowledge graph reasoning to address the constraints faced by path-based methods and propose a novel method KnowFormer. KnowFormer utilizes a transformer architecture to perform reasoning on knowledge graphs from the message-passing perspective, rather than reasoning by textual information like previous pretrained language model based methods. Specifically, we define the attention computation based on the query prototype of knowledge graph reasoning, facilitating convenient construction and efficient optimization. To incorporate structural information into the self-attention mechanism, we introduce structure-aware modules to calculate query, key, and value respectively. Additionally, we present an efficient attention computation method for better scalability. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of KnowFormer compared to prominent baseline methods on both transductive and inductive benchmarks.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph reasoning uses relationships among entities to infer further connections. Path-based methods have performed well, but their message-passing machinery can miss useful paths or compress too much information into limited representations. KnowFormer revisits Transformers as a way to address these constraints through reasoning over graph structure.

The model defines attention around the query structure of knowledge graph reasoning. It introduces structure-aware modules for computing queries, keys, and values, allowing self-attention to incorporate information about the graph. This makes its use of a Transformer distinct from approaches that rely on pretrained language models to reason through textual information.

The authors also provide an efficient attention computation method to improve scalability. Experiments show that KnowFormer outperforms prominent baselines on both transductive and inductive benchmarks, covering both evaluation settings reported in the paper. The results support adapting attention specifically to graph reasoning queries and structure, while the efficient computation addresses the practical cost of applying that mechanism at greater scale.
summary.tldr: KnowFormer uses efficient, structure-aware Transformer attention for knowledge graph reasoning and outperforms prominent baselines on the reported benchmarks.

title: KnowFormer: Revisiting Transformers for Knowledge Graph Reasoning

abstract: With tremendous efforts on developing effective e-commerce models, conventional e-commerce models show limited success in generalist e-commerce modeling, and suffer from unsatisfactory performance on new users and new products – a typical out-of-domain generalization challenge. Meanwhile, large language models (LLMs) demonstrate outstanding performance in generalist modeling and out-of-domain generalizability in many fields. Toward fully unleashing their power for e-commerce, in this paper, we construct ECInstruct, the first open-sourced, large-scale, and high-quality benchmark instruction dataset for e-commerce. Leveraging ECInstruct, we develop eCeLLM, a series of e-commerce LLMs, by instruction-tuning general-purpose LLMs. Our comprehensive experiments and evaluation demonstrate that eCeLLM models substantially outperform baseline models, including the most advanced GPT-4, and the state-of-the-art task-specific models in in-domain evaluation. Moreover, eCeLLM exhibits excellent generalizability to out-of-domain settings, including unseen products and unseen instructions, highlighting its superiority as a generalist e-commerce model. Both the ECInstruct dataset and the eCeLLM models show great potential in empowering versatile and effective LLMs for e-commerce. ECInstruct and eCeLLM models are publicly accessible through this link.

paragraphs: E-commerce models must support varied tasks and cope with products or requests outside their training experience. The paper identifies limited generalist capability and weak out-of-domain performance as problems for conventional approaches. It explores whether instruction-tuned language models can provide a more broadly useful foundation for e-commerce applications.

The authors construct ECInstruct, an openly available, large-scale instruction dataset for e-commerce, described as the first of its kind. They use it to instruction-tune general-purpose language models, producing the eCeLLM model family. The dataset and models form a combined contribution: domain-focused instructions provide the training material for adapting general language capabilities to e-commerce tasks.

In the reported in-domain evaluations, eCeLLM substantially outperforms the compared baselines, including GPT-4 and state-of-the-art task-specific models. It also generalizes well to unseen products and unseen instructions. These findings support its proposed role as a generalist e-commerce model across the evaluated settings. Public availability of both ECInstruct and eCeLLM makes the training resource and resulting models accessible for further work.
summary.tldr: eCeLLM uses the ECInstruct dataset to adapt language models for e-commerce, reporting strong in-domain results and generalization to unseen products and instructions.

title: eCeLLM: Generalizing Large Language Models for E-commerce from Large-scale, High-quality Instruction Data

abstract: Environment annotations are essential for the success of many out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization methods. Unfortunately, these are costly to obtain and often limited by human annotators’ biases. To achieve robust generalization, it is essential to develop algorithms for automatic environment discovery within datasets. Current proposals, which divide examples based on their training error, suffer from one fundamental problem. These methods introduce hyper-parameters and early-stopping criteria, which require a validation set with human-annotated environments, the very information subject to discovery. In this paper, we propose Cross-Risk Minimization (XRM) to address this issue. XRM trains twin networks, each learning from one random half of the training data, while imitating confident held-out mistakes made by its sibling. XRM provides a recipe for hyper-parameter tuning, does not require early-stopping, and can discover environments for all training and validation data. Algorithms built on top of XRM environments achieve oracle worst-group-accuracy, addressing a long-standing challenge in OOD generalization.
originalAbstract: Environment annotations are essential for the success of many out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization methods. Unfortunately, these are costly to obtain and often limited by human annotators’ biases. To achieve robust generalization, it is essential to develop algorithms for automatic environment discovery within datasets. Current proposals, which divide examples based on their training error, suffer from one fundamental problem. These methods introduce hyper-parameters and early-stopping criteria, which require a validation set with human-annotated environments, the very information subject to discovery. In this paper, we propose Cross-Risk Minimization (XRM) to address this issue. XRM trains twin networks, each learning from one random half of the training data, while imitating confident held-out mistakes made by its sibling. XRM provides a recipe for hyper-parameter tuning, does not require early-stopping, and can discover environments for all training and validation data. Algorithms built on top of XRM environments achieve oracle worst-group-accuracy, addressing a long-standing challenge in OOD generalization.

paragraphs: Many methods for generalizing beyond the training distribution rely on environment labels that identify different conditions within a dataset. Obtaining these labels can be expensive and shaped by annotator bias. Existing automatic discovery methods can also create a circular dependency: tuning their settings requires validation data with the environment labels they aim to discover.

Cross-Risk Minimization addresses this problem with two networks trained on separate random halves of the training data. Each network imitates confident mistakes its sibling makes on held-out examples. This unusual use of errors forms the basis of the environment-discovery procedure, which also supplies a recipe for hyperparameter tuning and avoids early stopping.

XRM can assign discovered environments to both training and validation data. The authors report that downstream algorithms using these environments achieve oracle worst-group accuracy. That finding supports the usefulness of the discovered divisions for robust learning: they enable performance on the weakest group comparable to the oracle result reported in the study.
summary.tldr: XRM discovers environments through twin networks that learn from each other's confident mistakes, supporting robust learning without human-labeled environments for tuning.

title: Discovering Environments with XRM

abstract: We propose to understand Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining model (CLIP) from the Optimal Transport (OT) perspective. Specifically, we show that training of CLIP is an embodiment of inverse OT and the adopted two InfoNCE losses in CLIP correspond to a special case of bilevel optimization of modified entropic OT. We then generalize the original CLIP loss to an OT-based loss family using variants of Regularized OT (e.g. Fused Gromov OT, unbalanced OT, etc.), and demonstrate their superior performance on public datasets for both image and text downstream tasks. We also rethink the inference stage of CLIP by using the tool of OT, and propose to adopt the fused Gromov OT for (zero-shot) classification, in which the prediction is based on the graph representation whereby images and texts are nodes for graph matching. By our new technique, we show how to generalize zero-shot classification to other more flexible zero-shot tasks with competitive performance: long-tailed classification and selective classification. The former assumes the known prior distribution of labels, while in the latter case, only a subset of samples are asked to predict, yet with high prediction confidence.

paragraphs: The paper interprets CLIP's image-text learning through optimal transport, a framework for matching distributions. It shows that CLIP training can be understood as inverse optimal transport, with its two contrastive losses corresponding to a particular bilevel formulation of modified entropic transport. This provides a mathematical starting point for changing the training objective.

The authors use that connection to construct a family of losses based on regularized transport variants, including fused Gromov and unbalanced transport. These alternatives outperform the original approach on public datasets for both image and text downstream tasks. The same perspective also motivates a revised inference procedure based on matching graphs whose nodes represent images and texts.

This graph-matching formulation extends zero-shot classification to more flexible settings with competitive reported performance. For long-tailed classification, the method assumes a known prior distribution over labels. For selective classification, it predicts only a subset of samples with high confidence. The contribution therefore spans both how image-text representations are trained and how they are used for prediction.
summary.tldr: An optimal transport interpretation of CLIP yields new training losses and graph-matching inference for flexible zero-shot classification.

title: OT-CLIP: Understanding and Generalizing CLIP via Optimal Transport

abstract: We study the problem of preferential Bayesian optimization (BO), where we aim to optimize a black-box function with only preference feedback over a pair of candidate solutions. Inspired by the likelihood ratio idea, we construct a confidence set of the black-box function using only the preference feedback. An optimistic algorithm with an efficient computational method is then developed to solve the problem, which enjoys an information-theoretic bound on the total cumulative regret, a first-of-its-kind for preferential BO. This bound further allows us to design a scheme to report an estimated best solution, with a guaranteed convergence rate. Experimental results on sampled instances from Gaussian processes, standard test functions, and a thermal comfort optimization problem all show that our method stably achieves better or competitive performance as compared to the existing state-of-the-art heuristics, which, however, do not have theoretical guarantees on regret bounds or convergence.

paragraphs: Preferential Bayesian optimization searches for a good solution when feedback only indicates which of two candidates is preferred. The learner does not receive direct function values. This paper develops a principled way to manage uncertainty and guide that search using pairwise preference information alone.

Inspired by likelihood ratios, the authors construct a confidence set of possible black-box functions. An optimistic algorithm then uses that uncertainty representation to choose promising candidates, supported by an efficient computational method. The analysis gives an information-theoretic bound on cumulative regret and uses it to derive a procedure for reporting an estimated best solution with a guaranteed convergence rate.

Experiments include functions sampled from Gaussian processes, standard test functions, and a thermal comfort optimization problem. The method consistently performs better than or competitively with the compared leading heuristics. Its significance is the combination of practical search performance and theoretical control over accumulated regret and final-solution convergence, guarantees that the compared heuristics do not provide.
summary.tldr: A preference-only Bayesian optimization method combines competitive empirical search with regret and convergence guarantees.

title: Principled Preferential Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Most studies on causal inference tackle the issue of confounding bias by reducing the distribution shift between the control and treated groups. However, it remains an open question to adopt an appropriate metric for distribution shift in practice. In this paper, we define a generic balancing error on reweighted samples to characterize the confounding bias, and study the connection between the balancing error and the Wasserstein discrepancy derived from the theory of optimal transport. We not only regard the Wasserstein discrepancy as the metric of distribution shift, but also explore the association between the balancing error and the underlying cost function involved in the Wasserstein discrepancy. Motivated by this, we propose to reduce the balancing error under the framework of optimal transport with learnable marginal distributions and the cost function, which is implemented by jointly learning weights and representations associated with factual outcomes. The experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

paragraphs: Causal inference methods often try to reduce confounding by making treated and control groups more comparable. A central difficulty is deciding how to measure the remaining difference between their distributions. This paper defines a general balancing error for reweighted samples and uses it to study how distribution matching relates to confounding bias.

The authors connect this error to Wasserstein discrepancy, an optimal-transport measure of distribution differences. They also examine the cost function underlying that discrepancy. This matters because the cost determines how differences between samples contribute to the overall measure, so choosing a distribution distance also involves choosing which sample differences it emphasizes.

The proposed method learns both the marginal distributions and the transport cost. It implements this through joint learning of sample weights and representations associated with factual outcomes. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach’s effectiveness. The contribution is a formulation that connects weighting and representation learning to the balancing error the method aims to reduce, rather than treating the discrepancy metric as an isolated choice.
summary.tldr: A causal inference method jointly learns sample weights and representations to reduce balancing error through optimal transport.

title: Reducing Balancing Error for Causal Inference via Optimal Transport

abstract: AUC maximization is an effective approach to address the imbalanced data classification problem in federated learning. In the past few years, a couple of federated AUC maximization approaches have been developed based on the minimax optimization. However, directly solving a minimax optimization problem to maximize the AUC score cannot achieve satisfactory performance. To address this issue, we propose to maximize AUC via optimizing a federated multi-level compositional minimax problem. Specifically, we develop a novel federated multi-level compositional minimax algorithm with rigorous theoretical guarantees to solve this new learning paradigm in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work studying the multi-level minimax optimization problem. Additionally, extensive empirical evaluations confirm the efficacy of our proposed approach.

Specifically, we develop a novel federated multi-level compositional minimax algorithm with rigorous theoretical guarantees to solve this new learning paradigm in both algorithmic design and theoretical analysis. paragraphs: The paper studies federated classification when the available data are imbalanced. It focuses on maximizing AUC, an objective the authors identify as useful for this problem. Their starting point is that existing federated approaches based on directly solving a minimax problem have not delivered satisfactory performance. This motivates changing the optimization formulation itself.

The proposed formulation is a multi-level compositional minimax problem. In plain language, it combines nested stages of computation with an optimization structure involving opposing minimization and maximization objectives. The contribution therefore includes both a new way to express the learning problem and a federated stochastic algorithm designed to solve that formulation.

The authors provide rigorous theoretical guarantees for their algorithm and report extensive empirical evaluations supporting its effectiveness. These are complementary contributions: the analysis supports the proposed optimization procedure, while the experiments support its usefulness for learning. The paper positions multi-level compositional minimax optimization as a promising route for improving federated AUC maximization, and describes its study of multi-level minimax optimization as a first to the authors’ knowledge.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a federated multi-level compositional minimax algorithm for AUC maximization, supported by theoretical guarantees and empirical evaluations.

title: A Federated Stochastic Multi-level Compositional Minimax Algorithm for Deep AUC Maximization

abstract: We propose a computationally efficient alternative to generalized random forests (GRFs) for estimating heterogeneous effects in large dimensions. While GRFs rely on a gradient-based splitting criterion, which in large dimensions is computationally expensive and unstable, our method introduces a fixed-point approximation that eliminates the need for Jacobian estimation. This gradient-free approach preserves GRF’s theoretical guarantees of consistency and asymptotic normality while significantly improving computational efficiency. We demonstrate that our method achieves a speedup of multiple times over standard GRFs without compromising statistical accuracy. Experiments on both simulated and real-world data validate our approach. Our findings suggest that the proposed method is a scalable alternative for localized effect estimation in machine learning and causal inference applications.

This gradient-free approach preserves GRF’s theoretical guarantees of consistency and asymptotic normality while significantly improving computational efficiency. We demonstrate that our method achieves a speedup of multiple times over standard GRFs without compromising statistical accuracy. Experiments on both simulated and real-world data validate our approach. Our findings suggest that the proposed method is a scalable alternative for localized effect estimation in machine learning and causal inference applications.

paragraphs: Generalized random forests estimate effects that can vary across different parts of a dataset. Their tree-building procedure uses a gradient-based rule to decide where to split. In large dimensions, computing that rule can become expensive and unstable. This paper targets that computational bottleneck while retaining the statistical foundations of the original approach.

The proposed trees replace the gradient-based calculation with a fixed-point approximation. This removes the need to estimate a Jacobian, the collection of derivatives used in the original calculation. The resulting splitting approach is gradient-free. The authors show that it preserves the generalized random forest guarantees of consistency and asymptotic normality, maintaining the theoretical basis for estimation as data grows.

Experiments on simulated and real-world data show speedups of multiple times over standard generalized random forests without compromising statistical accuracy. The findings suggest that changing the internal approximation used to build trees can substantially reduce computational demands. The authors position the method as a scalable alternative for localized effect estimation in machine learning and causal inference.
summary.tldr: Fixed-point trees avoid Jacobian estimation in generalized random forests, improving speed while preserving statistical guarantees and reported accuracy.

title: Generalized Random Forests Using Fixed-Point Trees

abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum acceleration in addressing infinite horizon Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to enhance average reward outcomes. We introduce an innovative quantum framework for the agent’s engagement with an unknown MDP, extending the conventional interaction paradigm. Our approach involves the design of an optimism-driven tabular Reinforcement Learning algorithm that harnesses quantum signals acquired by the agent through efficient quantum mean estimation techniques. Through thorough theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the quantum advantage in mean estimation leads to exponential advancements in regret guarantees for infinite horizon Reinforcement Learning. Specifically, the proposed Quantum algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$[$\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ conceals logarithmic terms of $T$.], a significant improvement over the $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ bound exhibited by classical counterparts, where $T$ is the length of the time horizon.

Through thorough theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that the quantum advantage in mean estimation leads to exponential advancements in regret guarantees for infinite horizon Reinforcement Learning. Specifically, the proposed Quantum algorithm achieves a regret bound of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$[$\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\cdot)$ conceals logarithmic terms of $T$.], a significant improvement over the $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T})$ bound exhibited by classical counterparts, where $T$ is the length of the time horizon.

paragraphs: This paper investigates quantum acceleration for reinforcement learning in an unknown Markov decision process with an infinite-horizon average-reward objective. It introduces a framework that extends conventional agent-environment interaction to include quantum signals. That interaction framework is an important part of the setting in which the paper establishes its theoretical advantage.

The proposed algorithm is tabular and driven by optimism. It uses efficient quantum mean estimation to extract information from the available quantum signals. The analysis connects the advantage of quantum mean estimation to improved regret guarantees, where regret measures the reward shortfall accumulated while the agent learns.

The stated bound is constant order up to factors logarithmic in the horizon length, compared with the square-root horizon dependence of the cited classical counterparts. The authors characterize this as an exponential improvement in regret guarantees. Because the notation suppresses logarithmic terms, the result should not be read as strictly constant regret. It is a theoretical improvement under the proposed quantum interaction framework.
summary.tldr: Under a quantum interaction framework, quantum mean estimation yields average-reward reinforcement-learning regret with only suppressed logarithmic horizon dependence.

title: Quantum Speedups in Regret Analysis of Infinite Horizon Average-Reward Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Randomized dimensionality reduction is a widely-used algorithmic technique for speeding up large-scale Euclidean optimization problems. In this paper, we study dimension reduction for a variety of maximization problems, including max-matching, max-spanning tree, as well as various measures for dataset diversity. For these problems, we show that the effect of dimension reduction is intimately tied to the doubling dimension $\lambda_X$ of the underlying dataset $X$—a quantity measuring intrinsic dimensionality of point sets. Specifically, the dimension required is $O(\lambda_X)$, which we also show is necessary for some of these problems. This is in contrast to classical dimension reduction results, whose dependence grow with the dataset size $|X|$. We also provide empirical results validating the quality of solutions found in the projected space, as well as speedups due to dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: Randomized dimensionality reduction can speed up geometric optimization by moving data into a space with fewer coordinates. This paper studies that approach for Euclidean maximization problems, including maximum matching, maximum spanning trees, and measures of dataset diversity. The central question is how many dimensions these tasks require after projection.

The authors show that the answer is closely connected to the dataset's doubling dimension, a measure of its intrinsic dimensionality. The required projected dimension scales linearly with that quantity. They also establish that this dependence is necessary for some of the problems considered. This differs from classical dimension-reduction results whose dimensional requirements grow with the number of data points.

The distinction matters because dataset size and intrinsic geometric complexity describe different aspects of the input. The theory ties compression requirements to the latter for the studied objectives. Empirical results additionally support the quality of solutions obtained in the projected space and demonstrate speedups from dimensionality reduction, connecting the geometric analysis to computational benefits.
summary.tldr: For several geometric maximization tasks, useful projection dimension scales with intrinsic doubling dimension rather than dataset size.

title: Randomized Dimensionality Reduction for Euclidean Maximization and Diversity Measures

abstract: Complex query answering (CQA) on knowledge graphs (KGs) is gaining momentum as a challenging reasoning task. In this paper, we show that the current benchmarks for CQA might not be as complex as we think, as the way they are built distorts our perception of progress in this field. For example, we find that in these benchmarks most queries (up to 98% for some query types) can be reduced to simpler problems, e.g., link prediction, where only one link needs to be predicted. The performance of state-of-the-art CQA models decreses significantly when such models are evaluated on queries that cannot be reduced to easier types. Thus, we propose a set of more challenging benchmarks composed of queries that require models to reason over multiple hops and better reflect the construction of real-world KGs. In a systematic empirical investigation, the new benchmarks show that current methods leave much to be desired from current CQA methods.

paragraphs: Complex query answering is intended to test reasoning over knowledge graphs, including questions involving several connections. This paper finds that existing benchmark construction can make such tasks easier than their form suggests. A query that appears to require several reasoning steps may reduce to predicting a single missing link.

The authors report that up to 98% of queries for some benchmark query types can be simplified into easier problems. When state-of-the-art models are evaluated on queries that cannot be reduced this way, performance falls significantly. This means strong aggregate scores on those benchmarks can give an inflated impression of progress on genuinely multi-step reasoning.

The paper introduces harder benchmarks whose queries require reasoning across multiple hops and whose construction better reflects real-world knowledge graphs. A systematic empirical evaluation reveals substantial remaining weaknesses in current methods. The contribution changes what the evaluation demands: it makes successful performance depend more directly on the reasoning capability the task is supposed to measure.
summary.tldr: Many complex-query benchmarks admit simpler solutions, and new benchmarks requiring multiple hops expose substantial weaknesses in current methods.

title: Is Complex Query Answering Really Complex?

abstract: Model merging based on task vectors, i.e., the parameter differences between fine-tuned models and a shared base model, provides an efficient way to integrate multiple task-specific models into a multitask model without retraining. Recent works have endeavored to address the conflicts between task vectors, one of the significant challenges faced by model merging, through sparsification; however, two issues significantly limit their performance: high parameter overlap and unbalanced weight distribution. To address these issues, we propose a simple yet effective framework called CABS (Conflict-Aware and Balanced Sparsification), consisting of Conflict-Aware Sparsification (CA) and Balanced Sparsification (BS). CA reduces parameter overlap by applying masks during sequential pruning, ensuring that each task vector retains distinct, non-overlapping parameters. BS leverages $n$:$m$ pruning to preserve critical weights while maintaining an even distribution across layers. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that CABS outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse tasks and model sizes.

To address these issues, we propose a simple yet effective framework called CABS (Conflict-Aware and Balanced Sparsification), consisting of Conflict-Aware Sparsification (CA) and Balanced Sparsification (BS). paragraphs: Model merging combines models trained for different tasks into a single multitask model without retraining. In the setting studied here, each specialized model shares a base model, and its task vector records the parameter changes made during fine-tuning. Combining these vectors can create conflicts when different tasks depend on incompatible changes to the same parameters.

The paper identifies two problems with existing attempts to reduce those conflicts through sparsification: retained parameters still overlap substantially, and the remaining weights are distributed unevenly. CABS addresses them with two components. Conflict-Aware Sparsification applies masks during sequential pruning so that task vectors retain distinct, non-overlapping parameters. Balanced Sparsification uses n:m pruning to preserve important weights while keeping their distribution across layers even.

These components address different aspects of the merge: which tasks retain particular parameter locations, and how the retained weights are distributed. Experiments across varied tasks and model sizes report improvements over leading merging methods. The findings support treating overlap and balance together when deciding which fine-tuning changes should survive a merge.
summary.tldr: CABS improves model merging by assigning task vectors non-overlapping parameters and balancing retained weights across layers.

title: CABS: Conflict-Aware and Balanced Sparsification for Enhancing Model Merging

abstract: We propose S3 (Specialization, Selection, Sparsification), a framework that rethinks multimodal learning through a structural perspective. Instead of encoding all signals into a fixed embedding, S3 decomposes multimodal inputs into semantic experts and selectively routes them for each task. Specialization forms concept-level experts in a shared latent space, Selection adapts routing for task-specific needs, and Sparsification prunes low-utility paths to yield compact, information-minimal representations. Across four MultiBench benchmarks, S3 improves accuracy and exhibits consistent sparsity-performance dynamics, exhibiting a reverse U-shaped trend, with performance peaking at intermediate sparsity. These results suggest that structuring multimodal representations as selectable semantic components provides a practical and principled alternative to contrastive learning or InfoMax-driven approaches.

Specialization forms concept-level experts in a shared latent space, Selection adapts routing for task-specific needs, and Sparsification prunes low-utility paths to yield compact, information-minimal representations. Across four MultiBench benchmarks, S3 improves accuracy and exhibits consistent sparsity-performance dynamics, exhibiting a reverse U-shaped trend, with performance peaking at intermediate sparsity. paragraphs: Multimodal learning combines information from different input types, often by encoding their signals into a fixed representation. S3 instead organizes that information into semantic experts that can be selected according to the task. The aim is to give the representation an internal structure whose components can be used selectively.

The framework has three connected stages. Specialization creates concept-level experts in a shared latent space. Selection determines which experts should contribute for a particular task. Sparsification then removes low-utility paths, producing compact representations with less retained information. These stages make the organization and routing of semantic components part of the learning approach, rather than treating the final embedding as a single fixed package.

Across four MultiBench benchmarks, S3 improves accuracy and shows a consistent reverse-U relationship between sparsity and performance. Intermediate sparsity performs best, so the observed benefit does not increase indefinitely as more paths are removed. The findings suggest that selectively retaining useful semantic components offers a practical alternative to contrastive or information-maximization-driven approaches to multimodal representation learning.
summary.tldr: S3 structures multimodal representations into selectable semantic experts, with evaluated performance peaking at intermediate levels of sparsity.

title: Toward Structural Multimodal Representations: Specialization, Selection, and Sparsification via Mixture-of-Experts

abstract: Recent progress in large-scale flow and diffusion models raised two fundamental algorithmic challenges: $(i)$ control-based reward adaptation of pre-trained flows, and $(ii)$ integration of multiple models, i.e., flow merging. While current approaches address them separately, we introduce a unifying probability-space framework that subsumes both as limit cases, and enables reward-guided flow merging, allowing principled, task-aware combination of multiple pre-trained flows (e.g., merging priors while maximizing drug-discovery utilities). Our formulation renders possible to express a rich family of operators over generative models densities, including intersection (e.g., to enforce safety), union (e.g., to compose diverse models), interpolation (e.g., for discovery), their reward-guided counterparts, as well as complex logical expressions via generative circuits. Next, we introduce Reward-Guided Flow Merging (RFM), a mirror-descent scheme that reduces reward-guided flow merging to a sequence of standard fine-tuning problems. Then, we provide first-of-their-kind theoretical guarantees for reward-guided and pure flow merging via RFM. Ultimately, we showcase the capabilities of the proposed method on illustrative settings providing visually interpretable insights, and apply our method to high-dimensional de-novo molecular design and low-energy conformer generation.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained generative flow to a reward and combining several flows are usually treated as separate problems. This paper places both inside one framework that operates on probability distributions. That formulation also supports doing both together: combining pretrained models while steering the resulting distribution toward a task-specific objective.

The framework expresses several ways to combine model densities. Intersections represent overlapping requirements, unions combine alternatives, and interpolation blends distributions. Reward-guided versions add a preference for desirable outputs. The authors also describe generative circuits that compose these operations into more complex logical expressions, giving model combination a richer vocabulary than a single blending rule.

To make the formulation usable, the paper introduces Reward-Guided Flow Merging, a mirror-descent procedure that turns the overall problem into successive standard fine-tuning tasks. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for both reward-guided merging and merging without rewards. They illustrate the method in visually interpretable settings and apply it to molecular design and low-energy conformer generation, demonstrating its use beyond simple examples.
summary.tldr: A probability-space framework unifies flow adaptation and model merging, with an algorithm that reduces reward-guided combination to repeated fine-tuning.

title: A Unified Density Operator View of Flow Control and Merging

abstract: Accurate prediction in survival analysis with competing risks is challenged by rare event rates and limited effective sample sizes. Knowledge distillation offers a promising way to transfer information from an external teacher to improve a local student, but existing methods are overwhelmingly developed for uncensored outcomes and do not directly extend to survival analysis, where censored observations provide only partial information. Moreover, prior work often assumes that teacher and student share identical outcome definitions, whereas in competing risks settings, they may differ in outcome granularity and event definitions, further complicating knowledge transfer. To address these gaps, we propose DiSKD (Discrete Survival Knowledge Distillation), a deep learning framework for discrete-time competing risks that integrates teacher predictions via a cause-specific, time-dependent Kullback-Leibler divergence. DiSKD enables flexible and privacy-conscious transfer without requiring raw data sharing, remains robust to model misspecification or outcome-definition heterogeneity, and adaptively weights teacher guidance by emphasizing compatible teachers while down-weighting less relevant ones. Simulation studies and real-world applications demonstrate improved discrimination and calibration.

paragraphs: Predicting time to an event becomes harder when events are rare and several event types compete. Censoring adds another complication because some observations provide only partial outcome information. DiSKD addresses how an external predictive model can help a local model in this setting, including when their definitions of outcomes do not align exactly.

The framework works in discrete time and transfers teacher predictions through a Kullback–Leibler divergence that varies by event cause and time. This gives the transfer mechanism a structure suited to competing risks. It also adapts the strength of teacher guidance, placing more weight on compatible teachers and less on teachers whose information is less relevant.

The authors report robustness to model misspecification and differences in outcome definitions, alongside improved discrimination and calibration in simulations and real-world applications. Those improvements concern both distinguishing outcomes and making probabilities agree with observed outcomes. Because transfer uses predictions without requiring raw-data sharing, the framework offers a privacy-conscious route to incorporating external information, without the abstract claiming a formal privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: DiSKD transfers external predictions into competing-risk survival models using cause- and time-specific guidance that adapts to teacher compatibility.

title: Discrete Survival Knowledge Distillation for Competing Risks Analysis

abstract: We introduce Hybrid Space-aware Stochastic Convolution Attention Noise (HySCAN), a hybrid randomized defense that helps close the long-standing gap between provable robustness under $\ell$2 certificates and empirical robustness against strong $\ell$$\infty$ attacks, while maintaining strong generalization across diverse imaging benchmarks. HySCAN jointly explores complementary sources of stochasticity at both training and inference: (i) implicit weight-space randomness via stochastic-aware Random Weights, and (ii) explicit feature-space randomness via Stochastic Attention Noise Injection modules. By incorporating randomness at both the parameter and representation levels, HySCAN enables meaningful certified guarantees while improving empirical robustness in practice. Comprehensive experiments on diverse imaging datasets, e.g., CelebA, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, HAM10000, and NIH Chest X-ray, demonstrate that HySCAN outperforms existing certified and empirical defenses, improving certified robustness by up to $\approx$ 9.6% and empirical robustness by up to $\approx$ 5% without reducing clean accuracy.

paragraphs: HySCAN targets two aspects of adversarial robustness: mathematically certified protection under an l2 measure and observed resistance to strong attacks under an l-infinity measure. These evaluate different properties of a defense. The paper aims to narrow the gap between them while preserving performance on ordinary, unperturbed images.

The approach combines randomness in two parts of the model. Stochastic-aware random weights introduce randomness at the parameter level, while stochastic attention noise modules introduce it into internal feature representations. The framework uses these complementary sources during training and inference, seeking both meaningful certificates and stronger practical resistance to attacks.

Experiments span several imaging datasets, including CelebA, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1k, HAM10000, and NIH Chest X-ray. The authors report improvements over existing certified and empirical defenses of up to approximately 9.6% in certified robustness and 5% in empirical robustness, without reducing clean accuracy. These are maximum reported improvements across the experiments, supporting the combined design without establishing equal gains for every dataset or attack.
summary.tldr: HySCAN combines parameter and feature randomness to improve certified and empirical adversarial robustness without reducing clean accuracy in reported experiments.

title: Does a Hybrid Space-Aware Randomized Defense Improve Empirical and Certified Adversarial Robustness?

abstract: Neural Flows efficiently model irregular multivariate time series by directly learning ODE solution trajectories with neural networks, bypassing step-by-step numerical solvers. Despite their efficiency, many existing approaches treat variables independently, leaving inter-variable interactions underexplored. Moreover, their one-step mapping makes interaction modeling inherently challenging, as it removes the iterative refinement of interactions during learning. To address this challenge, we propose one-step Graph-Structured Neural Flows (GSNF), which introduce two auxiliary-trajectory self-supervision strategies to strengthen interaction learning: (i) interaction-aware trajectory generation via re-initialization, which induces trajectory divergence to expose graph-induced interactions, with a theoretically derived lower bound on divergence; and (ii) reverse-time trajectory generation, which enforces forward–backward consistency to regularize graph learning, enabled by flow invertibility. Experiments on five real-world datasets show that GSNF achieves state-of-the-art classification performance with highly competitive training time and memory usage. The code is available at https://github.com/mzgaooo/GSNF.

paragraphs: Neural flows model irregularly sampled time series by directly learning trajectories that would otherwise require numerical differential-equation solvers. This provides efficiency, but many approaches underuse relationships among variables. Learning those relationships is particularly challenging when a single mapping replaces the repeated interaction refinement available in step-by-step methods.

Graph-Structured Neural Flows add two forms of auxiliary trajectory supervision. Re-initializing trajectories makes their divergence reveal graph-driven interactions, with a theoretical lower bound characterizing that divergence. Generating trajectories backward in time adds a consistency requirement between forward and reverse evolution. The latter uses flow invertibility to help regularize the learned graph.

These auxiliary tasks give interaction learning additional structure while preserving the one-step flow approach. On five real-world datasets, GSNF achieves state-of-the-art classification performance with highly competitive training time and memory usage. The reported results suggest that direct trajectory models can capture useful variable relationships when their training includes explicit signals about how interactions affect trajectory changes and reversibility.
summary.tldr: GSNF uses auxiliary forward and reverse trajectories to strengthen interaction learning in efficient one-step time-series models.

title: One-Step Graph-Structured Neural Flows for Irregular Multivariate Time Series Classification

abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have substantially expanded the scope of Table Question Answering (TableQA). However, existing benchmarks primarily treat TableQA as a passive, single-turn natural language understanding task, lacking the capacity to evaluate autonomous reasoning and tool-call trajectories in realistic, multi-turn scenarios. To bridge this gap, we introduce TableAgent-Bench, a large-scale bilingual benchmark that reformulates TableQA as proactive, agentic interactions over structurally complex, multi-table environments. With a topology-aware construction strategy, TableAgent-Bench captures dynamic intent evolution through 1,310 multi-turn dialogues grounded in 2,275 industrial tables. Furthermore, we propose the Table-centric Agent Evaluation Framework (TAEF) to assess agent interactions with complex table structures. Specifically, TAEF integrates a specialized agent toolset and 4 metric categories to systematically diagnose intermediate failure modes, assessing performance across table localization, tool-invocation rationality, and trajectory-level pass rate. Extensive experiments with 25 state-of-the-art LLM agents reveal a substantial capability gap, with even the strongest model Gemini-3-Pro-Preview achieving only 53.4% information coverage. We expect TableAgent-Bench to serve as a rigorous testbed for developing and evaluating agents capable of robust table-centric reasoning.

paragraphs: Answering questions about tables can require more than interpreting a single question and returning one answer. An agent may need to locate relevant tables, choose tools, and respond as the user’s intent changes over several turns. TableAgent-Bench is designed to evaluate this more active setting, which existing single-turn benchmarks largely miss.

The bilingual benchmark contains 1,310 multi-turn dialogues grounded in 2,275 industrial tables. Its construction accounts for table topology and includes structurally complex environments involving multiple tables. summary.tldr: TableAgent-Bench exposes weaknesses in agents’ multi-turn table reasoning by evaluating table selection, tool use, and interaction trajectories.

title: How Far Can LLM Agents Reason with Tables? Benchmarking Multi-Turn Agentic Table Question Answering in the Wild

abstract: LLM agents operate in two distinct regimes: open-weight agents amenable to reinforcement learning (RL) and black-box agents whose behaviour must be controlled purely at test time. Although black-box agents are often backed by state-of-the-art proprietary LLMs, API-only access precludes parameter-level optimization, rendering most RL methods inapplicable. To address this limitation, we turn to a known equivalence between RL and Bayesian inference. We propose Agentic Monte Carlo (AMC) to directly sample from the optimal policy of a black-box agent rather than training it through RL. The optimal policy is a posterior over trajectories whose prior we define as the fixed black-box LLM agent. We employ Sequential Monte Carlo to sample from this posterior by learning a value function to steer the agent while leaving the underlying black-box model unchanged. We validate AMC on three diverse environments from the AgentGym benchmark, demonstrating significant improvements over prompting baselines and even outperforming Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) as we scale the test-time compute of our method. AMC demonstrates the feasibility of performing principled RL-style optimization of black-box LLM agents.

paragraphs: An agent accessed only through an API cannot have its model parameters updated through ordinary reinforcement learning. This creates a gap between the capabilities of powerful proprietary models and the training methods available to improve their behavior. Agentic Monte Carlo addresses that gap by moving optimization to test-time sampling.

The method uses an equivalence between reinforcement learning and Bayesian inference. It treats the fixed agent as a prior over possible trajectories and represents the optimal policy as a posterior over those trajectories. Sequential Monte Carlo samples from this posterior, with a learned value function guiding the process. The underlying language model stays unchanged, although the steering value function is learned.

These results support the feasibility of reinforcement-learning-style optimization through guided trajectory sampling, showing how additional computation and a learned steering component can improve an agent without parameter access.
summary.tldr: Agentic Monte Carlo improves API-only agents through value-guided trajectory sampling, achieving reinforcement-learning-style optimization without updating the underlying model.

title: Agentic Monte Carlo: Simulating Reinforcement Learning for Black-Box Agents

abstract: Code translation transforms source code from one programming language (PL) to another. Validating the functional equivalence of translation and repairing, if necessary, are critical steps in code translation. Existing automated validation and repair approaches struggle to generalize to many PLs due to high engineering overhead, and they rely on existing and often inadequate test suites, which results in false claims of equivalence and ineffective translation repair. To bridge this gap, we develop MatchFixAgent, a large language model (LLM)-based, PL-agnostic framework for equivalence validation and repair of translations. MatchFixAgent features a multi-agent architecture that divides equivalence validation into several sub-tasks to ensure thorough and consistent semantic analysis of the translation. We compare MatchFixAgent’s validation and repair results with four repository-level code translation techniques. Our results demonstrate that MatchFixAgent produces (in)equivalence verdicts for $99.2$% of translation pairs, with the same equivalence validation result as prior work on $72.8$% of them. When MatchFixAgent’s result disagrees with prior work, we find that $60.7$% of the time MatchFixAgent’s result is actually correct. In addition, we show that MatchFixAgent can repair $50.6$% of inequivalent translation, compared to prior work’s $18.5$%.

paragraphs: Translating a software repository into another programming language requires checking whether the translated code preserves behavior. Existing validation and repair approaches can be costly to adapt across languages and depend on test suites that miss important differences. Passing those tests can therefore produce an incorrect conclusion that two versions are equivalent.

MatchFixAgent uses a language-model-based multi-agent architecture to divide equivalence checking into several subtasks. The framework is designed to work across programming languages and to repair translations judged inequivalent. Its emphasis on semantic analysis addresses the difficulty of determining whether translated code means and does the same thing.

It agrees with prior work on 72.8%; among disagreements, its judgment is correct 60.7% of the time. It also repairs 50.6% of inequivalent translations, versus 18.5% for prior work. These figures distinguish verdict availability, agreement, correctness in disputed cases, and repair success, rather than treating them as a single accuracy measure.
summary.tldr: MatchFixAgent uses multiple language-model agents to validate translated repositories and repairs more inequivalent translations than the evaluated prior approaches.

title: MatchFixAgent: Language-Agnostic Autonomous Repository-Level Code Translation Validation and Repair

abstract: Modern cloud systems rely on architectures with many interconnected microservices, which enable scalability and flexibility but make troubleshooting failures difficult. Identifying the root cause requires navigating complex dependencies, often beyond the capacity of domain experts. Causal models offer a principled approach to root cause analysis (RCA), but prior methods are typically sample inefficient, as they assume access to the full causal graph or require large numbers of post-failure interventions. We introduce Bayesian Root Cause Discovery (BRCD), which leverages a partial causal structure (a CPDAG learned during the pre-failure period) and performs Bayesian inference without enumerating all DAGs from each interventional Markov equivalence class ($\mathcal{I}$-MEC) for each root cause candidate. Using a recent uniform DAG sampling framework (Wienöbst et al., 2023), BRCD provides the first statistical consistency guarantees for nonparametric RCA, with both identifiability and finite-sample posterior bounds under $\varepsilon$-vanishing approximation. Empirically, across synthetic benchmarks and three microservice systems (Online Boutique, Sockshop, Petshop), BRCD achieves state-of-the-art top-$l$ accuracy while remaining effective in low-failure-sample regimes and scaling to large graphs.

paragraphs: Failures can propagate through interconnected microservices, making the original cause hard to distinguish from downstream symptoms. Causal approaches help, but often assume a complete graph or require many interventions after a failure. Bayesian Root Cause Discovery uses partial structure learned before failure to reduce that burden.

The method starts from a CPDAG representing causal ambiguity and performs Bayesian inference over candidate causes without enumerating every compatible directed graph. A uniform DAG-sampling framework supports the computation. The authors establish identification, consistency, and finite-sample posterior guarantees under an approximation condition.

Synthetic tests and the Online Boutique, Sockshop, and Petshop systems show state-of-the-art top-list accuracy, including with few failure samples and large graphs. The contribution combines uncertainty over causal structure with sample-efficient diagnosis. Its causal guarantees depend on the analyzed model and approximation conditions, rather than treating every statistical dependency in operational telemetry as a confirmed causal link.
summary.tldr: BRCD uses partial pre-failure causal structure and Bayesian graph sampling to identify microservice root causes with limited failure data.

title: Root Cause Analysis of Failures in Microservices via Bayesian Root Cause Discovery

abstract: Despite a large corpus of recent work on scaling up Gaussian processes, a stubborn trade-off between computational speed, prediction, and uncertainty quantification accuracy, and customizability persists. This is because the vast majority of existing methodologies exploit various levels of approximation that lower accuracy and limit the flexibility of kernel and noise-model designs — an unacceptable drawback at a time when expressive non-stationary kernels are on the rise in many fields. Here, we propose a methodology we term gp2Scale that scales exact Gaussian processes to more than 10 million data points without relying on inducing points, kernel interpolation, or neighborhood-based approximations, and instead leverages the existing capabilities of a GP: its kernel design. Highly flexible, compactly supported, and non-stationary kernels lead to the identification of naturally occurring sparse structure in the covariance matrix, which is then exploited to compute the linear system solution and the log-determinant for training. We demonstrate our method’s functionality on several real-world datasets and compare it with state-of-the-art approximation algorithms. Although we show superior approximation performance in many cases, the method’s real power lies in its agnosticism toward arbitrary GP customizations — core kernel design, noise, and mean functions — and the type of input space, making it optimally suited for modern Gaussian process applications.

It uses flexible, non-stationary kernels with compact support, so the sparsity belongs to the specified model itself.

The method exploits that structure to compute the linear-system solution and log-determinant needed for training, alongside distributed computation. It scales exact Gaussian processes beyond 10 million data points without inducing points, kernel interpolation, or neighborhood-based approximations. They emphasize its flexibility toward kernel, noise, and mean-function customization and different input spaces. The broader contribution is a route to large-scale Gaussian processes that preserves expressive modeling choices while obtaining computational savings from the covariance structure.
summary.tldr: gp2Scale uses naturally sparse covariance matrices and distributed computation to scale exact Gaussian processes beyond 10 million data points.

title: gp2Scale: A Class of Compactly Supported Non-Stationary Kernels and Distributed Computing for Exact Gaussian Processes on 10 Million Data Points

abstract: The Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Hidden Markov Model (HDP-HMM) is a Bayesian nonparametric extension of the classical Hidden Markov Model, well-suited for learning from (spatio-)temporal data. To relax the restrictive geometric assumption on state durations, the HDP Hidden Semi-Markov Model was introduced. However, both models assume stationary state durations, which limits their expressive power. In this work, we extend the HDP-HMM framework by incorporating recurrent explicit duration modeling, resulting in a more general and flexible model: the Recurrent Explicit Duration HDP-HMM (RED-HDP-HMM). We propose a Gibbs sampling method for efficient inference in this model. Empirical results on both synthetic and real-world segmentation tasks demonstrate that RED-HDP-HMM consistently outperforms the disentangled sticky HDP-HMM and the standard sticky HDP-HMM.

To relax the restrictive geometric assumption on state durations, the HDP Hidden Semi-Markov Model was introduced. However, both models assume stationary state durations, which limits their expressive power. In this work, we extend the HDP-HMM framework by incorporating recurrent explicit duration modeling, resulting in a more general and flexible model: the Recurrent Explicit Duration HDP-HMM (RED-HDP-HMM). We propose a Gibbs sampling method for efficient inference in this model. paragraphs: Sequential models need to represent both which hidden state is active and how long that state persists. The Hierarchical Dirichlet Process Hidden Markov Model provides a Bayesian nonparametric approach to temporal data, but its state durations follow a restrictive geometric assumption. A semi-Markov extension relaxes that restriction, yet both models still assume stationary durations.

The paper introduces RED-HDP-HMM, which adds recurrent, explicit duration modeling to the HDP-HMM framework. Its observation-dependent durations provide a more flexible account of persistence than the stationary assumptions of the earlier models. The authors also propose a Gibbs sampling procedure for efficient inference, making the expanded model usable for learning from sequences.

Tests on synthetic and real-world segmentation tasks show consistent improvements over the disentangled sticky HDP-HMM and standard sticky HDP-HMM. These findings support treating duration behavior as a richer component of the sequential model. In segmentation, that matters because identifying a sequence's underlying states involves understanding their persistence as well as distinguishing their observations.
summary.tldr: RED-HDP-HMM adds observation-dependent duration modeling and improves segmentation over two sticky HDP-HMM variants.

title: RED-HDP-HMM: Observation-Dependent Durations for Bayesian Nonparametric Sequential Models

abstract: We present Reading Observed At Mindless Moments (ROAMM), a multimodal dataset comprising 50 hours of simultaneous EEG and eye-tracking recordings collected during naturalistic multi-page reading from 44 participants. ROAMM includes synchronized physiological recordings, eye-movement events, page-level comprehension scores, and span-level mind-wandering (MW) annotations obtained using a retrospective self-report paradigm. We introduce a standardized leave-one-subject-out benchmark for MW detection and achieve up to 0.609 AUROC using supervised models. We additionally evaluate EEG-to-text decoding on reading segments with and without MW labels, showing that decoding performance decreases during MW episodes. ROAMM enables research on MW detection, EEG-to-text decoding, multimodal representation learning, and attention-related degradation of language representations during naturalistic reading.
originalAbstract: We present Reading Observed At Mindless Moments (ROAMM), a multimodal dataset comprising 50 hours of simultaneous EEG and eye-tracking recordings collected during naturalistic multi-page reading from 44 participants. ROAMM includes synchronized physiological recordings, eye-movement events, page-level comprehension scores, and span-level mind-wandering (MW) annotations obtained using a retrospective self-report paradigm. We introduce a standardized leave-one-subject-out benchmark for MW detection and achieve up to 0.609 AUROC using supervised models. We additionally evaluate EEG-to-text decoding on reading segments with and without MW labels, showing that decoding performance decreases during MW episodes. ROAMM enables research on MW detection, EEG-to-text decoding, multimodal representation learning, and attention-related degradation of language representations during naturalistic reading.

paragraphs: ROAMM is a dataset for studying attention during naturalistic reading across multiple pages. It contains 50 hours of simultaneous EEG and eye tracking from 44 participants. The synchronized recordings connect brain activity and eye movements with page-level comprehension scores and annotations identifying spans of mind-wandering.

The mind-wandering labels come from retrospective self-reports. The authors introduce a standardized leave-one-subject-out evaluation, testing detection on a participant excluded from model training. Supervised models achieve up to 0.609 AUROC. This supplies a benchmark for comparing detection approaches under a participant-transfer setting, alongside the physiological and behavioral measurements needed to investigate them.

The paper also evaluates decoding text from EEG during reading segments with and without mind-wandering labels. Decoding performance decreases during mind-wandering episodes, linking the annotated attention state to differences in text-decoding performance. Together, the dataset and evaluations support research on attention detection, multimodal representations, and how attention-related changes affect language information recoverable from EEG during reading.
summary.tldr: ROAMM pairs EEG, eye tracking, and mind-wandering annotations to benchmark attention detection and EEG-to-text decoding during reading.

title: ROAMM: A Benchmark Dataset for Multimodal Human Attention Decoding and EEG-to-Text Modeling During Naturalistic Reading

abstract: Speech Large Language Models (SLLMs) enable high-level emotion reasoning, but often produce ungrounded, text-biased judgments without verifiable acoustic evidence. In contrast, SSL encoders such as WavLM yield strong acoustic representations yet remain opaque discriminative models that offer limited interpretability. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Agentic Decoding of Emotion via Probing Tools (ADEPT) framework, which reframes emotion recognition as a multi-turn inquiry process rather than a single-pass prediction. ADEPT transforms an SLLM into an agent that maintains an evolving candidate set and adaptively invokes dedicated semantic and acoustic probing tools within a structured pipeline of candidate generation, evidence collection, and adjudication. Crucially, ADEPT enables a paradigm shift from consensus learning to ambiguity-driven emotion reasoning. Since human affect exhibits complexity and co-occurrence of emotions, we leverage minority annotations as informative signals instead of discarding them as noise. Finally, we integrate Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with the Evidence Trust Gate to explicitly couple tool-usage behaviors with prediction quality and enforce evidence-based reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that ADEPT improves in most cases the primary emotion accuracy while substantially improving minor emotion characterization, producing explanations grounded in auditable evidence.

In contrast, SSL encoders such as WavLM yield strong acoustic representations yet remain opaque discriminative models that offer limited interpretability. To bridge this gap, we introduce the Agentic Decoding of Emotion via Probing Tools (ADEPT) framework, which reframes emotion recognition as a multi-turn inquiry process rather than a single-pass prediction. ADEPT transforms an SLLM into an agent that maintains an evolving candidate set and adaptively invokes dedicated semantic and acoustic probing tools within a structured pipeline of candidate generation, evidence collection, and adjudication. Crucially, ADEPT enables a paradigm shift from consensus learning to ambiguity-driven emotion reasoning. Since human affect exhibits complexity and co-occurrence of emotions, we leverage minority annotations as informative signals instead of discarding them as noise. Finally, we integrate Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with the Evidence Trust Gate to explicitly couple tool-usage behaviors with prediction quality and enforce evidence-based reasoning. Experiments demonstrate that ADEPT improves in most cases the primary emotion accuracy while substantially improving minor emotion characterization, producing explanations grounded in auditable evidence.

paragraphs: ADEPT treats recognizing emotion in speech as a process of gathering and weighing evidence. The paper addresses a gap between speech language models, which can explain judgments but may rely too heavily on words, and acoustic encoders, which capture useful sound information but provide limited interpretability.

The system maintains several candidate emotions and revises them through multiple rounds. It calls specialized tools to examine semantic and acoustic evidence, then uses that evidence to adjudicate between candidates. It also treats minority human annotations as potentially informative. This matters because disagreement can reflect overlapping or ambiguous emotions rather than simply incorrect labeling.

Training combines Group Relative Policy Optimization with an Evidence Trust Gate to connect tool use to prediction quality and evidence-based reasoning. Experiments report improvements in primary-emotion accuracy in most cases, alongside substantial gains in characterizing minor emotions. The contribution is therefore both a recognition framework and a way to produce explanations whose supporting evidence can be inspected.
summary.tldr: ADEPT uses iterative semantic and acoustic probing to recognize overlapping emotions and explain its judgments with auditable evidence.

title: ADEPT: RL-Aligned Agentic Decoding of Emotion via Evidence Probing Tools — From Consensus Learning to Ambiguity-Driven Emotion Reasoning

abstract: DeepSeek-OCR leverages visual–text compression to reduce long-text processing costs and accelerate inference, yet visual tokens remain prone to redundant textual and structural information. Moreover, current token pruning methods for conventional vision–language models (VLMs) fail to preserve textual fidelity due to improper compression mechanisms. By analyzing the decoding process of DeepSeek-OCR, we find that a distinct two-stage reading trajectory: the model initially prioritizes the majority of high-norm tokens, then subsequently redistributes its attention to the remaining ones. Motivated by this insight, we propose RTPrune, a two-stage token pruning method tailored for DeepSeek-OCR. In the first stage, we prioritize high-norm visual tokens that capture salient textual and structural information. In the second stage, the remaining tokens are paired and merged based on optimal transport theory to achieve efficient feature aggregation. We further introduce a dynamic pruning ratio that adapts to token similarity and textual density for OCR tasks, enabling a better efficiency–accuracy trade-off. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, as evidenced by 99.47% accuracy and 1.23$\times$ faster prefill on OmniDocBench, achieved with 84.25% token retention when applied to DeepSeek-OCR-Large. Code is released.

A dynamic pruning ratio responds to token similarity and textual density, adapting the amount of compression to the document’s information rather than applying a single fixed ratio.

The speed figure refers specifically to prefill, not the entire inference process. These results support designing pruning around the OCR model’s observed reading behavior to improve efficiency while preserving textual accuracy.
summary.tldr: RTPrune follows DeepSeek-OCR’s two-stage reading pattern to reduce visual tokens while preserving accuracy and accelerating prefill.

title: RTPrune: Reading-Twice Inspired Token Pruning for Efficient DeepSeek-OCR Inference

abstract: Flow-based text-to-image models follow deterministic trajectories, making it costly to explore diverse modes under limited sampling budgets. Existing approaches to improving diversity often rely on retraining or degrade image fidelity. To address this limitation, we present a training-free, inference-time control mechanism that makes the flow itself diversity-aware. Our core insight is to encourage diversity through guidance that is geometrically decoupled from the model’s quality-seeking direction. Our method simultaneously encourages lateral spread among trajectories via a feature-space objective and reintroduces uncertainty through a time-scheduled stochastic perturbation. Crucially, this perturbation is projected to be orthogonal to the generation flow, a geometric constraint that allows it to boost variation without degrading image details or prompt fidelity. Theoretically, we show that this design monotonically increases a volume surrogate while approximately preserving the marginal distribution, providing a principled explanation for the robustness of generation quality. Empirically, across multiple text-to-image settings under fixed sampling budgets, our method consistently improves diversity metrics such as the Vendi Score and Brisque over strong baselines, while upholding image quality and alignment.
