paragraphs: Flow-based image generators follow deterministic generation trajectories, which can make exploring varied outputs costly when only a limited number of samples is available. This paper introduces an inference-time method that encourages trajectories to spread apart without retraining the model. Its organizing idea is to separate diversity-promoting changes geometrically from the flow’s quality-seeking direction.

The method combines a feature-space objective that pushes trajectories laterally apart with stochastic perturbations whose strength is scheduled over time. These perturbations are projected perpendicular to the generation flow. The intention is to introduce variation while protecting image details and fidelity to the prompt, addressing the quality tradeoff that can accompany diversity interventions.

The theoretical result shows monotonic growth of a volume surrogate while approximately preserving the marginal distribution. That approximation is part of the stated guarantee. Across multiple text-to-image settings with fixed sampling budgets, the authors report improvements in metrics including Vendi Score and Brisque over strong baselines while maintaining image quality and alignment. Together, the analysis and experiments support geometric control as a practical way to obtain more varied samples.
summary.tldr: An inference-time geometric control method increases flow-model output diversity while maintaining quality and prompt alignment in the reported experiments.

title: Letting Trajectories Spread: Quality-Preserving Control for Diverse Flow Matching

abstract: Learning mappings between infinite-dimensional function spaces, or operator learning, is essential for many machine learning applications. Although transformer-based operators are popular, they often rely on token-wise attention. These methods treat continuous fields as discrete tokens and usually ignore the global functional structure. We introduce Functional Attention, which reinterprets attention as a functional correspondence between adaptive bases. Inspired by geometric functional maps, our method replaces softmax affinities with structured linear operators. This yields a compact, generalizable, resolution-invariant representation that explicitly captures global dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that Functional Attention can match state-of-the-art performance in many operator learning tasks, including solving PDEs, 3D segmentation, and regression, while remaining robust to varying discretizations. Project page is available at https://github.com/xjffff/FUNCATTN.

paragraphs: Functional Attention targets operator learning, where a model learns mappings between functions rather than only between fixed collections of values. Transformer-based approaches often turn a continuous field into discrete tokens and compare those tokens through attention. This representation can overlook the field’s global functional structure, making the choice of representation central to the task.

The proposed method expresses attention as a correspondence between adaptive bases, which provide learned ways to represent functions. Inspired by geometric functional maps, it replaces softmax-based pairwise affinities with structured linear operators. This allows attention to describe relationships at the level of the represented functions and explicitly capture global dependencies in a compact form.

The paper reports that this representation is resolution-invariant and generalizable. Across operator-learning tasks that include solving partial differential equations, three-dimensional segmentation, and regression, Functional Attention can match state-of-the-art performance while remaining robust to different discretizations. The results support functional correspondences as a useful alternative when the same underlying information may be sampled at different resolutions.
summary.tldr: Functional Attention models relationships between function representations to capture global structure and remain robust across discretizations.

title: Functional Attention: From Pairwise Affinities to Functional Correspondences

abstract: Mean-field variational inference (VI) is scalable, but its independence assumption can severely limit inference when the posterior is inherently coupled across instances especially for correlated data. Existing structured VI approaches either impose simple dependence patterns or incur substantial cost as dependence becomes richer, leaving efficient higher-order instance-level dependence modeling largely unresolved. We propose Copula-SVI, which augments amortized marginals with an explicit vine-copula posterior and refines joint samples with Stein updates toward the true posterior. The vine construction makes dependence learning and sampling practical by decomposing it into bivariate copula factors, enabling edge-minibatched training with variance-aware level-wise sampling and efficient dependence-aware initialization via a sparse vine built from the same sampled edges. Experiments on constrained clustering and time series modeling show consistent improvements over strong structured VI baselines and demonstrate efficient higher-order instance-level dependence modeling.

paragraphs: Copula-SVI improves approximate probabilistic inference when different data instances are strongly related. Mean-field variational inference is scalable because it assumes independence, but that simplification can miss important relationships in a coupled posterior. More structured alternatives can capture dependence, although richer relationships often bring substantial computational costs.

The method combines learned marginal distributions with a vine copula, an explicit construction for connecting those distributions. The vine represents complex dependence through a collection of two-variable factors, making learning and sampling more manageable. It then refines joint samples with Stein updates that move them toward the true posterior. This separates modeling individual distributions from learning how their outcomes vary together.

For efficiency, training uses minibatches of vine edges and a sampling strategy that accounts for variance at different levels. A sparse vine constructed from the same sampled edges also provides an initialization that incorporates dependence. Experiments on constrained clustering and time-series modeling report consistent improvements over strong structured inference baselines, supporting the approach as an efficient way to capture higher-order relationships between instances.
summary.tldr: Copula-SVI combines vine-based dependence modeling with Stein refinement to improve inference on correlated data efficiently.

title: Copula-SVI: Vine-Copula Variational Inference with Stein Refining for Instance-Level Correlation Capturing

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strengths across diverse domains. However, achieving strong performance across these domains with a single general-purpose model typically requires scaling to sizes that are prohibitively expensive to train and deploy. On the other hand, while smaller domain-specialized models are much more efficient, they struggle to generalize beyond their training distributions. To address this dilemma, we propose FusionRoute, a robust and effective token-level multi-LLM collaboration framework in which a lightweight router simultaneously (i) selects the most suitable expert at each decoding step and (ii) contributes a complementary logit that refines or corrects the selected expert’s next-token distribution via logit addition. Unlike existing token-level collaboration methods that rely solely on fixed expert outputs, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that pure expert-only routing is fundamentally limited: unless strong global coverage assumptions hold, it cannot in general realize the optimal decoding policy. By augmenting expert selection with a trainable complementary generator, FusionRoute expands the effective policy class and enables recovery of optimal value functions under mild conditions. Empirically, across both Llama-3 and Gemma-2 families and diverse benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, FusionRoute outperforms both sequence- and token-level collaboration, model merging, and direct fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with domain experts on their respective tasks.

paragraphs: Specialized language models can be efficient within their domains but struggle outside them. FusionRoute combines their strengths during generation through a lightweight router that makes a new choice at every token. The router both selects an expert and contributes an additional logit signal that adjusts the expert’s next-token distribution.

The corrective signal is central to the method. The theoretical analysis shows that routing among fixed expert outputs generally cannot realize the optimal decoding policy unless strong global coverage assumptions hold. Adding a trainable complementary generator expands the available policy class and permits recovery of optimal value functions under mild conditions.

Experiments use both Llama-3 and Gemma-2 model families across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following. FusionRoute outperforms the evaluated sequence-level and token-level collaboration methods, model merging, and direct fine-tuning, while remaining competitive with specialists on their own tasks. These findings support combining expert selection with learned correction, rather than treating selection alone as sufficient for broad capability.
summary.tldr: FusionRoute selects an expert for each token and learns a corrective logit signal to expand what their collaboration can achieve.

title: Token-Level LLM Collaboration via FusionRoute

abstract: Distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) models the full return distribution, but typically relies on finite-dimensional categorical or quantile approximations, often involving projection or quantile-regression approximations to the Bellman target, together with independently sampled bootstrap targets that obscure transport structure and add variance. We present Path-Coupled Bellman Flows (PCBF), a continuous-time DRL method that encodes Bellman endpoint consistency and pathwise Bellman-coupled geometry within generative flow trajectories. PCBF represents return distributions via flow matching and couples the paths of consecutive states through shared base noise, yielding a geometric Bellman flow relation between velocity fields. This structure enables a $\lambda$-parameterized control-variate target that reduces training variance while preserving the source and Bellman endpoint geometry. Experiments on analytically tractable MRPs, OGBench, and D4RL show improved distributional fidelity, training stability, and competitive offline RL performance.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning predicts the full distribution of future returns. Common methods approximate that distribution with categories or quantiles, and independently sampled training targets can introduce variance while obscuring relationships between consecutive states. Path-Coupled Bellman Flows instead represents return distributions using continuous generative flows trained through flow matching.

The method connects the flow paths for consecutive states by giving them shared starting noise. This coupling creates a Bellman relation between their velocity fields, linking the geometry along the paths as well as consistency at their endpoints. A control-variate target, adjustable through a parameter called lambda, uses this structure to reduce training variance while preserving the source and Bellman endpoint geometry.

Experiments include analytically tractable Markov reward processes, OGBench, and D4RL. They show better fidelity to return distributions, more stable training, and competitive offline reinforcement learning performance. These findings support using the relationship between whole generative paths to improve distribution learning, with benefits in both the represented distributions and the training process.
summary.tldr: Path-Coupled Bellman Flows links generative return-distribution paths across states to reduce variance and improve distributional fidelity.

title: Path-Coupled Bellman Flows for Distributional Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advances in generative models, such as diffusion models, have raised concerns related to privacy, copyright infringement, and data curation. Prior work has shown that training data can be reconstructed from such models, but existing attacks typically rely on substantial computational resources, access to the training set, or carefully engineered prompts. In this work, we present a low-resource reconstruction attack that operates through seemingly benign prompts and requires little to no access to the training data. Our attack targets template-memorized images (TMI), where recurring layouts and visual structures are memorized during training. We show that such memorization manifests under potentially realistic usage. This raises a possibility of unintentional reconstruction by naive users that don’t carry explicit adversarial intent. For example, we observe that a simple prompt such as "blue Unisex T-Shirt" can reproduce visual content depicting a real individual. Beyond extraction, we observe novel phenomena occurring in TMI (e.g., interpolation), raising questions about the novelty of generated content and the effectiveness of established methods for detecting memorized content. Our code is available at https://github.com/TheSolY/lr-tmi.

paragraphs: This paper studies a form of image memorization centered on recurring layouts and visual structures. The authors call these template-memorized images. Their concern is that an image generator can reproduce memorized visual content through ordinary-looking prompts, even when the person prompting it has little or no access to the training data.

The proposed reconstruction attack requires few resources and does not depend on carefully engineered prompts or extensive training-set access. In one reported example, a simple request for a blue unisex T-shirt reproduces visual content depicting a real individual. The observation raises the possibility that users without adversarial intent could unintentionally reconstruct memorized content during plausible everyday use.

The authors also observe interpolation phenomena in template memorization. These findings raise questions about how to judge the novelty of generated images and whether established memorization detectors capture this form of reproduction effectively. The paper’s contribution is to demonstrate an accessible reconstruction pathway and characterize behavior that extends beyond straightforward extraction of an obviously memorized image.
summary.tldr: Ordinary-looking prompts can reconstruct template-memorized visual content with few resources and little or no training-data access.

title: Reconstructing Template-Memorized Images from Natural Prompts

abstract: Any-to-any models predict any modality from any combination of others within a single network – a formulation used in multimodal vision and vision-language models, and increasingly in scientific domains such as ecology and astronomy. Existing any-to-any models are typically trained from scratch using encoder-decoder or diffusion architectures, impacting their performance and preventing them from using strong pre-trained decoder-only models as a prior. In this work, we investigate decoder-only any-to-any multimodal modeling, which treats all modalities symmetrically and supports arbitrary modalities as inputs and outputs without modality-specific heads, losses, or task pipelines. Because every modality is both an input and an output of the same model, the resulting model, named MODUS, can support a range of applications, such as chained generation through intermediate modalities or cross-modal self-verification by scoring the model’s own outputs with another generated modality. MODUS demonstrates strong out-of-the-box performance and is competitive with specialist and multitask baselines using a single model across various benchmarks. All materials are open-sourced.

paragraphs: Any-to-any modeling aims to predict one modality from any combination of other modalities using a single network. This paper explores a decoder-only approach to that goal. The motivation is that common encoder-decoder and diffusion approaches are typically trained from scratch, preventing them from using strong pretrained decoder-only models as a starting prior.

MODUS treats modalities symmetrically: every modality can serve as both input and output within the same model. It does so without separate modality-specific heads, losses, or task pipelines. This shared formulation makes it possible to reuse one model for different directions of prediction instead of organizing each direction as a separate task-specific system.

That symmetry also supports chained generation through intermediate modalities and cross-modal self-verification, where another generated modality helps score the model’s outputs. Across several benchmarks, MODUS reports strong out-of-the-box performance and competitiveness with specialist and multitask baselines. The findings show that a single decoder-only model can support diverse multimodal prediction roles while enabling these additional ways to generate and assess outputs.
summary.tldr: MODUS uses one decoder-only model for symmetric any-to-any multimodal prediction, enabling chained generation and cross-modal self-verification.

title: MODUS: Decoder-only Any-to-Any Modeling of Diverse Modalities

abstract: Generative tabular augmentation is appealing in data-scarce domains, yet the prevailing focus on distributional fidelity does not reliably translate into better downstream models. We formalize a fidelity-utility gap: common generative objectives prioritize distributional plausibility, whereas augmentation succeeds only when injected samples reduce the current learner’s held-out evaluation loss. This gap motivates learning not just how to generate, but what to generate and when to inject as training evolves. We propose TAP (Tabular Augmentation Policy), which couples diffusion inpainting with a lightweight, learner-conditioned policy to steer generation toward high-utility regions and controls safe injection via explicit gating and conservative windowed commitment. Under severe data scarcity, TAP consistently outperforms strong generative baselines on seven real-world datasets, improving classification accuracy by up to 15.6 percentage points and reducing regression RMSE by up to 32%.

paragraphs: Generating realistic table rows does not necessarily improve a model trained on them. This paper formalizes that distinction as a gap between fidelity and utility: a generator can reproduce plausible data while failing to reduce the learner’s loss on held-out examples. The useful augmentation target therefore depends on the learner, not just on the original data distribution.

The proposed Tabular Augmentation Policy, or TAP, couples diffusion inpainting with a lightweight policy informed by the current learner. The policy steers generation toward regions expected to help learning and determines when generated samples enter training. Explicit gating and conservative commitment over windows regulate injection, making sample selection and timing part of the augmentation process.

Under severe data scarcity, TAP consistently outperforms strong generative baselines on seven real-world datasets. Reported improvements reach 15.6 percentage points in classification accuracy and a 32% reduction in regression RMSE. These results support treating augmentation as an adaptive training decision, where the value of synthetic examples is assessed through their contribution to the downstream learner.
summary.tldr: TAP adapts what synthetic tabular data to generate and when to use it, improving downstream learning under severe data scarcity.

title: Active Tabular Augmentation via Policy-Guided Diffusion Inpainting

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated exceptional capabilities when trained within executable runtime environments, notably excelling at software engineering tasks through verified feedback loops. Yet, scalable and generalizable execution-grounded environments remain scarce, limiting progress in training more capable ML agents. We introduce CTF-Dojo, the first large-scale executable runtime tailored for training LLMs with verifiable feedback, featuring 658 fully functional Capture-The-Flag (CTF)-style challenges containerized in Docker with guaranteed reproducibility. To enable rapid scaling without manual intervention, we develop CTF-Forge, an automated pipeline that transforms publicly available artifacts into ready-to-use execution environments in minutes, eliminating weeks of expert configuration traditionally required. We trained LLM-based agents on just 486 high-quality, execution-verified trajectories from CTF-Dojo, achieving up to 11.6% absolute gains over strong baselines across three competitive benchmarks: InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench, and Cybench. Our best-performing 32B model reaches 31.9% Pass@1, establishing a new open-weight state-of-the-art that rivals frontier models like DeepSeek-V3-0324 and Gemini-2.5-Flash. By framing CTF-style tasks as a benchmark for executable-agent learning, CTF-Dojo demonstrates that execution-grounded training signals are not only effective but pivotal in advancing high-performance ML agents without dependence on costly proprietary systems.

paragraphs: Training agents through executable tasks provides feedback that can verify whether their actions worked. CTF-Dojo expands this kind of training infrastructure with 658 functional Capture-The-Flag challenges packaged in Docker for reproducibility. The environment targets a shortage of scalable execution-grounded tasks for developing language-model agents.

An accompanying pipeline, CTF-Forge, converts publicly available artifacts into executable environments automatically. The paper reports that this takes minutes, replacing configuration work that traditionally required weeks of expert effort. This automation matters because the training resource includes runnable challenges and verifiable interaction outcomes, rather than only static descriptions of tasks.

Agents trained on 486 high-quality, execution-verified trajectories achieve gains of up to 11.6 percentage points over strong baselines across InterCode-CTF, NYU CTF Bench, and Cybench. The best 32B model reaches 31.9% Pass@1, which the paper reports as an open-weight state of the art rivaling named frontier models. These results support the effectiveness of verified execution feedback for training capable agents.
summary.tldr: CTF-Dojo provides reproducible executable security challenges whose verified training trajectories improve agent performance across three CTF benchmarks.

title: Training Language Model Agents to Find Vulnerabilities with CTF-Dojo

abstract: This position paper argues that building a reliable agentic Web requires shifting from low-level interaction primitives to typed actions supported by a semantic layer. Today’s web agents primarily operate through clicks, keystrokes, and DOM manipulation, which leads to brittle long-horizon behavior, high execution cost, and limited auditability. We propose web verbs as a concrete design for this layer. A verb exposes a web operation as a typed function with structured inputs, structured outputs, and documented behavior, whether it is backed by a server-side Web API or a maintained client-side workflow. Verb calls can carry preconditions, postconditions, policy tags, and logging hooks, allowing agents to synthesize concise programs with explicit control flow and data flow and to produce checkable execution traces. Using representative case studies, we illustrate how verb-level composition can produce correct, reproducible outcomes, while browser agents using low-level interaction primitives may produce brittle behavior or incorrect reasoning. We conclude with a call to action on standardization, developer tooling, and community processes needed to make this semantic layer deployable and trustworthy at web scale.

paragraphs: This paper argues that reliable web agents need operations expressed at a higher level than clicks, keystrokes, and page manipulation. Long sequences of these low-level interactions can be fragile, expensive, and difficult to audit. The proposed alternative is a semantic layer that gives web operations explicit meaning and structured interfaces.

The authors call these operations web verbs. Each verb is a typed function with structured inputs and outputs plus documented behavior. It may use a server API or a maintained client-side workflow underneath. Preconditions, postconditions, policy tags, and logging hooks can make requirements and outcomes explicit, allowing agents to compose concise programs with inspectable control and data flow.

Representative case studies illustrate how composing verbs can yield correct, reproducible outcomes where low-level browser interactions may become brittle or support incorrect reasoning. The paper then calls for standards, developer tools, and community processes to make the approach deployable at web scale. Its contribution combines an interface design with an agenda for making those interfaces trustworthy and broadly usable.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes typed web operations with explicit contracts and logging to make agent workflows more reliable and auditable.

title: Position: Web Agents Should Use Typed Actions Instead of Click-Based Browsing

abstract: Agentic AI systems behave through trajectories: they plan, invoke tools, update memory, and coordinate over multiple steps. However, interpretability remains largely model-centric, focused on explaining single predictions rather than tracing long-horizon behavior and responsibility across interacting components. As a result, critical failures, such as tool misuse, coordination breakdowns, or goal drift, often evade existing audits until harm occurs. We argue that interpretability for agentic systems must become system-centric, addressing trajectories, responsibility assignment, and lifecycle dynamics rather than internal model mechanisms alone. We advance three claims: interpretability must (1) co-design with agentic capabilities, (2) address distinct layers of opacity with tailored methods, and (3) integrate across the deployment lifecycle. To operationalize this position, we introduce ATLIS (Agentic Trajectory and Layered Interpretability Stack), a framework integrating five interpretability layers across a five-stage deployment lifecycle. ATLIS enables lightweight continuous monitoring with risk-aware escalation to deeper system-level analysis when incidents are detected. ATLIS provides a blueprint for closing the growing gap between agentic capabilities and the interpretability infrastructure needed to govern them. Project Page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/ATLIS/.

paragraphs: An AI agent’s behavior unfolds through sequences of planning, tool use, memory updates, and coordination. This position paper argues that explaining individual model predictions does not adequately account for these longer trajectories. Failures such as tool misuse, coordination breakdowns, and goal drift can involve interactions across components and escape existing audits.

The authors propose that interpretability should develop alongside agent capabilities, use methods suited to different layers of opacity, and operate throughout deployment. The emphasis is on tracing behavior over time and assigning responsibility across the system. Internal model analysis remains relevant, but it sits within a broader account of how the agent acts.

Their ATLIS framework organizes five interpretability layers across five deployment stages. It supports lightweight continuous monitoring, with deeper system-level analysis triggered by incidents according to risk. The paper presents this as a blueprint for accountable deployment: routine observation and more intensive investigation are connected within one framework for understanding agent behavior throughout its lifecycle.
summary.tldr: ATLIS proposes layered, lifecycle-wide interpretability for tracing agent behavior and escalating from continuous monitoring to deeper incident analysis.

abstract: Many applications in text and speech processing require the analysis of distributions of variable-length sequences. We recently introduced a general kernel framework, 'rational kernels', to extend kernel methods to the analysis of such variable-length sequences or more generally weighted automata. These kernels are efficient to compute and have been successfully used in applications such as spoken-dialog classification using Support Vector Machines. However, the rational kernels previously introduced do not fully encompass distributions over alternate sequences. Prior similarity measures between two weighted automata are based only on the expected counts of co-occurring subsequences and ignore similarities (or dissimilarities) in higher order moments of the distributions of these counts. In this paper, we introduce a new family of rational kernels, 'momentkernels', that precisely exploit this additional information. These kernels are distribution kernels based on moments of counts of strings. We describe efficient algorithms to compute moment kernels and apply them to several difficult spoken-dialog classification tasks. Our experiments show that using the second moment of the counts of n-gram sequences consistently improves the classification accuracy in these tasks.

paragraphs: Text and speech applications may involve distributions over alternative sequences, rather than one fixed sequence. Earlier rational kernels allowed kernel methods to work with variable-length sequences and weighted automata. However, their comparisons used expected counts of shared subsequences, leaving higher-order information about the distribution of those counts unused.

The paper introduces moment kernels to capture this additional information. These kernels compare distributions through moments of string counts, extending the information available beyond average occurrence counts. This matters because similarity in expected counts does not by itself account for similarities or differences in higher moments. The authors also describe efficient algorithms for computing the new kernels.

The evaluation applies the method to several difficult spoken-dialog classification tasks. Using the second moment of n-gram counts consistently improves classification accuracy in those tasks. The stated finding therefore supports adding second-moment information for the evaluated problems, while the broader methodological contribution is a family of kernels designed to represent richer aspects of distributions over sequences.
summary.tldr: Moment kernels enrich sequence-distribution comparisons, with second-moment n-gram information consistently improving the evaluated spoken-dialog classifiers.

title: Distribution kernels based on moments of counts

abstract: This paper introduces an approach for clustering/classification which is basedon the use of local, high-order structure present in the data. For someproblems, this local structure might be more relevant for classification thanother measures of point similarity used by popular unsupervised andsemi-supervised clustering methods. Under this approach, changes in the classlabel are associated to changes in the local properties of the data. Usingthis idea, we also pursue to learn how to cluster given examples of clustereddata including from different datasets. We make these concepts formal bypresenting a probability model that captures their fundamentals and show thatin this setting, learning to cluster is a well defined and tractable task.Based on probabilistic inference methods, we then present an algorithm forcomputing the posterior probability distribution of class labels for each datapoint. Experiments in the domain of spatial grouping and functional geneclassification are used to illustrate and test these concepts.

paragraphs: The paper explores clustering and classification through the structure of local neighborhoods. Its premise is that, for some problems, patterns involving several nearby data points can be more informative than the point similarity measures used by other clustering methods. Under this approach, changes in class labels are linked to changes in local data properties.

The authors also investigate learning how to cluster from examples that have already been grouped, including examples drawn from different datasets. They formalize the idea in a probability model and show that learning to cluster is well defined and tractable within that setting. This turns neighborhood structure into something a learner can use systematically.

A probabilistic inference algorithm computes a posterior distribution over class labels for each data point, expressing uncertainty about assignments. Experiments in spatial grouping and functional gene classification illustrate and test the framework. The contribution is a model and learning procedure for exploiting local structure; the abstract's motivation remains conditional on that structure being relevant to the particular classification or clustering problem.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic framework learns clustering behavior from local neighborhood structure and previously clustered examples, including examples from different datasets.

title: Learning to cluster using local neighborhood structure

abstract: Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) model sequential data in many fields such as text/speech processing and biosignal analysis. Active learning algorithms learn faster and/or better by closing the data-gathering loop, i.e., they choose the examples most informative with respect to their learning objectives. We introduce a framework and objective functions for active learning in three fundamental HMM problems: model learning, state estimation, and path estimation. In addition, we describe a new set of algorithms for efficiently finding optimal greedy queries using these objective functions. The algorithms are fast, i.e., linear in the number of time steps to select the optimal query and we present empirical results showing that these algorithms can significantly reduce the need for labelled training data.

We introduce a framework and objective functions for active learning in three fundamental HMM problems: model learning, state estimation, and path estimation. paragraphs: Hidden Markov models are used for sequential data, but obtaining labels for those sequences can be costly. This paper studies active learning, where the learner chooses informative examples instead of treating data gathering as fixed. The key question is how to choose queries that serve a particular HMM learning or estimation objective.

The authors introduce a framework with objective functions for three problems: learning the model, estimating states, and estimating paths. Keeping these objectives distinct makes query selection responsive to what the learner is trying to improve. They also develop algorithms that efficiently find optimal greedy queries according to the proposed objectives.

Selecting an optimal query takes time linear in the number of sequence steps. The optimality statement concerns the greedy query choice, rather than an entire future sequence of queries. Empirical results show that the algorithms can significantly reduce the need for labeled training data. Together, the objective functions and efficient selection procedures connect targeted data gathering with practical savings in annotation.
summary.tldr: Objective-specific active-learning algorithms choose optimal greedy HMM queries in linear time and can substantially reduce labeled-data requirements.

title: Active learning for Hidden Markov Models: objective functions and algorithms

abstract: We introduce models for density estimation with multiple, hidden, continuous factors. In particular, we propose a generalization of multilinear models using nonlinear basis functions. By marginalizing over the weights, we obtain a multifactor form of the Gaussian process latent variable model. In this model, each factor is kernelized independently, allowing nonlinear mappings from any particular factor to the data. We learn models for human locomotion data, in which each pose is generated by factors representing the person’s identity, gait, and the current state of motion. We demonstrate our approach using time-series prediction, and by synthesizing novel animation from the model.

paragraphs: This paper develops density models in which several hidden, continuous factors jointly explain the observed data. The motivation is to represent different sources of variation separately, as suggested by separating style from content. The proposed construction generalizes multilinear models by introducing nonlinear basis functions, allowing a richer relationship between the hidden factors and observations.

By marginalizing over the weights, the authors obtain a multifactor version of a Gaussian Process Latent Variable Model. Each factor is kernelized independently, so the mapping from an individual factor to the data can be nonlinear. The model therefore preserves separate factors while allowing each to influence the observations through more flexible mappings.

The application is human locomotion. Each pose is modeled through factors representing the person's identity, gait, and current state of motion. The authors demonstrate the approach through time-series prediction and the synthesis of new animation. These demonstrations show how the factorized model can support both predicting motion over time and generating poses within an animation, connecting its probabilistic formulation to concrete uses.
summary.tldr: A multifactor Gaussian process model separates hidden sources of variation and demonstrates motion prediction and novel animation synthesis.

title: Multifactor Gaussian process models for style-content separation

abstract: After a classifier is trained using a machine learning algorithm and put to use in a real world system, it often faces noise which did not appear in the training data. Particularly, some subset of features may be missing or may become corrupted. We present two novel machine learning techniques that are robust to this type of classification-time noise. First, we solve an approximation to the learning problem using linear programming. We analyze the tightness of our approximation and prove statistical risk bounds for this approach. Second, we define the online-learning variant of our problem, address this variant using a modified Perceptron, and obtain a statistical learning algorithm using an online-to-batch technique. We conclude with a set of experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms.
originalAbstract: After a classifier is trained using a machine learning algorithm and put to use in a real world system, it often faces noise which did not appear in the training data. Particularly, some subset of features may be missing or may become corrupted. We present two novel machine learning techniques that are robust to this type of classification-time noise. First, we solve an approximation to the learning problem using linear programming. We analyze the tightness of our approximation and prove statistical risk bounds for this approach. Second, we define the online-learning variant of our problem, address this variant using a modified Perceptron, and obtain a statistical learning algorithm using an online-to-batch technique. We conclude with a set of experiments that demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classifiers whose inputs become less reliable after training. A deployed system may encounter missing or corrupted features even when that kind of noise was absent from its training data. The learning objective is therefore to obtain a classifier that remains robust to this form of classification-time disruption.

The authors develop two approaches. The first uses linear programming to solve an approximation of the learning problem. They analyze how tight that approximation is and prove statistical risk bounds. This provides both a computational route to a solution and a theoretical account of its relationship to the learning objective.

The second approach formulates an online version of the problem and adapts the Perceptron to address it. An online-to-batch conversion then turns that procedure into a statistical learning algorithm. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods. The contribution combines optimization-based and online-learning routes to handling the same practical mismatch: feature information available during training may become unavailable or unreliable when predictions are needed.
summary.tldr: Linear-programming and modified-Perceptron methods learn classifiers robust to missing or corrupted features at prediction time.

title: Learning to classify with missing and corrupted features

abstract: Optimization problems with a nuclear norm regularization, such as e.g. low norm matrix factorizations, have seen many applications recently. We propose a new approximation algorithm building upon the recent sparse approximate SDP solver of (Hazan, 2008). The experimental efficiency of our method is demonstrated on large matrix completion problems such as the Netflix data set. The algorithm comes with strong convergence guarantees, and can be interpreted as a first theoretically justified variant of Simon-Funk-type SVD heuristics. The method is free of tuning parameters, and very easy to parallelize.

We propose a new approximation algorithm building upon the recent sparse approximate SDP solver of (Hazan, 2008). The experimental efficiency of our method is demonstrated on large matrix completion problems such as the Netflix data set. The algorithm comes with strong convergence guarantees, and can be interpreted as a first theoretically justified variant of Simon-Funk-type SVD heuristics. The method is free of tuning parameters, and very easy to parallelize.

paragraphs: The paper proposes an approximation algorithm for optimization problems that use nuclear-norm regularization, including low-norm matrix factorization. Large matrix completion problems provide a practical motivation: the method must handle substantial matrices while optimizing an objective that includes this regularizer. The authors aim to combine computational usefulness with a rigorous account of convergence.

Their algorithm builds on a sparse approximate solver for semidefinite programming. The resulting method comes with strong convergence guarantees and requires no tuning parameters. The authors also describe it as easy to parallelize, a useful property when the scale of the matrix makes computation a central concern.

Experiments demonstrate efficiency on large matrix completion tasks, including the Netflix dataset. Beyond those results, the authors interpret the algorithm as a theoretically justified variant of Simon-Funk-type singular-value-decomposition heuristics. That connection matters because it relates a practical family of factorization approaches to an algorithm with formal convergence support. The empirical efficiency and theoretical guarantees are distinct contributions that the proposed method brings together.
summary.tldr: A tuning-free approximation algorithm makes nuclear-norm optimization practical while providing strong convergence guarantees.

title: A Simple Algorithm for Nuclear Norm Regularized Problems

abstract: We consider apprentice learning — i.e., having an agent learn a task by observing an expert demonstrating the task — in a partially observable environment when the model of the environment is uncertain. This setting is useful in applications where the explicit modeling of the environment is difficult, such as a dialogue system. We show that we can extract information about the environment model by inferring action selection process behind the demonstration, under the assumption that the expert is choosing optimal actions based on knowledge of the true model of the target environment. We show that our proposed algorithms can estimate the parameters of the environment model with much shorter demonstration compared to learning the model only from the reaction from the environment.
originalAbstract: We consider apprentice learning — i.e., having an agent learn a task by observing an expert demonstrating the task — in a partially observable environment when the model of the environment is uncertain. This setting is useful in applications where the explicit modeling of the environment is difficult, such as a dialogue system. We show that we can extract information about the environment model by inferring action selection process behind the demonstration, under the assumption that the expert is choosing optimal actions based on knowledge of the true model of the target environment. We show that our proposed algorithms can estimate the parameters of the environment model with much shorter demonstration compared to learning the model only from the reaction from the environment.

paragraphs: Learning from an expert's demonstration becomes harder when an agent cannot fully observe its environment and does not know the environment's model. This paper studies how demonstrations can help estimate that model. Dialogue systems motivate the setting because explicitly specifying how the environment behaves can be difficult.

The key idea is to learn from the expert's choice of actions, as well as from the environment's reactions. The method infers the action-selection process behind a demonstration to extract information about model parameters. Its stated assumption is that the expert knows the true environment model and chooses optimal actions using that knowledge. Under this assumption, the choices themselves carry information about the environment.

The authors show that their algorithms can estimate model parameters from much shorter demonstrations than methods learning only from environmental reactions. The finding highlights an additional source of evidence in expert behavior: an action can reveal something about the model that made it optimal. The result depends on the stated interpretation of the expert's knowledge and decision-making.
summary.tldr: Assuming a knowledgeable, optimal expert, inferring why demonstration actions were chosen can reduce the data needed to learn an environment model.

title: Apprenticeship Learning for Model Parameters of Partially Observable Environments
